clat-bootcamp-mock-37-p4.title: Sarnath on the UNESCO World Heritage List Where the Wheel Was First Turned
clat-bootcamp-mock-37-p4.text:
The news came from a harbour city on the lower lip of an Asian peninsula, where heritage's great jury was sitting in its late-forties session: the deer park beside the Ganga's ancient twin would finally wear the blue-and-white shield. For twenty-eight summers the site had queued upon the waiting list, and now, judged on yardsticks that prize testimony to a living tradition and kinship with an extraordinary life, it was in.

History's logic was simpler. Here, in a park once reserved for deer its very name means 'gift of stags' a wanderer, newly illumined beneath a distant fig tree, found the band of companions who had abandoned him when he abandoned austerities. He turned the wheel of the law for them; and in that turning, the first brotherhood of monks was born. An emperor, penitent after a terrible eastern war, raised the place to glory: a pillar crested by lions facing the four winds a quartet of beasts that would, twenty-four centuries later, be stamped above the seals of a republic and stupas raised over relics, of which one great brick drum still towers where the teaching began and one moundish tower, crowned with an octagonal turret a Mughal governor's son once added, stands half a kilometre off; these two protected halves form the property. In the gallery nearby, hands of the Gupta age have left the Teacher's earliest calm in buff sandstone, and today lamas, bhikkhus and village grandmothers from a dozen nations circle the brick drum while kites wheel above. Pilgrims have since trodden it without pause, save for a twelfth-century ruin and a nineteenth-century rediscovery, and it now joins the cradle in the Himalayan foothills and the fig tree in Bihar of the four stations the Master named, only the sal-grove of the final rest still awaits its badge.

clat-mock-23-p4.text: India's transition towards cleaner and more sustainable sources of energy has increasingly focused on reducing dependence on imported crude oil while simultaneously supporting farmers through alternative markets for agricultural produce. One of the most significant initiatives in this direction has been the promotion of ethanol-blended petrol. Over the past decade, blending levels have risen substantially owing to policy support, expansion of domestic distillation capacity, and greater participation of sugar mills and grain- based distilleries. The programme is expected to contribute to multiple national objectives, including lowering greenhouse gas emissions, improving energy security, reducing the country's import bill, and creating additional income opportunities for farmers. Alongside sugarcane-based feedstocks, policymakers have encouraged diversification towards food grains and agricultural residues in order to reduce excessive dependence on a single crop. The initiative forms an important component of India's broader strategy to promote biofuels and a circular economy. Technological developments have also facilitated the introduction of vehicles capable of operating on higher ethanol blends. Nevertheless, experts continue to debate several challenges associated with the programme, including concerns regarding water-intensive cultivation, food security, regional disparities in feedstock availability, and the environmental sustainability of large-scale ethanol production. As India accelerates its clean energy transition, the ethanol blending programme has emerged as an important example of balancing environmental objectives with economic development and rural livelihoods. The success of the initiative will ultimately depend upon technological innovation, sustainable agricultural practices, and the ability to diversify raw materials without compromising food or ecological security.

clat-mock-19-p4.title: Base Year of Wholesale Price Index Revised
clat-mock-19-p4.text:
India recently initiated a major reform in its system of measuring price movements in the economy. The exercise forms part of a broader effort to modernize official statistics and align domestic practices with evolving international standards. Policymakers have increasingly emphasized the need for inflation indicators that capture production-stage price changes more accurately, particularly in an economy witnessing rapid diversification of manufacturing, services, and energy sectors.

The reform comes at a time when governments across the world are re-evaluating traditional measures of inflation to better understand how rising costs faced by producers eventually influence prices paid by consumers. Such measures are important not only for macroeconomic policy but also for infrastructure contracts, industrial planning, and assessment of economic competitiveness. Economists argue that modern inflation tracking should reflect changes in technology, production structures, and the growing role of services in national output.

The revised framework also seeks to improve the treatment of emerging industries and energy sources while incorporating more sophisticated statistical techniques. International organizations have repeatedly encouraged countries to strengthen producer-level price indicators as a complement to consumer inflation measures. Such indicators are often used to analyse cost pressures within supply chains and assess whether inflationary shocks are temporary or likely to persist.

The initiative reflects a broader trend in economic governance where statistical systems are periodically updated to remain representative of contemporary economic realities. Similar revisions have been undertaken by many countries as part of efforts to improve evidence-based policymaking and economic forecasting.

clat-mock-15-p1.title: The Launch of the India-Middle East-Europe Economic Corridor (IMEC) Portal
clat-mock-15-p1.text:
The Ministry of External Affairs (MEA), in collaboration with the Ministry of Ports, Shipping and Waterways, announced the operationalization of the unified digital transit portal for the India- Middle East-Europe Economic Corridor (IMEC). This milestone follows high-level diplomatic engagements held between India, the United Arab Emirates (UAE), and Saudi Arabia to fast- track the multimodal transport corridor initially conceptualized on the sidelines of the New Delhi G20 Summit. The newly deployed digital framework integrates customs clearance, real-time tracking, and unified bill of lading protocols across maritime and rail networks.

Geopolitical experts view the rapid deployment of IMEC’s digital architecture as a calculated strategic counterweight to China’s expanding footprint through its Belt and Road Initiative (BRI). Diplomatic friction, however, continues to simmer in the background, particularly regarding trade tariff adjustments along the proposed European terminal points. Amid mounting regional complexities in West Asia, New Delhi has maintained a steadfast focus on securing structural maritime agreements. Backed by institutional support, the IMEC infrastructure framework aims to reduce transit times between India and Europe by 40%, optimizing supply chain resilience and bolstering indigenous industrialization under the Sagarmala architecture.

clat-real-mock-01-p3.text: I rise to inform this august House of the resolute diplomatic countermeasures initiated by the Government of India in response to the continued lack of cooperation from Canada regarding extremist elements operating from its soil. Despite repeated demarches and the sharing of actionable intelligence, the safety of our diplomats has been compromised. Consequently, a meeting of the Cabinet Committee on Security was convened to recalibrate our engagement. To safeguard our national security and uphold the dignity of our diplomatic missions, the following decisions have been enforced: • One, the issuance of visas to Canadian nationals has been temporarily suspended until the security situation improves. • Two, adhering to the principle of parity, we have demanded the repatriation of 41 Canadian diplomats to ensure mutual equivalence in diplomatic presence. • Three, the electronic travel authorization for OCI cardholders with Canadian passports will be subject to stricter scrutiny. • Four, we have formally reminded the Canadian administration of their obligations under the Vienna Convention on Diplomatic Relations. • Five, we have rejected the allegations stemming from the 'Five Eyes' intelligence sharing network as unsubstantiated and politically motivated. (Excerpts from a hypothetical Statement made by Minister of External Affairs on diplomatic tensions, dated October 15, 2025)

clat-mock-35-p1.title: Vikram-1 — India's First Private Orbital Rocket (Skyroot Aerospace)
clat-mock-35-p1.text: History does not always arrive with noise; sometimes it lifts off past noon from a barrier island on the Coromandel coast. On the eighteenth of July, a seven-storey, all-carbon-composite rocket rose from the First Launch Pad of the Satish Dhawan Space Centre, and within a quarter of an hour had slipped its payloads into an orbit some 450 kilometres up. Mission Aagaman, its builders declared, had met every objective. The architect of this triumph is a Hyderabad startup founded eight years ago by two engineers who once drew ISRO salaries, born of the 2020 reforms that unlocked the space sector for private enterprise; earlier this year it crossed the billion-dollar valuation mark, a first for any Indian spacetech firm. The vehicle pairs solid muscle with additive brains: three stages of solid propellant, capped by a liquid orbital- adjustment module whose 3D-printed engine coaxed the payloads into their precise slots — technologies flown for the first time in India. The manifest was suitably mixed: a German customer's satellite, an orbital bodyguard in the form of a robotic arm designed to snare debris, an Indian Earth-observation camera, and a diamond-themed artwork headed for weightlessness. The date carried a quiet symmetry: exactly forty-six years earlier, from the same coast, India's first home-grown satellite launcher had risen, dragging the nation into an elite club. Now private enterprise has repeated the rite, admitting India — behind superpowers — into a still more exclusive club: countries whose companies can hurl satellites into orbit themselves. Regulator, promoter and landlord watched together: the national space-promotion centre authorised the flight, the national space agency's range hosted it. Its suborbital forerunner had already kissed space from this shore; a heavier sibling now sits on the drawing board for next year.

clat-mock-27-p3.title: Third India–Nordic Summit, 2026
clat-mock-27-p3.text: The Third India–Nordic Summit, held on 19 May 2026, marked a significant expansion of India’s engagement with northern Europe. The participating leaders elevated the relationship to Strategic Partnership, seeking to combine India’s market, manufacturing capacity and skilled workforce with Nordic expertise in sustainability and advanced technology. The discussions covered renewable energy, green hydrogen, low-emission industries, water management and the circular economy. Maritime cooperation included green shipping, shipbuilding, sustainable ship recycling and ocean-based industries. The leaders also supported deeper collaboration between universities, laboratories, start- ups and business incubators, including research in emerging communication technologies. Trade and investment formed another important component. The leaders proposed using India’s recent trade arrangements with European partners to improve market access, encourage investment and create resilient supply chains. Nordic firms were invited to explore opportunities in India’s green transition, defence manufacturing and financial-services ecosystem. Greater movement of students, researchers and skilled professionals was also encouraged. The partnership has a wider strategic dimension. Changes in the polar region affect climate systems, shipping routes and access to natural resources, making scientific cooperation increasingly important. India and the Nordic countries consequently supported joint polar research and continued engagement through established multilateral institutions. They also discussed the conflicts in Europe and West Asia, terrorism and the need to reform global governance institutions. The summit reflects a broader diplomatic strategy in which India works with small but technologically advanced economies on issue-specific cooperation. Nordic countries possess substantial expertise and investment capital but comparatively limited domestic markets. India offers scale and talent but requires technology and long-term financing for its development transition. Converting summit declarations into projects will depend on regulatory certainty, protection of intellectual property, commercial viability and the ability to manage geopolitical differences.

clat-mock-31-p0.title: Indonesia's Volcanic Eruption & the Ring of Fire
clat-mock-31-p0.text:
On September 2026, a small volcanic island rising out of the narrow waterway that separates Java from Sumatra began hurling lava fountains and booming across the region. By Sunday, a second ash cloud had punched fifty thousand feet into the sky, drifting over Banten, Lampung and Bengkulu provinces and out across the Indian Ocean. Ash was detected in the airspace over the capital, forcing authorities to shut Jakarta's main international gateway along with several other airports; over 1,500 flights were grounded, schools in the capital moved their classes online, and services as far away as Bali and Medan were disrupted. The Transport Minister, Dudy Purwagandhi, conceded that no one could say when the disruption would end "due to the dynamic weather." Mercifully, no casualties were reported, no evacuation was ordered the nearest settlement lies over sixteen kilometres away — and, unlike the December 2018 episode when this very volcano demonstrated that it could kill hundreds without the warning of an earthquake, no tsunami alert was issued this time.

The volcano itself is a child in geological terms, having emerged from the sea less than a century ago, growing out of the submerged caldera left behind by its parent, whose late-nineteenth-century explosion remains among the loudest sounds in recorded history and altered global climate for years. Its alert status had already been raised to Level III in July 2026 after a surge in activity, even as Java's highest peak continued its own months-long eruption further east. None of this is unusual for Indonesia, the country with more active volcanoes than any other, sitting on the world's most violent tectonic arc — a horseshoe of subduction zones that hosts the overwhelming majority of the planet's earthquakes and eruptions.

clat-mock-24-p4.title: India's Digital Payment Revolution: Building an Inclusive Financial Ecosystem
clat-mock-24-p4.text: Over the past decade, digital payment systems have transformed the way financial transactions are conducted in India. Advances in digital public infrastructure, increasing smartphone penetration, expanding internet connectivity, and wider access to banking services have enabled millions of individuals and businesses to shift from cash-based transactions to electronic modes of payment. This transformation has contributed to greater financial inclusion while encouraging innovation in the country's rapidly growing financial technology ecosystem. India's digital payments architecture has been designed to promote interoperability, allowing users of different banks and payment applications to transfer funds seamlessly. Such an ecosystem has encouraged competition among service providers while enabling merchants, consumers, and small enterprises to adopt digital payments with minimal infrastructure. The expansion of digital transactions has also supported formalisation of the economy by creating reliable digital records that can facilitate access to financial services, including credit for small businesses. As digital payment systems continue to expand, policymakers are increasingly focusing on strengthening cybersecurity, consumer protection, and the resilience of payment infrastructure. At the same time, efforts are being made to improve cross-border payment connectivity and extend the benefits of digital finance to international travellers and other eligible users. These developments reflect India's broader objective of building secure, efficient, and globally interoperable digital public infrastructure. Despite remarkable progress, challenges remain. Uneven digital literacy, disparities in internet access, and the dominance of a limited number of service providers continue to generate important policy debates. Addressing these issues is considered essential for ensuring that future growth in digital payments remains competitive, inclusive, and secure.

clat-mock-13-p1.title: YELLOW LINE
clat-mock-13-p1.text:
The term "Yellow Line" holds a specific and critical place in the geopolitical and military lexicon of the Middle East, serving as the easternmost operational boundary of Israeli civil administration and military deployment in the strategically vital Golan Heights. Established in the aftermath of the 1973 Yom Kippur War under the 1974 Agreement on Disengagement between Israeli and Syrian forces, this line delineates the western edge of the United Nations-monitored buffer zone. Positioned just west of the historical 1967 ceasefire "Purple Line," the Yellow Line effectively marks the physical limit beyond which Israeli heavy weaponry and armored divisions cannot pass without violating international disengagement protocols. From a tactical standpoint, the line is heavily fortified with advanced electronic surveillance arrays, thermal imaging networks, and early-warning radar systems anchored along the high volcanic plateaus and the ridges of Mount Hermon, providing an indispensable look-down capability over the plains extending toward Damascus. Over the decades, Israel has seamlessly integrated the territory behind this perimeter into its domestic legal framework via the Golan Heights

Law, fostering local agricultural development and wine industries alongside a unique demographic mix of Jewish communities and indigenous Druze populations. While the international status of the region within the Yellow Line remains a point of deep diplomatic contention, formal recognition of Israeli sovereignty over the zone by the United States in recent years has reinforced its permanence on the ground. Today, the Yellow Line stands as a heavily monitored, frozen yet highly volatile frontier where high-readiness military patrols operate in lockstep with United Nations Disengagement Observer Force (UNDOF) monitors to prevent localized border frictions from escalating into a broader regional conflict.

clat-aiom-mock-02-p3.text:
The Biological Weapons Convention (BWC) stands as the foundational global treaty prohibiting the development and stockpiling of biological agents. However, its effectiveness is often questioned due to a significant structural deficit: unlike the Chemical Weapons Convention, the BWC lacks a binding verification mechanism or provisions for on-site inspections, relying instead on voluntary confidence-building measures.

This regulatory gap is increasingly perilous in the age of rapid biotechnological advancement, giving rise to the "dual-use research" dilemma—where legitimate scientific work intended for civilian benefits, such as vaccine development, can be repurposed for weaponization. The catastrophic reach of the recent global pandemic further exposed the fragility of this architecture. In response, India has advocated for bolstering the treaty through robust National Implementation Frameworks, arguing that effective biosecurity relies on harmonizing international commitments with stringent domestic legal oversight.

clat-mock-14-p3.text:
Religious Site Disputes, Shahi Jama Masjid, Bhojshala and the Places of Worship Act Recent court proceedings concerning disputed religious sites have once again brought the Places of Worship Act, 1991 into public debate. In Uttar Pradesh, the Allahabad High Court upheld a trial court’s decision to appoint an advocate commissioner to survey the Shahi Jama Masjid in Sambhal district. The survey order is a fact- finding step and does not by itself decide ownership or religious character, but it has triggered wider legal discussion on how courts should handle claims relating to historical places of worship.

This issue is closely connected with the Places of Worship Act, 1991, which was enacted to preserve the religious character of places of worship. The law generally prohibits conversion of any place of worship from one religious denomination to another. Its larger objective was to prevent reopening of historical religious disputes and to maintain communal harmony.

The relevance of the Babri Masjid–Ram Janmabhoomi dispute is central to understanding this law. The 1991 Act specifically excluded the Ayodhya dispute from its operation because litigation over that site was already pending. In its 2019 Ayodhya judgment, the Supreme Court described the Places of Worship Act as an important constitutional commitment to secularism and non-retrogression. The Court also emphasized that historical wrongs cannot be used as a basis to disturb the present constitutional order. Therefore, while the Ayodhya dispute was treated as an exceptional case, the Act was intended to ensure that similar disputes over other religious sites are not repeatedly reopened.

The recent Bhojshala–Kamal Maula Mosque matter in Madhya Pradesh adds another dimension because the site is a protected monument under heritage law. Courts in such cases must balance religious claims, archaeological evidence, preservation duties, and public order. Together, the Sambhal, Bhojshala and Babri-related debates show the complex intersection of history, faith, constitutional secularism, and judicial process in India.

clat-additional-mock-01-p3.text: The Supreme Court on Wednesday (May 13, 2026) asked teachers not to be “self- centered” and think only about their job security, but spare a thought for children in need of quality education, a right protected under the Constitution and the Right to Education Act. The court’s oral observations came while hearing a series of petitions filed by States of Madhya Pradesh and Uttar Pradesh and teachers’ associations from West Bengal and Kerala, seeking a review of a September 2025 judgment requiring in-service teachers of classes one to eight in non-minority schools across the country to clear the Teachers’ Eligibility Test (TET) in two years or be “compulsorily retired”. Tamil Nadu had argued that the judgment affected about four lakh teachers in the State alone. If implemented on the ground, the State would have to bear witness to “classrooms without teachers”, it had contended. “The Right of Children to Free and Compulsory Education Act [Right to Education Act. 2009] exists for the children. Do not be self-centered to say ‘I will only get orders from the court protecting my security of tenure, but will not think about the children',” Justice Dipankar Datta, heading a Bench comprising Justice Manmohan, addressed the review petitioners. Justice Datta referred to Section 23(2) of the 2009 Act, which gave teachers five years’ time to get the “mandatory” qualification of TET in cases of shortage of trained teachers and the inadequacy of teacher education institutions. The judge drew attention to the second proviso to Section 23(2) which was inserted in an amendment to the Act in 2017. It gave a further leeway by allowing teachers appointed or in position as of March 31, 2015, and who did not possess the required minimum academic qualifications, to acquire them within four years. clat-aiom-mock-01-p1.text:
A recent report of the Parliamentary Standing Committee on Science and Technology, Environment, Forests and Climate Change has drawn renewed attention to the air quality crisis in Delhi–NCR. It notes that pollution in the region is the outcome of multiple interacting sources particularly road transport, certain industrial activities, crop‑residue burning and adverse winter weather conditions that trap pollutants close to the surface. The committee argues that, within this mix, emissions from vehicles remain a critical driver of both fine particulate matter and harmful gases.

The panel has called for a thorough overhaul of India’s vehicular emission framework so that norms keep pace with advances in science and technology as well as international practice. It points out that the rapid push towards fuel blending and alternative fuels, though important for energy security, must be accompanied by careful monitoring of their impact on nitrogen oxides and vapour losses from fuel systems. The report also endorsed innovative ecological solutions for urban centers, such as the rapid-growth Miyawaki method. In this context, it urges the introduction of tighter limits on evaporative losses and more advanced control systems in new vehicles. Taken together, the recommendations aim to steer India’s transport sector towards cleaner fuels and more sustainable mobility while closing regulatory gaps that currently undermine air‑quality goals.

clat-mock-22-p4.title: ELNINO
clat-mock-22-p4.text:
The El Niño-Southern Oscillation (ENSO) is a periodic fluctuation in sea surface temperatures and the air pressure of the overlying atmosphere across the equatorial. At its core, the phenomenon represents a dramatic shift in the "Walker Circulation"—a massive atmospheric loop that normally drives air westward across the tropical Pacific. Under neutral conditions, strong trade winds push warm surface waters, creating a "warm pool" near Indonesia and Australia, while cooler, nutrient-rich water upwells along the coast of South America.

When this system enters an El Niño phase, the trade winds weaken, allowing the accumulated warm water to surge eastward. Meteorologists distinguish "Super" events by the intensity of this warming, typically measuring deviations in sea surface temperatures in specific Pacific zones. This thermal shift disrupts global climate patterns by altering jet streams and heat distribution.

The ENSO cycle is monitored using the Southern Oscillation Index (SOI), which serves as an atmospheric barometer. By tracking the pressure gradient between the western and eastern Pacific, scientists can quantify the strength of the trade winds. When the SOI displays sustained negative values, it signals that the normal pressure "seesaw" has tilted, marking the onset of the warmer phase. Conversely, La Niña occurs when the trade winds intensify, pulling unusually cold water to the surface in the eastern Pacific. This atmospheric coupling creates a feedback loop that influences rainfall distribution, cyclone frequency, and agricultural outcomes across the globe, with distinct and often opposing impacts on the South Asian monsoon cycle.

clat-mock-30-p0.text:
Mohenjo-daro’s “Dancing Girl” and the Question of Interpretation The urban centres of the Harappan civilisation have yielded a wide range of material remains, including terracotta objects, stone sculptures, seals and metal artefacts. These objects are important not merely for their artistic qualities but also because they provide clues about the technological capabilities and social life of a civilisation whose script remains undeciphered. Among the better-known artefacts associated with Mohenjo-daro is a small female figurine discovered during archaeological excavations in the 1920s. Its unusual posture, ornaments and confident bodily stance have made it one of the most recognisable objects associated with the Indus civilisation. The figurine is particularly significant in discussions of early metalworking because of the sophisticated casting technique employed in its manufacture. The object is now preserved in India, while the archaeological site itself lies in present-day Pakistan. The interpretation of archaeological objects, however, is not always independent of the assumptions of the person studying them. In the absence of written records explaining the purpose of a particular object, archaeologists often rely upon posture, associated objects, artistic conventions and comparisons with other material remains. Such interpretations may subsequently become widely accepted even when the original evidence does not conclusively establish the object's function.

This issue is particularly relevant in the case of the Mohenjo-daro figurine. Its posture led early archaeologists to associate it with performance and movement. Later scholarship has questioned whether the label traditionally attached to the figurine necessarily represents the intention of its maker. Some scholars have suggested that the figure could have had an altogether different social or ritual significance. The debate illustrates a broader problem in archaeology: the difference between what an artefact objectively reveals and what modern observers infer from it.

The figurine has also generated debate in the modern educational and cultural sphere. Its physical appearance, particularly its unclothed form, has occasionally been viewed through contemporary social norms. In 2026, an altered representation of the artefact in a newly introduced school arts textbook attracted public discussion. The episode raised wider questions about whether historical artefacts should be represented in their original form or modified to conform to contemporary ideas of age-appropriateness and social sensitivity. The subsequent debate extended beyond the individual artefact to questions concerning historical accuracy, censorship, interpretation and the responsibilities of educational institutions.

The controversy therefore provides an opportunity to distinguish between preserving an archaeological object, interpreting its meaning, and representing it in educational material. These are related but distinct questions. A museum may preserve an artefact in its original form, an archaeologist may debate its function, and an educational institution may make choices about how the artefact is visually presented. Each decision involves a different set of considerations. Following the controversy, NCERT decided to restore the original image in the textbook.

clat-mock-40-p0.title: From Kerala to Keralam
clat-mock-40-p0.text: In 2026, the Union government moved forward with a long-pending proposal concerning the official name of one of India’s southern States. The initiative followed a resolution adopted by the State legislature and revived discussion on how linguistic identity, federal consultation and constitutional procedure interact when the name of a State is altered. The proposal was subsequently considered by the Union Cabinet and taken through the parliamentary process. Press Information Bureau The development was rooted in a broader historical context. The State had been reorganised in the 1950s as part of the restructuring of India’s internal boundaries largely on linguistic lines. Over the decades, questions of language and regional identity continued to influence demands relating to the names of States, cities and other geographical entities. Unlike an ordinary administrative change, however, altering the official name of a State involves a constitutionally prescribed process in which both Union institutions and the concerned State legislature have defined roles. The Constitution gives Parliament significant authority over the formation of States and changes relating to their areas, boundaries and names. At the same time, the federal structure requires consultation with the legislature of the affected State before Parliament proceeds with such legislation. The State’s opinion forms part of this process, although the Constitution does not place the final legislative decision solely in its hands. The 2026 development therefore illustrates an important feature of Indian federalism: changes to the political map or constitutional identity of a State may originate from regional aspirations, but their formal recognition requires action through national constitutional institutions. The episode also highlights how India’s constitutional framework accommodates territorial and nomenclatural changes without necessarily invoking the procedure used for every formal constitutional amendment.

clat-mock-03-p4.text:
In a defining moment for Asian geopolitics, the freeze in India-China relations witnessed a significant thaw on the sidelines of the SCO Summit 2025 in Tianjin. Marking their first bilateral summit since 2018, the Indian Prime Minister and the Chinese President announced a "reset" in ties, moving beyond the shadow of the 2020 Galwan Valley clashes. The leaders endorsed the outcomes of the 24th Special Representatives’ Dialogue, which established a new framework for disengagement and coordinated patrolling along the 3,488-km Line of Actual Control (LAC), adhering to the 2005 Political Parameters.

The diplomatic breakthrough acknowledges the complex economic reality: despite border tensions, China recently overtook the US to reclaim its position as India’s largest trading partner, with the bilateral trade deficit touching USD 99 billion. To address this, both sides agreed to resume the High-Level Economic Dialogue. In a symbolic gesture marking the 75th anniversary of diplomatic ties, the leaders announced the resumption of the Kailash Mansarovar Yatra by 2026 and the reopening of border trade via the Nathu La and Shipki La passes. While contentious issues like the CPEC and river water sharing remain, the joint statement emphasized 'Strategic Autonomy,' asserting that the 'Dragon-Elephant' dynamic would be steered independently of third-party influence to stabilize the multipolar world order.

clat-mock-27-p0.title: India–Nepal Border Dispute: Lipulekh Pass & The Kailash Mansarovar Yatra
clat-mock-27-p0.text: In 2026, an annual event of deep religious significance once again placed one of South Asia's oldest and most sensitive boundary disputes in the spotlight. When India announced the resumption of the famous Himalayan pilgrimage to two sacred sites, using a high-altitude mountain pass in the Kumaon region of Uttarakhand as one of its principal gateways, the government of Nepal formally objected — to New Delhi and, notably, to the third country that controls the far side of the pass, which lies at the junction of the borders of three nations. The dispute traces back more than two centuries, to a treaty signed in the aftermath of an Anglo-Nepalese war. That treaty fixed Nepal's boundary along the course of a river, but the two neighbours have never agreed on precisely where that river begins. India maintains that the river rises near a particular valley, placing the contested settlements — including the strategically important pass itself within Indian territory; Nepal contends that its source lies further west, which would place all of the disputed places within Nepal. Because both countries read the same treaty differently, the boundary has never been definitively settled. The disagreement was sharply aggravated in 2020, when India inaugurated a road through the disputed area and Nepal, in response, formally incorporated the territories into its official map. The latest friction over the pilgrimage route reflects a recurring tension: New Delhi insists it has used the pass for the pilgrimage for decades, while Kathmandu argues that no bilateral arrangement with the third country can legitimise the use of territory it claims as its own.

clat-mock-21-p1.text:
INDIA-UAE Relations The bilateral relationship between India and the United Arab Emirates has undergone a profound strategic metamorphosis, evolving from a traditional energy-buyer dynamic into a multidimensional Comprehensive Strategic Partnership. The economic cornerstone of this transition is the Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreement (CEPA) implemented in 2022, which fundamentally realigned market access and slashed tariffs. Defying conservative timelines, the bilateral trade corridor successfully breached the $100 billion milestone in early 2026—years ahead of its original 2030 schedule—prompting the leadership to establish an ambitious new target of $200 billion.

Beyond conventional merchandise trade, the partnership is increasingly anchored in deep institutional and technological integration. This is evidenced by pioneering agreements linking national digital payment infrastructures to facilitate seamless cross-border transactions. Furthermore, the relationship has expanded into critical resource security, marked by long- term Liquefied Natural Gas (LNG) supply pacts and unprecedented foreign participation in India’s domestic energy stockpiling initiatives. As a vital node in emerging geopolitical frameworks like the India-Middle East-Europe Economic Corridor (IMEC) and minilateral blocs like I2U2, the India-UAE axis exemplifies a modern template for Global South cooperation, bridging the gap between capital-rich Gulf economies and India’s rising technological and manufacturing sectors.

clat-mock-03-p3.text:
Prime Minister Shri Narendra Modi participated in the 6th BIMSTEC Summit, hosted by Thailand. The leaders adopted the ‘Bangkok Vision 2030’, outlining a comprehensive roadmap for regional integration and resilience against global challenges. Emphasizing the alignment with India’s ‘Act East Policy’, the Prime Minister highlighted that the region, representing 22% of the world’s population and a combined GDP of USD 5.2 trillion, serves as a bridge between South and Southeast Asia. To foster human resource development, India introduced the BODHI Program, offering training and scholarships to professionals across member nations.

Addressing critical infrastructure and health needs, the Prime Minister announced the operationalization of the BIMSTEC Energy Centre in Bengaluru and proposed a specialized capacity-building program for Cancer Care. To boost intra-regional commerce, the establishment of a BIMSTEC Chamber of Commerce and an annual Business Summit was mooted. Furthermore, a pilot study on Digital Public Infrastructure (DPI) was proposed to enhance governance. Strengthening cultural and youth engagement, India announced it would host the First BIMSTEC Games in 2027 to mark the grouping's 30th anniversary. On the sidelines, India and Thailand elevated their relationship to a Strategic Partnership, focusing on defense dialogues, joint exercises like ‘Maitree’, and cooperation under the Indo-Pacific Oceans Initiative (IPOI). (214 words)

clat-mock-25-p2.title: Diplomacy, Maritime Security and Regional Stability in West Asia
clat-mock-25-p2.text: A recent diplomatic initiative in West Asia has drawn international attention as an effort to reduce tensions following an extended period of military confrontation. The understanding reached between the principal parties seeks to create conditions for sustained negotiations while simultaneously addressing issues that have implications far beyond the region. Governments and international organizations have viewed the initiative as an opportunity to prevent further escalation and restore confidence through phased implementation of mutually agreed commitments. Among the principal concerns discussed during the negotiations were maritime security, freedom of international commerce, regional energy supplies and mechanisms for monitoring sensitive strategic activities. Because a substantial proportion of global energy trade passes through this region, any disruption to commercial shipping has consequences for freight costs, insurance premiums and international commodity markets. Countries heavily dependent on imported energy have therefore closely monitored developments and their possible economic impact. The diplomatic process also places considerable emphasis on internationally supervised verification arrangements intended to enhance confidence among the negotiating parties. Observers note that technical oversight, phased implementation and reciprocal confidence-building measures are often regarded as essential elements in resolving complex international disputes involving security and economic interests. Beyond the immediate participants, the developments are expected to influence broader regional connectivity and trade. Analysts have suggested that improved stability could facilitate commercial activity, strengthen transport corridors and encourage investment in infrastructure projects connecting South Asia, Central Asia and West Asia. Nevertheless, many experts caution that the long-term success of any interim understanding will depend upon continued political dialogue, effective implementation and sustained international cooperation rather than the initial agreement alone.

clat-mock-10-p3.text: The Supreme Court's refusal to grant bail in the Delhi communal violence conspiracy case — involving former university students and activists charged under India's primary anti-terrorism statute — has crystallized a profound doctrinal shift toward what legal scholars term security- centric jurisprudence, where the sanctity of individual liberty under Article 21 yields to statutory constraints during national security prosecutions. The bench applied a proportionality framework distinguishing between accused persons occupying architect-level roles within the alleged conspiracy and those functioning as subsidiary facilitators, holding that identical charges do not mandate identical bail outcomes — a departure from the conventional "bail is the rule" principle. Central to this reasoning was the statute's definition of terrorist acts under a broadly drafted provision encompassing threats to sovereignty through "any other means," language critics have persistently condemned as constitutionally vague. The law itself has undergone four transformative amendments since its original enactment targeting unlawful activities threatening India's integrity: the first introduced terrorism as a standalone legal category under the earlier United Progressive Alliance dispensation; subsequent modifications broadened definitional scope, shifted evidentiary burdens onto the accused, and extended custodial periods: while the most recent, enacted during the current administration, empowered the national counter-terrorism investigation agency to seize properties unilaterally without state government concurrence — overriding federalism principles and provoking fierce Centre-state friction. Crucially, the court distinguished its reasoning from a previous judgment recognizing exceptional bail relief for prolonged incarceration, insisting that delay alone cannot override statutory embargo when national security remains imperilled. However, the ruling's acceptance of prosecution narratives at face value during bail hearings, without rigorous evidentiary scrutiny, risks transforming pre-trial detention into de facto punishment — a concern particularly acute given India's already overwhelming undertrial population comprising nearly three-quarters of all prisoners nationwide.

clat-mock-25-p1.text:
SIPRI Yearbook and the Changing Global Security Landscape The Stockholm International Peace Research Institute (SIPRI) publishes an annual assessment of global security trends covering military expenditure, arms transfers, nuclear forces, disarmament initiatives, and emerging strategic technologies. Widely regarded as one of the most authoritative independent sources on international security, the Yearbook provides governments, researchers, and policymakers with comparative data for analysing changes in the global strategic environment. The latest assessment indicates that geopolitical rivalry continues to reshape defence policies across the world. Rising regional conflicts, technological competition, cyber capabilities, and concerns over supply-chain security have encouraged many countries to increase investments in military modernization. Several States have accelerated procurement of advanced missile systems, unmanned platforms, space-based assets, and integrated command-and-control networks while simultaneously strengthening domestic defence industries. The report also notes continuing developments in global nuclear deterrence. Although international arms-control efforts remain important, many nuclear-armed States are modernising delivery

systems and improving operational preparedness. These developments have renewed debates over strategic stability, crisis management, and the future of multilateral disarmament initiatives. In addition to military capabilities, the Yearbook examines broader dimensions of international security, including cyber operations, emerging technologies, and regional security partnerships. It observes that contemporary conflicts increasingly combine conventional military force with information warfare, electronic capabilities, and digital infrastructure, making modern security challenges far more complex than traditional interstate wars. For countries such as India, the evolving global security environment presents both opportunities and challenges. Policymakers continue to balance national security requirements with technological self-reliance, strategic partnerships, and responsible nuclear stewardship while navigating an increasingly uncertain international order. Consequently, annual assessments such as the SIPRI Yearbook remain important reference documents for understanding long-term trends rather than merely recording military statistics.

clat-mock-05-p3.text:
The Indian subcontinent, owing to its unique tectonic placement, has long been susceptible to seismic volatility. Recognising this, authorities have recently unveiled a modernized risk map that redefines the country's vulnerability landscape. A crucial addition to this framework is the introduction of a new, hyper-sensitive Zone VI, designed to cover the most tectonically active northern frontiers where the Indian plate presses relentlessly against the Eurasian plate. This reclassification aims to enforce rigorous construction standards in areas previously underestimated by older surveys.

Central to this new approach is a robust legal and administrative structure. The country's primary disaster management body operates under the direct leadership ensuring that disaster resilience is integrated into national development goals rather than treated as an afterthought. Complementing this high-level oversight is the role of the national organization, which has codified the new safety parameters that engineers must now adhere to.

On the technical front, understanding the impact of tremors has become more nuanced. Seismologists distinguish between the energy released at the source and the severity of shaking experienced on the ground. For practical damage assessment, experts rely on a descriptive scale that ranks earthquakes from I to XII based on observed structural damage and human perception, distinct from the logarithmic scales used for magnitude. To bridge the gap between science and the public, the government has also deployed dedicated digital platforms to provide citizens with immediate earthquake notifications.

clat-mock-19-p0.title: G7 Summit 2026 and Emerging Global Priorities
clat-mock-19-p0.text:
The 52nd G7 Summit was held in Évian-les-Bains, France, in June 2026 under the French presidency. Besides the seven member countries, several partner nations, including India, Brazil, South Korea, and Kenya, participated as invited guests. The summit took place amid significant geopolitical and economic uncertainty, with discussions focusing on Ukraine, developments in West Asia, critical mineral supply chains, artificial intelligence governance, debt vulnerabilities in developing countries, and global economic imbalances.

A major theme of the summit was reducing excessive dependence on concentrated supply chains for critical minerals essential to clean energy technologies, semiconductors, and advanced manufacturing. Leaders also discussed the growing strategic significance of artificial intelligence and the need to balance innovation with accountability and safety. Ukraine remained a central agenda item, while concerns over maritime trade routes and energy security featured prominently in discussions concerning the Middle East.

India used the platform to highlight the concerns of the Global South and engaged in multiple bilateral meetings with G7 leaders. The summit also reflected broader debates regarding the future of global governance, as emerging economies continue to seek a greater voice in institutions originally designed in the post-Second World War era. India further expressed support for Canada becoming a Dialogue Partner of the Indian Ocean Rim Association (IORA) and welcomed the establishment of "Raisina Americas" to promote strategic dialogue and policy engagement across the Americas.

clat-mock-20-p0.title: Dancing Girl Controversy
clat-mock-20-p0.text:
The recent controversy surrounding the depiction of the Harappan bronze figurine popularly known as the "Dancing Girl" has revived larger questions concerning the representation of history in educational material. A Class IX textbook published by the National Council of Educational Research and Training (NCERT) carried a digitally version of the figurine in which parts of the sculpture appeared to be covered. Following criticism from archaeologists, historians, and educators, the original image was restored. The episode has prompted renewed discussion on whether educational resources should adapt historical artefacts to contemporary sensibilities or preserve them in their original archaeological form.

The debate extends beyond a single sculpture. Archaeological interpretation frequently involves balancing scientific evidence with public understanding. Artefacts recovered from ancient civilisations are not merely artistic objects; they constitute material evidence through which historians reconstruct technology, economy, social organisation, belief systems, and cultural practices. Consequently, even seemingly minor alterations may influence how future generations perceive the past.

The Indus Valley Civilisation, one of the world's earliest urban cultures, has yielded a remarkable range of artefacts, including bronze sculptures, stone figures, seals, pottery, jewellery, terracotta objects, and sophisticated urban architecture. Despite decades of excavation, its script remains undeciphered, compelling scholars to rely heavily on material remains rather than written records. As archaeological research continues, debates over authenticity, conservation, interpretation, and public presentation remain central to understanding India's ancient heritage.

clat-additional-mock-01-p4.text:
The UAE's Role in Global Energy Markets: Production Strategy, Regional Geopolitics, and Producer Dynamics The United Arab Emirates has emerged as one of the world's most significant crude oil producers, commanding substantial proven reserves and advanced production infrastructure. With decades of experience in hydrocarbon extraction and refining, the UAE has continuously invested in upgrading and expanding its oil production facilities. These capital-intensive projects reflect the nation's commitment to maximizing the economic value of its petroleum resources and maintaining technological competitiveness in global energy markets.

OPEC, the Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries, has historically served as the primary forum through which major oil-producing nations coordinate supply policies and attempt to influence international market dynamics. The organization brings together diverse members with varying economic priorities, production capabilities, and long-term strategic visions. Coordination among member states seeks to achieve price stability, market influence, and collective bargaining power against consuming nations.

Within the Middle East, Saudi Arabia has traditionally held prominent influence in producer organizations, wielding significant geopolitical leverage through its vast reserves and production capacity. The region's energy politics remain complex, with individual producers navigating competing objectives: maximizing revenues, managing domestic economies, and positioning themselves within evolving global energy markets.

Producer nations face ongoing strategic decisions regarding their roles in collective frameworks. Major oil exporters must balance collective coordination benefits—such as market influence and coordinated pricing policies—against individual national priorities. These priorities include capitalizing on production capacity, responding to shifting market conditions, and adjusting strategies according to updated long-term projections.

Modern energy geopolitics reflect dynamic tensions as producers pursue independent strategies while also recognizing mutual interdependence. Market volatility, supply predictability, and supply-chain confidence remain central concerns shaping how nations approach energy cooperation and competition in global markets. Source: Reuters

clat-aiom-mock-01-p4.text: Indian sports witnessed a paradigm shift in 2025 as Sheetal Devi, the teenage sensation from Kishtwar, redefined the boundaries of athletic potential. The bow, which demanded immense patience from her in the early years, finally delivered historic results as she claimed the world title at the World Archery Para Championships. Her precise shooting style, unique for being the only active female international archer to shoot without arms, captivated the global audience. However, her journey did not stop at the para-sport podium. Later in the year, Sheetal shattered a significant glass ceiling when she was selected for India’s able-bodied team for the Asia Cup. This selection made her the first para-archer in Indian history to be included at that level, competing directly against athletes with full upper-body function. Her inclusion was not a token gesture but a result of her consistent scores that rivalled the best in the business. For the sporting community, Sheetal’s achievement went beyond medals; it expanded how excellence and ability are understood in Indian sport, proving that precision is a product of focus and will, irrespective of physical constraints.

clat-mock-14-p4.title: The Global Dawn of Artemis II: A New Deep-Space Era
clat-mock-14-p4.text:
The launch of NASA’s Artemis II mission on April 1, 2026, marks a historic milestone in human spaceflight, breaking a five-decade hiatus in deep-space exploration since the Apollo era. By carrying a diverse, international four-person crew into the Moon's vicinity via a free-return trajectory, the mission does more than validate advanced life support systems and Orion’s spacecraft performance—it signals a profound geopolitical and scientific shift that reverberates globally.

On the world stage, Artemis II is viewed as a definitive symbol of shared human progress and strategic international collaboration. The inclusion of a Canadian Space Agency astronaut alongside historic NASA crew members showcases a collaborative framework built on global partnerships, which also integrates secondary payloads from nations.

Beyond its technical achievements, the global community sees Artemis II as the ultimate testing ground for sustainable deep-space infrastructure. The deployment of revolutionary technologies—such as the 260 Mbps. Ultimately, the world watches Artemis II not merely as an American milestone, but as a gateway to the broader solar system.

clat-mock-30-p2.text:
U.S.–Saudi Civil Nuclear Agreement: The “123 Agreement” and the Non-Proliferation Question Civil nuclear cooperation has increasingly become part of the strategic relationships that the United States builds with its partners. Such cooperation, however, involves more than the transfer of reactors or nuclear technology. It also requires arrangements governing safeguards, fuel-cycle activities, nuclear security and the possibility of diversion of civilian material towards military purposes.

The recent U.S.–Saudi nuclear agreement illustrates this tension particularly clearly. Saudi Arabia has sought to develop a civilian nuclear programme as part of its broader plans for energy diversification and technological development. For Washington, cooperation offers an opportunity to strengthen strategic and commercial ties with a major Middle Eastern partner while maintaining safeguards against nuclear proliferation.

The agreement has attracted attention because of the sensitive nature of activities. These activities can have legitimate civilian applications but can also produce materials or capabilities relevant to nuclear weapons programmes. Consequently, the extent of international verification and the conditions attached to U.S. nuclear cooperation have become central issues in assessing the arrangement.

The agreement operates within a specific framework of U.S. nuclear law. The framework derives its popular name from a provision of American legislation that governs significant nuclear cooperation with foreign countries. Under this system, an agreement is subject to congressional review before it can enter into force.

The debate ultimately illustrates the difficulty of reconciling energy security, commercial interests, strategic partnerships and nuclear non-proliferation. The central question is not whether Saudi Arabia can develop civilian nuclear power, but under what safeguards and conditions such cooperation should proceed.

clat-mock-13-p0.title: Defeat of the 131 Amendment Bill
clat-mock-13-p0.text:
The Legislative Context The dramatic defeat of Bill 131 marks a significant turning point in recent legislative history, exposing deep ideological fissures and reshaping the political landscape. Introduced with the intent of overhaul, Bill 131 was envisioned by its architects as a sweeping piece of reform designed to modernize regulatory frameworks and streamline administrative protocols. Proponents championed the bill as a necessary corrective to institutional inertia, arguing that its passage would catalyze economic efficiency and strengthen accountability. However, the sheer scope of the proposed changes quickly drew intense scrutiny from a broad coalition of critics, transforming the legislative process into a highly contentious battleground.

The Dynamics of Opposition As the bill progressed through committee stages, structural flaws and unintended consequences began to dominate the debate. Opponents, ranging from civil society organizations to legal experts and opposition lawmakers, argued that the bill lacked essential safeguards. Critics contended that the centralized authority proposed in Bill 131 would inadvertently dismantle critical checks and balances, leaving vulnerable sectors exposed to systemic overreach. Furthermore, grassroots mobilization intensified as public awareness grew regarding the bill's potential impact on regional autonomy and consumer protections. The debate ceased to be a routine policy discussion, evolving instead into a polarized referendum on governmental authority versus institutional oversight.

The Floor Vote and Aftermath The tension culminated on the chamber floor during the final reading of the bill. While the ruling coalition anticipated a narrow victory based on strict party lines, the momentum shifted during the final hours of debate. Several key centrist legislators and moderate crossbenchers broke ranks, expressing profound reservations over the lack of amendments addressing their core concerns. When the electronic voting board lit up, the definitive count revealed that Bill 131 had been soundly defeated. The failure of the legislation sent immediate shockwaves through political circles, forcing policymakers back to the drawing board and serving as a stark reminder of the challenges inherent in advancing complex, high-stakes legislative reform without broad-based consensus.

clat-mock-38-p1.text: The 18th BRICS Summit, hosted by India in New Delhi in September 2026, reflected the grouping’s growing ambition to shape global economic governance while giving greater representation to emerging and developing economies. Held under the theme of resilience, innovation, cooperation and sustainability, the summit brought together an expanded membership whose economic and political interests are not always identical. The New Delhi Declaration addressed global governance, development finance, trade, agriculture, technology and sustainable development. Members discussed ways to deepen cooperation among emerging economies while retaining the grouping’s consensus-based structure. Agriculture received particular attention through discussions on food security, farmer welfare, sustainability and innovation. Economic questions also featured prominently as members examined mechanisms for strengthening financial and commercial cooperation without eliminating national policy autonomy. Agriculture was another prominent area. Member countries endorsed initiatives covering food security, farmers’ rights, climate-resilient agriculture, digital farming and exchange of agricultural knowledge. A new farmer-centric network dealing with agricultural inputs, genetic resources and information was among the initiatives welcomed by leaders. India also used its chairship to promote digital public infrastructure, artificial intelligence, industrial cooperation, health and environmental conservation. The summit demonstrated BRICS’ increasing institutional reach, but its expanded membership also means that consensus must accommodate countries with very different strategic and economic priorities.

clat-mock-05-p2.text:
After more than fifteen years of on-again, off-again negotiations, India and the European Union are finally on the verge of signing one of the most ambitious trade agreements either side has ever concluded with a major economy.

Sources close to the talks say the deal will dramatically open doors that have remained heavily guarded for decades, especially in sectors where European companies have long complained of steep barriers. At the same time, Indian industry is being promised easier access to a market of 450 million affluent consumers at a moment when alternative export destinations have become unpredictable and expensive.

Both sides describe the timing as “strategically perfect”: Europe wants new growth engines beyond its slowing domestic markets, while India seeks to diversify its export basket just when some traditional routes are becoming costlier. If everything falls into place, the agreement will be formally announced in the first half of 2026.

clat-bootcamp-mock-37-p1.title: The Uniform Civil Code, Assam, 2026 One Law for the Valley
clat-bootcamp-mock-37-p1.text:
Approval came from the first Cabinet of a returned Chief Minister at the Koinadhara State Guest House; a fortnight later, on the session's closing day of May 2026, the Parliamentary Affairs Minister rose in Guwahati to table the Bill in the Chief Minister's name. Two days of debate, opposition walkouts, and one division vote later, the Vidhan Sabha passed it making the state the third in the Union to plant this flag, and the first in the Northeast. The path had been charted earlier: a pioneer Himalayan state had turned its 2024 law into a working code the following January, a western industrial state had passed its own version that very March, while one coastal enclave still lives under a Portuguese civil skeleton of 1867 the working model cited whenever Article 44's Directive-Principle dream is invoked.

The machinery is administrative before it is philosophical. Registrars in every district will now wait upon couples: memoranda must reach them within sixty days of the ceremony, with lapses costing ten thousand rupees. A parallel register opens for partnerships formed without pheras or vows, due within thirty days of domesticity minors may not enrol, nor the already-married, nor any consent extracted by force or fraud; children of such unions stand legitimate, and an abandoned partner may claim support in court. Ages are fixed at eighteen and twenty-one; monogamy is refitted into the new penal code, seven years the ceiling for a second union and as many for wedlock won by deception; three years for a counterfeit dissolution; three more with a lakh in fines for shackling a divorcee who remarries. The state's 2024 community-specific marriage-registration statute folds into the new architecture and stands repealed, while unions lawfully formed before commencement remain saved. Where custom, ritual and constitutional sanctuary begin, the framers insist, their Bill stops.

clat-mock-16-p2.title: LABOUR LAW
clat-mock-16-p2.text:
The manufacturing hubs of Noida and Greater Noida have recently faced structural labor unrest, highlighting the ongoing tension between rapid industrial expansion and workers' rights. As a primary economic zone attracting billions in foreign direct investment, the region relies on maintaining a highly competitive production ecosystem. However, factory floor disputes over wage stagnation, sudden mass layoffs, and the extensive use of temporary contract workers have triggered intense protests, temporarily disrupting key supply chains in the electronics and automotive sectors.

To resolve these recurring industrial disputes, local administrations and state labor departments are pushing for comprehensive statutory updates. These measures are designed to consolidate outdated, fragmented labor laws into a unified framework aimed at standardizing dispute resolution timelines, modernizing occupational safety guidelines, and regularizing contract hire conditions. A central feature of these updates is the transition toward a digital single-window compliance system, which streamlines mandatory corporate filings and reduces administrative burdens for employers. However, implementing these changes faces heavy resistance. Trade unions argue that the new rules tip the scale too far in favor of corporate management by easing rules around layoffs and changing trade union registration thresholds. Conversely, industrial associations contend that rigid local rules delay production cycles, emphasizing the delicate challenge of balancing labor protections with global economic competitiveness.

clat-aiom-mock-02-p4.text:
Bank of India’s recent ₹10,000 crore fundraise through infrastructure bonds spotlights the deepening pool of long-horizon capital for India’s build-out of roads, power, transit, and urban systems. Strong investor appetite—reflected in heavy bidding—signals confidence in the economy’s multi‑year infrastructure pipeline and in the capacity of large issuers to intermediate stable funding into projects with extended gestation.

Infrastructure bonds sit at the heart of this financing architecture. They channel patient capital into core assets, broaden banks’ funding mix beyond traditional deposits, and add depth to India’s corporate bond market. For investors, these instruments typically offer predictable cash flows and high-quality counterparties, but they still require careful assessment of market conditions, liquidity, and issuer strength over long holding periods. Alongside them, newer market structures and thematic instruments are evolving, and market participants increasingly compare bond- based funding with alternative vehicles that invest in operating infrastructure.

As the policy push toward large-scale capital formation gathers pace, a more diversified menu of instruments—and clearer disclosure standards—aim to align project timelines with financing horizons, distribute risks efficiently across investors, and sustain momentum toward national infrastructure goals.

clat-mock-15-p4.text:
The Global AI Safety Summit and Declarations on Frontier Artificial Intelligence The rapid acceleration of generative artificial intelligence models has prompted an unprecedented international legislative response to mitigate systemic existential risks. Leaders, policymakers, and tech executives gathered at a historic global AI Safety Summit to establish a unified framework for the oversight of "frontier AI"—defined as highly capable foundation models that can pose severe risks to public safety. The central discourse focused on the dual-use nature of advanced machine learning algorithms, which offer exponential breakthroughs in scientific

computing while simultaneously presenting threats regarding automated cyberattacks, state- level disinformation campaigns, and the democratization of hazardous biochemical blueprints.

The political climax of the summit was the historic, unanimous signing of a collaborative safety declaration by over twenty-five sovereign nations, including India, the United States, China, and members of the European Union. Named after the historic venue where the summit was hosted, the declaration formally acknowledged that substantial risks arise from potential intentional misuse or unintended issues of control regarding frontier AI capabilities. To institutionalize these safety thresholds, participating nations agreed to establish state-backed AI Safety Institutes designed to rigorously test and audit private models before their public release. Despite intense corporate lobbying, the summit concluded with a clear consensus that independent, public- interest scientific research must take absolute precedence over unregulated market deployment to preserve global geopolitical stability.

clat-mock-18-p3.title: Ambedkar Jayanti and the Legacy of Mahad Satyagraha
clat-mock-18-p3.text:
Every year, Ambedkar Jayanti is observed across India to commemorate the birth anniversary of Dr. B.R. Ambedkar, one of the principal architects of the Indian Constitution and a leading advocate of social justice. His contributions extended beyond constitutionalism to struggles against caste discrimination, social exclusion, and unequal access to public resources. Among the many movements associated with his leadership, one campaign in western India is often remembered for challenging entrenched social hierarchies and asserting the principle of equal civic rights.

Historians regard this movement as a turning point in India's anti-caste struggle because it transformed demands for social reform into a broader claim for equality and dignity. The event also highlighted the relationship between legal rights and social realities, a theme that continued to influence Ambedkar's later political and constitutional thought. Today, Ambedkar Jayanti serves not only as a commemoration of an individual leader but also as an occasion to reflect upon questions of equality, representation, and social justice in contemporary India.

clat-mock-03-p1.text:
Indian sport witnessed a historic milestone this week as India completed a rare double at the Kho Kho World Cup 2025, with both the men’s and women’s teams clinching gold. In a display that combined lightning-fast reflexes, diving tags and razor-sharp strategic acumen, the Indian sides outplayed their opponents in every department, reaffirming the country’s dominance in a sport that traces its roots to traditional village playgrounds. What was once seen largely as a rustic pastime has now emerged on the global stage as a

highly organised, camera-friendly contact sport, with international audiences getting a closer look at its speed and tactical depth. The World Cup triumph is being hailed as a breakthrough moment, comparable to earlier successes in kabaddi and hockey in terms of visibility and soft power. Several players, many of whom honed their craft on dusty school fields and in state-level camps, have now become overnight ambassadors of Indian sporting heritage. The victories are also expected to give a major boost to professional Kho Kho leagues, sponsorship interest and grassroots participation. More importantly, they signal that an indigenous gameonce confined to local tournaments and school meetscan stand shoulder to shoulder with global disciplines, blending cultural legacy with modern competitive excellence.

clat-mock-25-p4.text: Sarnath: Preserving a Legacy of Faith and Heritage Ancient places of worship often serve not only as centres of religious devotion but also as repositories of history, architecture and cultural exchange. In recent years, international efforts to preserve such sites have increasingly highlighted their importance as shared heritage transcending national boundaries. Recognition by global institutions reflects not only historical significance but also the continuing responsibility of governments to ensure conservation, scientific management and sustainable tourism. One such ancient settlement in northern India has recently received international recognition for its exceptional cultural value. Archaeological remains at the site reveal continuous development over many centuries through royal patronage, monastic activity and public contributions. Excavations have uncovered stupas, monasteries, sculptural remains, inscriptions and monumental pillars, providing valuable evidence regarding the evolution of religious architecture and artistic traditions in the Indian subcontinent. Historical records produced by foreign travellers who journeyed across Asia during the early medieval period offer important insights into the prosperity of the settlement. Their descriptions of religious institutions, monuments and scholarly activity have often supplemented archaeological discoveries in reconstructing the site's historical development. Modern conservation efforts have likewise relied upon a combination of scientific excavation, documentary evidence and international evaluation. The process through which culturally significant places receive global heritage recognition is itself rigorous. Before inscription, nominated sites undergo extensive technical assessment by expert advisory bodies, which evaluate their authenticity, integrity and long-term conservation plans. Such recognition is intended not merely to honour the past but also to encourage responsible preservation for future generations. The renewed attention accorded to this ancient settlement has also reinforced broader discussions concerning India's cultural diplomacy and the protection of historical monuments. Conservation experts observe that safeguarding archaeological heritage requires balancing tourism, urban development and environmental sustainability while preserving the historical character of the site. As countries increasingly collaborate in protecting cultural heritage, ancient monuments continue to serve as enduring symbols of civilisational continuity and shared human history.

clat-mock-34-p2.title: Ancient Buddhist Site of Sarnath Inscribed on UNESCO World Heritage List
clat-mock-34-p2.text:
The ancient Buddhist site of Sarnath has been inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List. Welcoming the inscription of Uttar Pradesh’s Sarnath on the UNESCO World Heritage List, Prime Minister Narendra Modi described it as a proud moment for every Indian.

In a social media post, PM Modi said that Sarnath has a close association with Lord Buddha, whose timeless message of wisdom, compassion, and harmony continues to inspire the world. He added that the recognition celebrates India’s profound civilisational and spiritual heritage. The Prime Minister said that the inscription would inspire more people from across the world to visit Sarnath and connect with the ideals of Lord Buddha.

Culture and Tourism Minister Gajendra Singh Shekhawat described the inscription as a defining moment for India’s cultural heritage. In a social media post, Mr Shekhawat said that Sarnath is a timeless beacon of peace, wisdom, and compassion. He said that it reflects the profound spiritual and philosophical contributions of Indian civilisation to humanity. Mr Shekhawat added that the inscription reaffirms the nation’s enduring role as a cradle of ideas that continue to inspire the world across generations.

Extracted with edits and revisions from https://newsonair.gov.in/ancient-buddhist-site-of-sarnath-inscribed-on- unesco-world-heritage-list/

clat-additional-mock-01-p2.title: The Evolution of Global Technology Governance and India's Emerging Role
clat-additional-mock-01-p2.text:
The digital revolution has fundamentally altered how nations understand power, prosperity, and strategic positioning. As computing infrastructure, artificial intelligence systems, and advanced electronics become central to economic growth and national capacity, countries increasingly recognize that technology development operates within a complex web of geopolitical relationships.

Historically, technology advancement was viewed as a primarily domestic or purely commercial endeavor. Today, however, governments recognize that the sourcing, manufacturing, and distribution of technological components carry profound implications for national autonomy and international relationships. The flow of information, materials, and expertise across borders shapes which nations can innovate independently and which become dependent on external sources for critical capabilities.

India has emerged as a significant participant in the global technology ecosystem. With its substantial software engineering talent, growing interest in semiconductor manufacturing, and expanding artificial intelligence research capacity, the country occupies a distinctive position. Indian firms and research institutions contribute to worldwide technology supply networks, while Indian consumers and industries depend on imported technological goods and services.

International cooperation on technology matters has become increasingly common, with countries exploring various institutional frameworks to align their interests. These arrangements typically involve dialogue among nations with shared economic values and governance philosophies. The motivations underlying such partnerships are multifaceted: nations seek to strengthen mutual capabilities, reduce individual vulnerabilities, and create environments where innovation can flourish securely.

The minerals and materials that underpin modern electronics—including those essential for batteries, computing devices, and renewable energy systems—are unevenly distributed globally. This reality shapes economic relationships and requires ongoing attention from policymakers navigating the intersection of resource availability, technological advancement, and international commerce.

clat-mock-30-p3.text:
Guarantee for Rozgar and Ajeevika Mission (Gramin) (VB–G RAM G) Act The legislative overhaul of India’s rural employment framework under the Viksit Bharat – Guarantee for Rozgar and Ajeevika Mission (Gramin) (VB–G RAM G) Act, 2025 marks a structural shift toward outcome-driven asset creation and targeted decentralization. Positioned as a core instrument to ensure national progress is realized through local self-governance, the statutory architecture balances Union-level oversight with state-level administrative accountability. Implementation operates as a shared financial model, where the Union specifies unskilled wage rates while state governments remain legally obligated to formalize state- specific schemes within a strict statutory timeframe following enactment.
