While locals described it as a "solid wall of water," meteorological experts are currently analyzing data from local observatories to determine if the rainfall intensity met the specific hourly threshold required to technically classify the event as a 'cloudburst.'

The disaster has once again highlighted the unique vulnerability of this region, where moisture-laden winds are mechanically forced upwards by the mountain barriers, creating sudden atmospheric instability. In response to the crisis, the central administration has activated protocols under the statutory disaster management framework established in 2005. Specialized response teams have been deployed to the affected districts, including Chamoli, to assist in rescue operations. Meanwhile, the nodal ministry responsible for weather forecasting is facing scrutiny regarding the efficacy of its modern radar network. Critics argue that despite the ability of these radars to measure precipitation density and wind speed, the 'nowcast' warnings often arrive too late to save lives in such rugged terrain.

clat-mock-14-p0.title: Kerala to Keralam
clat-mock-14-p0.text:
The Linguistic Renaissance: Regaining "Keralam" The modern movement to officially rename the state of Kerala to "Keralam" is deeply rooted in linguistic pride and the historic consolidation of Malayalam-speaking communities. The familiar term "Kerala" is an anglicized adaptation popularized during British colonial rule to suit foreign accents. In contrast, "Keralam" is the authentic, classical name embedded in the state's native tongue, Malayalam, reflecting its geographical identity as the bountiful land (alam) of coconuts (kera).

This socio-linguistic change represents a vital structural shift toward cultural decolonization. It directly mirrors successful historical precedents where major Indian cities, regions, and states systematically shed their colonial mononyms—such as Bombay transforming to Mumbai, Madras changing to Chennai, Calcutta becoming Kolkata, and Mysore transitioning to Karnataka.

By pursuing this official transition, the state actively aims to align its statutory political identity with its living cultural soul. This necessary correction ensures that the region's official geography honors the linguistic heritage, literature, and daily identity of its citizens. Ultimately, this reclamation allows the state to permanently establish its indigenous nomenclature on the global map, celebrating its roots while stepping confidently into the future.

clat-mock-41-p1.text:
India and the European Union have moved closer to establishing one of their most significant economic partnerships following the conclusion of negotiations for an ambitious Free Trade Agreement (FTA) in 2026. The development followed years of negotiations that had earlier stalled before being formally revived. The agreement is intended to deepen trade and investment relations between two major economic markets at a time of increasing global protectionism and supply-chain uncertainty.

The proposed framework covers trade in goods and services, market access, rules of origin, intellectual property, sustainable development and provisions concerning movement of professionals. India has sought improved access for labour-intensive sectors such as textiles, garments, leather, footwear and marine products, while European businesses have emphasised greater access to India's expanding consumer market.

Agriculture and dairy products have remained particularly sensitive areas for India, while environmental trade measures, including the Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM), have also figured prominently in the broader economic relationship. The agreement therefore reflects an attempt to reconcile market liberalisation with domestic economic priorities.

Although negotiations have concluded and the treaty text has advanced into the approval process, further institutional procedures remain necessary before the agreement becomes legally binding on the parties. The development comes as India simultaneously expands its network of economic partnerships with other major trading blocs and countries.

clat-mock-21-p3.text: NFHS 6 The National Family Health Survey (NFHS) is India's largest nationally representative survey on population, health, and nutrition. Conducted under the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, the survey provides estimates that support evidence-based policymaking across the country. The latest NFHS-6 highlights significant progress in several health and demographic indicators. Institutional deliveries have crossed the 90% mark, reflecting improved access to maternal healthcare services. India's Total Fertility Rate (TFR) remains below the replacement level, indicating the country's continued demographic transition. Child nutrition has shown improvement, with declines in long-term stunting and severe acute wasting. The survey also reports higher coverage of childhood immunisation and greater utilisation of public healthcare facilities for vaccination services. Another notable trend is the growing digital inclusion of women, with internet usage increasing substantially compared to the previous survey. However, the survey also records a continued rise in Caesarean section deliveries, raising important public health concerns regarding the appropriate use of surgical interventions during childbirth. Overall, the findings provide valuable insights into India's changing demographic, nutritional, and healthcare landscape and serve as an important benchmark for evaluating public health programmes and monitoring progress towards national development objectives.

clat-bootcamp-mock-01-p1.title: Law of Sedition
clat-bootcamp-mock-01-p1.text: A frozen law rarely thaws quietly. Nearly four years after the Supreme Court sheathed the Republic's oldest speech offence — barring fresh FIRs, freezing investigations, stalling every pending trial — a late-May clarification this year allowed slumbering prosecutions to stir, on one curious condition: the accused himself must invite the trial back. The courtroom reprieve has split opinion. Can a prisoner angling for bail, critics ask, truly choose freely? And what of dockmates — two rivers flowing from one indictment — where one waves the trial onward while the other digs in? The clause was ever the Raj's favourite hook: twice fastened to a Poona editor and his vernacular daily, and once to the Mahatma's own weekly — earning him six years, and us an epigram about princes and political suppression that has outlived the empire. In the Republic's first summer, the young apex court refused to countenance speech- curbs unless the security of the State itself quaked; two high courts went further and voided the clause outright — until early-sixties surgery saved it by maiming it. Its recent interment borrowed, tellingly, a doctrine that laws must keep step with the march of time. Reform counsel already on record urged retention, but refurbished: the tendency-to-violence safeguard written into the text, and a double lock before any FIR. The reworded successor, meanwhile, guards a different deity altogether: not the government of the day, but the State itself — though listeners complain its vocabulary, all "subversive activities" and separatist "feelings", still begs for the chisel. The mother of the law buried her own version years ago, unlamented. A seven-judge bench still waits; so does a definitive epitaph — or a resurrection.

clat-aiom-mock-01-p2.text:
In a landmark diplomatic gathering held in Malaysia's capital, leaders from South and Southeast Asia convened to reinforce their long-standing partnership. This high-level dialogue, rooted in the principles of the Bangkok Declaration of 1967, highlighted the enduring relevance of regional solidarity. While the bloc originally began with a core group of five nations, it has since evolved into a formidable entity, recently expanding its footprint by formally inducting its newest member, thereby altering its traditional ten-member structure.

The summit focused on operationalizing strategic commitments, leading to the endorsement of a comprehensive roadmap for 2026–2030. This plan aims to translate the Comprehensive Strategic Partnership into tangible outcomes. Recognizing deep civilizational links, India proposed establishing a dedicated center for regional studies at the historic Nalanda University to foster intellectual exchange. Furthermore, acknowledging the vital maritime connection, the leaders declared 2026 as a special year dedicated to maritime cooperation. The summit concluded with a resolute affirmation of the ASEAN Outlook on the Indo-Pacific, setting the stage for a more integrated future.

clat-mock-08-p0.text:
India's democratic framework relies heavily on the integrity of its electoral rolls, which form the backbone of free and fair elections. The Election Commission of India (ECI), established as an autonomous constitutional body, exercises comprehensive authority over the preparation, revision, and maintenance of electoral rolls across the country. The Constitution empowers the Commission through specific provisions to ensure superintendence, direction, and control of the entire electoral process.

The Summary Revision of Electoral Rolls (SIR) is a critical periodic exercise undertaken before major elections to update voter lists by adding eligible new voters, removing deceased or shifted individuals, and correcting errors. This exercise carries significant advantages for electoral integrity and the broader democratic process.

To modernise operations, the ECI has deployed digital platforms like ECINet, which leverages technology for streamlining verification processes, enabling real-time status updates via SMS/Email, and facilitating online document uploads. Voter identification is anchored by the EPIC card system, which serves as the primary identity document for electors at polling stations.

The procedural framework governing enrolment and revision processes is codified under specific statutory rules. Additionally, the Chief Election Commissioner enjoys constitutional protection regarding removal from office, safeguarding the Commission's independence from political interference and ensuring impartial electoral governance nationwide.

clat-mock-29-p2.title: Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO) Summit 2026
clat-mock-29-p2.text: The Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO) remains an important multilateral platform bringing together countries across Eurasia. Its cooperation extends across areas such as regional security, counter-terrorism, connectivity, economic cooperation, technology, culture and people-to-people exchanges. The organisation has also developed various mechanisms involving ministers, experts, youth and other stakeholders. The 26th meeting of the Council of Heads of State was held in 2026 as the culmination of the organisation's annual chairmanship cycle. The summit adopted a declaration covering a range of regional and international issues, including terrorism, connectivity, scientific cooperation, climate-related concerns and economic development. Member states also reaffirmed their commitment to cooperation based on sovereignty, equality and mutual respect. India used the summit to emphasise its priorities within the organisation. Prime Minister Narendra Modi highlighted the importance of strengthening cooperation in security, connectivity and opportunities for development. He also stressed the role of technology, entrepreneurship, innovation, start-ups and youth engagement in expanding cooperation among SCO countries. India further placed emphasis on civilisational and people-to-people exchanges. Several India-led initiatives relating to youth, science, literature and cultural dialogue received attention during the summit. The proposed Civilisation Dialogue mechanism was presented as a platform for encouraging greater interaction among the diverse societies represented within the organisation. The summit also reaffirmed the SCO's institutional character. While security remains a major area of cooperation, the organisation does not function as a conventional collective-defence arrangement. Its agenda combines security concerns with economic, technological, cultural and developmental priorities. The meeting also marked the transition to the next annual chairmanship cycle, demonstrating the SCO's rotating institutional structure and its continuing emphasis on multilateral cooperation across Eurasia.

clat-mock-18-p2.title: Valuing Invisible Work
clat-mock-18-p2.text:
A recent judgment of the Supreme Court has renewed discussions about the economic and social significance of unpaid domestic labour. While household work has traditionally been viewed as a private responsibility rather than an economic activity, the Court observed that such work contributes substantially to family welfare, human development, and the functioning of the broader economy. The judgment arose from a compensation dispute involving the death of a woman who had devoted most of her time to managing household responsibilities and caring for family members.

The Court noted that activities performed within households often remain absent from conventional economic indicators despite requiring time, skill, and effort. It further observed that caregiving responsibilities enable other members of the household to participate in education, employment, and public life. The judgment also highlighted concerns regarding delays in compensation claims and emphasized the need for a more responsive legal framework. According to legal observers, the ruling may influence future debates concerning the valuation of unpaid care work and the recognition of contributions that have historically remained outside formal economic calculations.

clat-mock-06-p0.text:
The Union Budget 2026–27 outlines a comprehensive strategy aimed at accelerating India’s journey toward Viksit Bharat. In her opening remarks, the Finance Minister referred to the birth anniversary of a revered Bhakti-era spiritual reformer, linking ethical values and social justice with economic policymaking. The address set the tone for a reform-driven and citizen-focused governance framework built on three guiding principles that stress decisiveness, structural change, and inclusive development.

The macroeconomic outlook presented in the budget highlights sustained high growth, moderate inflation, and a calibrated path toward fiscal consolidation. The fiscal deficit is projected to decline steadily compared to previous years, reflecting adherence to fiscal discipline while preserving momentum in capital expenditure. Investments in infrastructure, logistics, and digital connectivity continue to form a cornerstone of the government’s long-term growth strategy.

Manufacturing and technological advancement receive significant attention. Plans include the development of multiple dedicated chemical parks to strengthen domestic industrial capacity and reduce import dependency. The next phase of a national semiconductor initiative has also been proposed to deepen India’s capabilities in advanced electronics and chip manufacturing. Overall, the budget emphasizes stability, structural reform, and production-led growth while maintaining a balance between ambition and inclusion in the development agenda.

clat-mock-09-p4.title: India's Indigenous Microprocessor Journey and DHRUV64
clat-mock-09-p4.text:
India's pursuit of technological sovereignty has gained significant momentum with the indigenous development of advanced microprocessors like DHRUV64. As part of the nation's broader semiconductor mission, this processor represents a shift away from reliance on foreign intellectual property towards a self-sustaining hardware ecosystem. Built upon the open-source RISC-V Instruction Set Architecture (ISA), DHRUV64 is engineered to prioritize security and customizability, addressing critical needs in strategic sectors such as defense, aerospace, and secure industrial automation.

Unlike traditional commercial processors that operate as "black boxes," indigenous designs offer transparency, ensuring that no hidden backdoors exist — a crucial requirement for national security infrastructure. The architecture focuses on high-performance computing capabilities while maintaining energy efficiency, making it adaptable for various embedded systems and server-grade applications. This initiative is supported by the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY) to foster a fabless design culture within the country. By mastering complex design flows and logical synthesis, India is not only creating hardware but also nurturing a skilled workforce capable of competing globally. DHRUV64 stands as a testament to the "Atmanirbhar Bharat" vision, laying the groundwork for a future where India is a global hub for semiconductor innovation rather than just a consumer.

clat-mock-28-p0.title: Scoring The Global GoalS
clat-mock-28-p0.text: In 2015 the world's governments adopted a blueprint for the following fifteen years: an agenda of seventeen sustainable development goals, from ending poverty and hunger to protecting the planet and strengthening global partnership. Performance against that agenda is measured each year by an international index, which scores and ranks the participating countries. The annual verdicts have been sobering. Even the countries that habitually lead the table remain far from their own targets, and at the present pace the majority of the goals will be missed across the world by the agreed deadline. India is a participant in every edition of that assessment, and its results are followed closely at home, where each release renews a familiar debate about how far the country has travelled and how far it still has to go. Commentary tends to turn on the same few points: the distance between India's score and the leading countries, the comparison with its regional neighbours, and the unevenness of progress across the goals themselves — with those tied to everyday well-being, such as poverty, hunger and nutrition, health, and water and sanitation, receiving the closest attention. The honest summary is one of persistence rather than completion; the targets of 2030 remain ahead. Measurement, however, is a machinery of its own. Alongside the global index, each country maintains a national framework of indicators, and the periodic progress reports that track them are compiled at home, institution by institution. The arrangement echoes an older architecture: the framework that preceded the present agenda carried a far smaller set of goals and targets, and the successor agenda deliberately enlarged both. As the ambition has grown, so has the business of counting it.

clat-mock-20-p3.title: The U.S.A. marked its 250th anniversary
clat-mock-20-p3.text:
The year 2026 marks an important milestone in the history of the United States as it commemorates two and a half centuries since the political event that laid the foundation of the modern American republic. The celebrations have prompted renewed reflection not only on the ideals of liberty, representative government, and constitutionalism but also on the evolution of the country's global partnerships. Among these, the relationship between India and the United States has emerged as one of the most significant strategic partnerships of the twenty-first century.

Although the two democracies experienced periods of political divergence during the Cold War, changing geopolitical realities, economic reforms, and shared security interests have gradually transformed bilateral relations. Today, cooperation extends beyond diplomacy into trade, defence, science and technology, education, critical and emerging technologies, clean energy, and resilient supply chains. Strategic dialogue has also intensified through various bilateral and multilateral mechanisms aimed at promoting regional stability and addressing transnational challenges.

The Indo-Pacific has become an important area of collaboration, where both countries work alongside like- minded partners to support a rules-based maritime order, freedom of navigation, disaster response, infrastructure development, and technological cooperation. Defence ties have similarly expanded through regular military engagements, increasing interoperability between armed forces, and collaboration in areas such as cybersecurity, space, logistics, and advanced defence technologies.

Economic relations have also continued to evolve despite occasional trade disagreements. Ongoing negotiations seek to improve market access, strengthen investment flows, diversify supply chains, and enhance cooperation in sectors such as semiconductors, pharmaceuticals, renewable energy, and digital innovation. As both nations navigate an increasingly complex international environment, their partnership reflects a broader convergence of strategic interests while preserving each country's independent foreign policy priorities. Consequently, the trajectory of India–United States relations remains an important subject for understanding contemporary international politics and the changing balance of power in the Indo-Pacific region.

clat-mock-17-p0.title: Tribal Self-Governance and Local Democracy
clat-mock-17-p0.text:
Recent debates concerning the implementation of tribal rights legislation have once again brought attention to the functioning of local self-governance institutions in Scheduled Areas. Civil society groups, tribal organizations, and policymakers have expressed differing views regarding the extent to which local communities should participate in decisions concerning land acquisition, mining activities, forest resources, and development projects.

Advocates of greater decentralization argue that local institutions possess a better understanding of ecological conditions, customary practices, and community needs. They contend that meaningful participation strengthens democratic governance and promotes sustainable development. Others emphasize the need to balance local decision-making with broader developmental objectives and national economic priorities.

The discussion has also highlighted questions regarding the relationship between constitutional provisions, traditional governance systems, and statutory institutions. In several regions, concerns have been raised regarding the consultation process adopted before undertaking projects that may affect tribal communities. At the same time, governments have pointed to ongoing efforts to improve infrastructure, public services, and economic opportunities in historically marginalized areas.

The issue reflects a broader challenge confronting democratic societies: how to reconcile economic development, environmental protection, and the rights of indigenous and tribal communities while ensuring that governance remains both effective and inclusive.

clat-real-mock-01-p4.text:
The post-operational analysis of 'Operation Sindoor' indicates a decisive shift in New Delhi’s strategic calculus regarding the western frontier. Following the neutralization of threats in the Pahalgam sector, the Ministry of External Affairs has adopted a multi-pronged diplomatic offensive. Sources in the South Block confirm that a formal demarche was issued to the adversary, citing irrefutable evidence of state complicity that violates the sanctity of the Line of Control (LoC) established by the historic 1972 agreement. Beyond the immediate military maneuvering in the Himalayas, the government is reportedly reviewing its riparian gestures, specifically concerning the tributaries of the Indus system that flow across the border.

Simultaneously, the geopolitical fallout has accelerated India’s pivot away from gridlocked regional forums. There is a renewed vigour to consolidate the Bay of Bengal Initiative for Multi-Sectoral Technical and Economic Cooperation (BIMSTEC) as the primary vehicle for regional integration, deliberately sidelining platforms held hostage by bilateral animosity. Analysts observe that this muscular foreign policy marks the final shed of the hesitation associated with the Non-Aligned Movement (NAM) era, moving towards a doctrine of proactive issue- based alignment.

Operation Sindoor also marked a shift in India’s counter-terror doctrine, reflecting a preference for proactive deterrence while remaining below the threshold of full-scale conflict. Analysts observed that the operation sought to balance domestic security imperatives with regional stability, signalling resolve without undermining India’s broader strategic and economic interests.

clat-mock-19-p2.title: 50th anniversary of Sikkim
clat-mock-19-p2.text:
This year marks the 50th anniversary of Sikkim’s integration with India, commemorating the events of 1975 when Sikkim became the 22nd State of the Indian Union. Prior to its integration, Sikkim was ruled by the Chogyal dynasty and functioned as an Indian protectorate under a special treaty arrangement. Political developments during the early 1970s, including demands for democratic reforms and greater political representation, altered the relationship between the monarchy and elected institutions.

In 1975, the Sikkim Assembly adopted a resolution seeking the abolition of the institution of the Chogyal and closer constitutional integration with India. Subsequently, a referendum was conducted in which an overwhelming majority reportedly supported the proposal. Parliament enacted the Constitution Amendment Act, 1975, granting Sikkim full statehood. The amendment also inserted Article 371F, providing special constitutional provisions for the state.

Sikkim occupies a strategically important position in the eastern Himalayas, sharing borders with Nepal, Bhutan, and China. The state is also associated with significant geographical features such as Kanchenjunga, India’s highest mountain peak. The anniversary has renewed discussions on federalism, constitutional integration, border security, and the unique historical processes through which different regions became part of the Indian Union.

clat-mock-28-p2.title: A Question Of Representation
clat-mock-28-p2.text:
India's constitutional map is far from uniform. Alongside the states stand the union territories, run by the Union through appointed officials. Most have no elected legislature; only a small number do, and the national capital enjoys a distinctive arrangement — a directly elected assembly and a council of ministers over a defined list of subjects, while the Union keeps public order, police and land. That arrangement was added by amendment decades after independence.

The same asymmetry lies at the heart of a grievance in the country's far north. In 2019 the former state there was split into two union territories: one kept an elected government, while the other — a high, cold Himalayan region — was placed directly under the Centre, with no assembly of its own. Residents who had once sent members to the state legislature now found decisions in appointed hands; local councils existed, but their powers fell far short of a legislature's. Campaigners call the result a representation deficit, and their demands — full statehood, seats in Parliament, a recruitment commission, safeguards for tribal identity and a fragile ecology — keep the region in the news. The Constitution, however, offers models of self-rule for tribal communities. In the north-east a special constitutional schedule created autonomous district councils for tribal areas of four states, empowered to legislate on land, forests, water, trade, marriage and customs, and to run village courts and schools. A parallel framework elsewhere gives village assemblies a decisive say over local resources. Advocates for the Himalayan territory argue that a comparable arrangement could secure local identity and national frontiers; the government, wary of constitutional complexity, prefers to strengthen the councils that exist and to protect local residents by regulation. The disagreement is over how much self-rule a strategically vital region can safely be given.

clat-mock-22-p2.title: Export Preparedness Index
clat-mock-22-p2.text:
The landscape of India’s international trade is increasingly defined by sub-national performance, a trend highlighted by the periodic release of the Export Preparedness Index (EPI). As the nation seeks to integrate more deeply into global value chains, this analytical framework has emerged as a essential tool for assessing how individual states facilitate and contribute to national export expansion. By offering a structured evaluation of regional trade readiness, the index assists policymakers in identifying barriers to commerce and optimizing local logistical frameworks.

The methodology behind the index is comprehensive, focusing on several foundational pillars that determine a state's capacity to engage in international trade. These pillars are designed to capture the multifaceted nature of export-oriented growth, ranging from governance structures and infrastructure development to the broader commercial climate. To ensure depth, these core pillars are further broken down into a variety of sub-pillars and specific indicators, allowing for precise, data-driven comparisons between states regardless of their industrial maturity or geographic location.

To facilitate better benchmarking, the index organizes states into specific performance tiers, distinguishing between those at different stages of their export journey. This classification system helps prioritize interventions, encouraging states to improve their trade facilitation measures and policy frameworks. Ultimately, the publication of this index by India's national policy think tank serves as a strategic compass, fostering healthy competition among states and providing a clear roadmap for enhancing India's overall export competitiveness on the global stage.

clat-mock-10-p0.text: The elimination of Iran's supreme spiritual authority in a coordinated aerial assault on the final day of February shattered decades of proxy-based confrontation, plunging the Middle East into its gravest conventional crisis since the Gulf War. Operating under dual codenames invoking both destructive force and foundational ambition, the strike decapitated Tehran's revolutionary command structure while Iranian retaliatory barrages struck American forward bases across the Gulf — from Qatar's sprawling desert airfield to Bahrain's Fifth Fleet headquarters, from Emirati staging grounds to Turkey's Incirlik installation where missile debris triggered NATO alert protocols. Tehran's Lebanese proxy simultaneously unleashed rockets across the Blue Line, provoking Israeli strikes on Beirut's southern suburbs while Houthis disrupted Red Sea shipping, rerouting nearly twelve percent of global trade through longer African passages. The maritime chokepoint connecting the Persian Gulf to the Indian Ocean — a 55-to-95-kilometre corridor bordered by Iran and Oman — became a combat zone where naval clashes sank multiple Iranian vessels, immediately spiking Brent crude past ninety dollars and grounding flights across Gulf hubs. At the gulf's northwestern end, two rivers sustaining the ancient Mesopotamian civilization merge through a contested delta before reaching these turbulent waters. India, importing ninety percent of its crude with ten million diaspora workers across the region, faces acute economic exposure as Chabahar Port operations and the INSTC corridor fall within conflict proximity. Russia and China condemned the strikes as sovereignty violations while the IAEA convened emergency consultations regarding Iran's compromised nuclear facilities, raising fears of radiological contamination across populated zones.

clat-mock-22-p1.title: Emergency
clat-mock-22-p1.text: The emergency provisions in the Indian Constitution, enshrined in Part XVIII (Articles 352 to 360), are fundamentally designed to safeguard the sovereignty, unity, integrity, and security of the nation. The framers of the Constitution recognized that extraordinary crises—such as war, external aggression, armed rebellion, or severe financial instability—demand swift and highly centralized responses. During normal times, India functions as a federal democracy, distributing power between the Centre and the states. However, declaring an emergency effectively transforms this federal structure into a unitary one without requiring formal constitutional amendments. This temporary mechanism is required to grant the Central government overriding executive and legislative powers, ensuring that the country can navigate grave national threats or the breakdown of constitutional machinery in specific states without being hindered by procedural delays or divided authority. To craft these crucial safeguards, the framers borrowed and adapted concepts from previous legislative frameworks. The primary structural foundation for the emergency provisions was directly taken from the Government of India Act, 1935. This colonial-era legislation contained specific sections granting the executive vast discretionary powers to assume centralized control during a failure of governance or internal disturbances. Furthermore, while the overarching emergency framework originates from the 1935 Act, a specific feature—the suspension of Fundamental Rights during an active emergency—was borrowed from the Weimar Constitution of Germany. By combining these historical precedents with strict parliamentary oversight, the Constitution ensures the state has the strength to survive existential crises.

clat-mock-34-p3.title: 26th Shanghai Cooperation Organisation Summit
clat-mock-34-p3.text:
Prime Minister Narendra Modi on Tuesday participated in the 26th Meeting of the Council of Heads of State of the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO) in Bishkek, calling for stronger cooperation on security, connectivity and development while urging member countries to take committed action against terrorism.

The summit, held from August 31 to September 1 in the Kyrgyz Republic, coincides with the 25th anniversary of the SCO. Leaders reviewed the organisation’s progress and discussed ways to strengthen its role in promoting peace, security, stability and prosperity in the region. In his address, PM Modi thanked Kyrgyz President Sadyr Zhaparov for his warmth and hospitality and said the SCO’s 25th anniversary provided an opportunity to prepare a roadmap for the next 25 years, building on the organisation’s tradition of dialogue and cooperation.

Recalling India’s vision presented at the previous summit, the Prime Minister said the grouping should now work towards achieving concrete outcomes under the three pillars of Security, Connectivity and Opportunity. On security, PM Modi reiterated India’s position that conflicts cannot be resolved through military means and that dialogue and diplomacy are the only way forward. He described terrorism as a grave threat to humanity and called for determined efforts to dismantle the entire terror ecosystem.

Extracted with edits and revisions from https://ddnews.gov.in/en/pm-modi-participates-in-26th-sco-summit-in- bishkek/

clat-mock-38-p0.text: India’s digital-payment ecosystem has undergone a remarkable transformation over the past decade. A major contributor to this change has been a real-time payment architecture developed by the National Payments Corporation of India, which allows customers of different banks to transact seamlessly through compatible mobile applications. Introduced in 2016, the platform has grown from a relatively small banking initiative into the backbone of India’s retail digital- payment system. Its rapid expansion was aided by interoperability, round-the-clock availability and the ability to conduct transactions without repeatedly entering conventional bank-account details. The system was designed to support multiple methods of initiating and receiving payments, making digital transfers considerably more convenient than many earlier electronic-payment arrangements. As transaction volumes increased, however, policymakers faced a new question: how should the infrastructure supporting such a large payment network be financed without undermining financial inclusion? In 2026, the government introduced a revised framework allowing a limited Merchant Discount Rate on certain merchant payments while continuing to protect consumers and a large proportion of smaller transactions from additional costs. The government clarified that the charge is not a tax collected by either the government or the payment-network operator. Instead, it is distributed among participants such as banks and payment-service providers to support the operation and expansion of the ecosystem. The policy debate therefore reflects UPI’s transition from a rapidly expanding public digital infrastructure to a mature payment system that must balance affordability, innovation, inclusion and long-term financial sustainability.

clat-mock-09-p1.title: Economic Survey 2025-26 — Key Highlights
clat-mock-09-p1.text:
The Economic Survey, India's flagship annual economic document, has a rich history dating back to 1950-51 when it was first presented as part of the Union Budget. Over the decades, it evolved into an independent publication, authored under the guidance of the Chief Economic Adviser (CEA) and tabled during the Budget Session of Parliament.

The Economic Survey 2025-26 presented a comprehensive assessment of India's economic performance, highlighting the country's resilience as the fastest-growing major economy for the fourth consecutive year. The First Advance Estimates placed FY26 real GDP growth at 7.4% and GVA growth at 7.3%, while the Survey assessed the economy's structural fundamentals as remaining strong for sustained medium-term performance.

On the demand side, Private Final Consumption Expenditure grew robustly at 7.0%, reaching 61.5% of GDP — the highest since 2012. Rural and urban consumption both contributed, driven by low inflation at a record 1.7%, stable employment, and increased purchasing power. Gross Fixed Capital Formation grew by 7.8%, maintaining its share at 30% of GDP.

India also established its first International Financial Services Centre to attract global capital, while the Survey recommended continued reforms to sustain growth momentum and build economic resilience.

clat-mock-20-p2.title: Severe El Niño
clat-mock-20-p2.text:
Climate variability has become one of the most significant challenges for governments, particularly those whose economies depend heavily on agriculture. Among the various climate systems influencing global weather, the El Niño–Southern Oscillation (ENSO) occupies a central place because of its far-reaching effects on rainfall, marine ecosystems, food production, and economic stability. Although ENSO originates in the tropical Pacific Ocean, its consequences are experienced across continents, influencing seasonal weather patterns in Asia, Africa, Australia, and the Americas.

Scientists rely on a combination of oceanic and atmospheric observations to monitor changes associated with ENSO. These include variations in sea surface temperatures, atmospheric pressure, wind circulation, and oceanic currents. Advances in satellite technology, climate models, and ocean-monitoring systems have considerably improved the ability to track these developments and issue seasonal forecasts, although predicting their exact regional impacts remains challenging.

Different phases of ENSO do not produce identical climatic outcomes. Researchers have identified multiple patterns within the phenomenon, each associated with distinct oceanic and atmospheric conditions. Consequently, the intensity and distribution of rainfall, agricultural productivity, fisheries, and temperatures may vary from one event to another. Since India's economy and food security remain closely linked with the performance of the southwest monsoon, developments in the Pacific Ocean continue to receive close attention from policymakers, farmers, economists, and disaster management authorities.

clat-mock-03-p2.title: A sombre shadow was cast over Indian aviation when an Air India Boeing 787
clat-mock-03-p2.text: Dreamliner, flight AI-171 bound for London Gatwick, crashed moments after takeoff in the Meghani Nagar area of Ahmedabad. The tragedy, which claimed the lives of 241 people, has reignited global scrutiny on Boeing, already reeling from the reputational damage of the 737 Max crisis. The aircraft involved had been in service since 2014. Aviation experts note that while the cruise phase constitutes the longest duration of a flight (57%), it accounts for less than 1% of fatalities. Conversely, the "Low and Slow" phasestakeoff and landingare the deadliest. IATA data indicates that over 50% of accidents occur during the landing phase alone. During takeoff, engines operate at maximum thrust, and the risk of a 'wing stall'where lift is lost due to a steep angle of attackis highest. Despite this incident, statistical trends from ICAO show that flying remains the safest mode of transport, with accidents per million departures dropping significantly over the last two decades due to advancements in carbon-fibre composite structures and rigorous safety protocols. (187 words)

clat-mock-28-p3.title: Remembering A Constitutional Crisis
clat-mock-28-p3.text: Constitutions are written against the memory of failure, and the Indian Constitution is no exception. It arms the Union with special powers intended for times of grave peril, yet it also assumes that such powers will be used sparingly and ended promptly. For about two years in the middle of the 1970s that assumption failed. The freedoms guaranteed by the Constitution were suspended on a vast scale: thousands of citizens — parliamentarians, journalists, students and workers — were detained without trial; the press was censored; the courts were pressed into acquiescence; Parliament was reduced to silence. What the framers had conceived as a last-resort fortress became the instrument of one party's rule. The memory of those years has been institutionalised. In the mid-2020s the government began observing a designated day each year, falling in the same season as the original events, to honour those who resisted and suffered and to pledge that such abuse never recur. Official programmes, exhibitions, publications and films mark the day, addressed by the country's most senior leaders. Opposition parties mark the same date in their own way, so the period has become a recurring touchstone of the country's political memory. The constitutional legacy is double-edged. One amendment, unmatched in sweep, recast the document's basic features; a corrective amendment under a successor government later restored much of what had been changed, narrowed the ground on which national power could be suspended, and returned legislatures to their ordinary terms. The detentions had rested on a preventive-detention statute long since repealed. Scholars debate whether the episode was an aberration of individuals or a warning about the fragility of legal safeguards. What is certain is that it remains the reference point for arguments about the limits of constitutional power.

clat-mock-33-p2.title: India to Assume Vice-Presidency of FATF for 1st Time
clat-mock-33-p2.text:
India has been chosen for the incoming vice presidency of the Financial Action Task Force (FATF), the global money laundering and terror financing watchdog. Vivek Aggarwal, a 1994-batch officer of the Indian Administrative Service (Madhya Pradesh cadre) and presently Secretary, Ministry of Culture, has been elected and appointed as the vice president of FATF from July 2026 to June 2027. This is the first time India will have a leadership position at the global body. The vice presidency for India also strengthens India’s chances for assuming the presidency role when the next switchover happens at the FATF after two years, officials said.

The FATF has 40 members, and over 200 jurisdictions have committed to the FATF recommendations through the FATF-style regional bodies. The FATF Presidency runs on a two-year term, and the vice-president assists the president in carrying out the organisation’s mandate. The Ministry of Finance in a statement released late Friday said that this decision marks a “landmark recognition” of India’s growing leadership in the global fight against money laundering and terrorist financing.

“The vice-president of the FATF is elected by the FATF Plenary from among its members and assists the president in steering the organisation’s work. The appointment places an Indian official at the apex of the global standard-setting body for anti-money laundering and counter-terrorist financing. India’s elevation to the vice- presidency reflects the credibility and trust the country has earned within the FATF Global Network of more than 200 jurisdictions,” the ministry said.

Extracted with edits and revisions https://indianexpress.com/article/business/india-fatf-vice-presidency-vivek- aggarwal-appointed-10748670/

clat-mock-39-p4.title: Greenland Issue & Arctic Governance
clat-mock-39-p4.text:
Greenland returned to the centre of international attention in 2026 as its geographical position, critical-mineral potential and importance to North Atlantic affairs generated renewed strategic interest. In September, the governments of the United States, Denmark and Greenland signed an agreement aimed at strengthening security cooperation in the Arctic and North Atlantic. The arrangement supplements an earlier defence framework and also addresses Greenlandic interests, sovereignty and self-determination. The development has also renewed discussion about the roles played by NATO, the Arctic Council and other mechanisms of regional cooperation. These institutions operate under different mandates and legal foundations, making Arctic governance an important subject in contemporary international relations. Climate change has added another dimension. Declining sea ice may affect shipping patterns, resource accessibility and scientific activity, while questions involving maritime boundaries and continental-shelf claims

bring the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS) into the debate. Comparisons with the legal arrangements governing Antarctica have consequently received greater attention. India also has a growing scientific interest in the region. Its Arctic research programme includes the Himadri research station, through which Indian researchers undertake studies relating to climate, atmosphere, glaciers and polar processes. The Greenland issue therefore brings together strategic competition, international law, scientific research, climate change and the evolving geopolitical importance of the polar regions.

clat-bootcamp-mock-01-p2.title: The 2026 Iran War — Decapitation & the Closed Strait (Hard Tier)
clat-bootcamp-mock-01-p2.text: At half past nine on the last Saturday morning of February 2026 — not under a concealing moon but in broad daylight, a choice as consequential as the ordnance — thirty precision munitions and air-launched ballistic missiles folded the Leader's House into rubble. The man who had ruled the Islamic Republic for thirty-seven years was found dead at his workplace, his death confirmed before midnight through tears on state television: forty days of mourning, a black flag over the shrine at Mashhad. Within hours, radio warnings crackled out to merchantmen off the Gulf: the waterway was shut. A council of three — the president, the chief justice, a jurist on loan from the electors' bench — held the tiller while the clerical electors, convening online under open threats that the victor and his choosers too would be hunted, took nine days to hand the republic. At sea, meanwhile, the decisive weapon proved to be paperwork: once war-risk underwriters walked away in early March, the strait remained legally open and effectively sealed; crude broke a hundred dollars within days and crested at levels unseen in four years, while mariners of fifty nations idled by the tens of thousands. A spring ceasefire briefly unlatched the gate — for a few hours one mid-April morning — until, the counter- blockade of Iranian ports persisting, it slammed shut again the next dawn, two Indian-flagged ships among those turned back under fire. A midsummer memorandum promised peace; yet by September, where a hundred hulls once passed daily, scarcely five did — some paying extravagant tolls — threading a narrow detour hugging the coast and a partner lane in Omani water. The world had suffered, said the energy watchers, the largest oil-supply disruption in market history.

clat-mock-30-p1.text:
Recasting India's Tribunal Architecture Tribunals occupy an unusual position in India’s constitutional and administrative landscape. They were created to provide specialised adjudication and, at least in principle, to reduce the pressure on conventional courts. Over time, however, their institutional design has generated a recurring debate: how can bodies performing adjudicatory functions remain sufficiently independent while also being administratively efficient and publicly accountable?

The latest legislative intervention seeks to address this tension by moving away from a framework in which important aspects of tribunal administration were closely connected with the executive. The reform attempts to create a more permanent institutional architecture for appointments, administration and oversight. It also reflects the judiciary’s continuing concern that the design of tribunals should not compromise principles associated with judicial independence and separation of powers.

The reform is significant for another reason. Instead of treating appointments, performance, complaints and administrative supervision as separate questions, it seeks to place them within a common institutional framework. At the same time, the proposed arrangement does not completely remove the executive from the system. Financial accountability, parliamentary oversight and certain governmental functions continue to have a role.

The legislation must therefore be viewed not simply as another attempt to reorganise tribunals, but as part of a longer institutional debate involving Parliament, the executive and the judiciary. Its success will ultimately depend on whether the new architecture can combine professional expertise, transparent appointments and institutional independence with timely adjudication and effective administrative functioning.

The broader question is consequently not whether tribunals should exist, but what institutional safeguards are necessary when adjudicatory power is exercised outside the ordinary court structure.

clat-mock-31-p4.title: The Anti-Paper Leak Law & Its 2026 Strengthening
clat-mock-31-p4.text:
Few pieces of legislation have travelled from cabinet table to both Houses of Parliament as quickly. Approved by the Union Cabinet on a Friday in late July 2026, circulated among Members the following day, introduced in the Lok Sabha on Monday by the Minister of State for Personnel, and passed by both Houses within the same week the amendment Bill was born of a crisis. Weeks of nationwide student protests over the alleged leak of a national medical entrance paper had already claimed a political casualty: the Education Minister had resigned, and his successor found himself defending the Bill through nearly eight hours of stormy debate, walkouts, and repeated adjournments in the Upper House.

The parent statute it amends is itself young enacted only in 2024, as India's first central law criminalising unfair means in public examinations, covering tests conducted by the major central recruitment and entrance bodies. But the events of 2026 convinced the government that its deterrents were too gentle. The amendment therefore raises the floor and the ceiling: for individuals, both the minimum and maximum terms of imprisonment go up, alongside a five-fold increase in fine; for organised examination crime, the minimum term is lengthened and the minimum fine multiplied ten-fold; for service providers — the companies that run centres, supply technology and manage logistics the maximum fine rises five-fold and the period of debarment from public examinations doubles.

Equally significant is the procedural machinery: investigations must now conclude within a fixed two-month timeline, Special Fast Track Courts are to be created for time-bound trials, and Special Task Forces will target organised syndicates. Critics in Parliament asked a harder question whether severity of punishment alone can secure what administration has failed to: the sanctity of the examination hall. After being passed by both Houses, the Bill received presidential assent in August 2026, bringing the strengthened framework into force.

clat-mock-40-p1.title: India’s Push Towards Ethanol Blending and Cleaner Mobility
clat-mock-40-p1.text: India’s transport-fuel policy has increasingly incorporated biofuels as part of a wider effort to diversify the country’s energy mix. Among the measures receiving sustained policy attention is the blending of ethanol with conventional petrol. The initiative has expanded progressively over the years, supported by changes in production capacity, fuel-distribution infrastructure and automobile standards. The transition involves several sectors simultaneously. Ethanol production depends on the availability of suitable domestic raw materials and sufficient processing capacity, while fuel suppliers must maintain prescribed quality and blending standards. At the same time, the automobile industry must ensure that vehicles placed on the market can operate efficiently with fuels containing a higher proportion of ethanol. These technical requirements have made coordination between government agencies, fuel companies, vehicle manufacturers and research institutions increasingly important. The policy also has wider economic implications. India remains heavily dependent on imported crude petroleum, making international price movements and supply disruptions important considerations in domestic energy planning. Greater use of alternative fuels is therefore viewed as one element of a broader strategy to improve resilience in the transport-energy sector. Parallel initiatives have also encouraged the development of newer generations of biofuels using technologies capable of converting different forms of biomass into usable energy products. These efforts seek to complement conventional fuel-blending programmes by encouraging innovation, investment and more efficient use of domestic resources. The expansion of ethanol-blended petrol thus reflects a broader transformation in India’s fuel policy, involving energy security, technological adaptation, domestic production and long-term changes in the transport sector. Its implementation continues to depend on coordination across multiple institutions and industries.

clat-mock-18-p1.title: India–Myanmar Relations: Strategic Imperatives and Emerging Challenges
clat-mock-18-p1.text:
Myanmar President U Min Aung Hlaing's recent visit to India has once again highlighted the strategic importance of India–Myanmar relations. As India's only ASEAN neighbour sharing a land border, Myanmar occupies a crucial position in India's Act East Policy and serves as a gateway connecting South Asia with Southeast Asia. Discussions during the visit focused on connectivity projects, border security, trade, energy cooperation, and regional stability.

The relationship is shaped by both opportunities and challenges. While India views Myanmar as essential for enhancing connectivity with ASEAN and developing its northeastern states, the political instability following the 2021 military coup has complicated bilateral engagement. Issues such as cross-border insurgency, refugee flows, narcotics trafficking, and China's growing strategic footprint in Myanmar continue to influence India's policy choices. At the same time, both countries cooperate on infrastructure development, defence coordination, and regional initiatives aimed at strengthening economic integration.

clat-mock-10-p1.text:
The National Quantum Mission represents a significant milestone in India’s quest to emerge as a key player in frontier technologies. Launched with an outlay of over ₹6,000 crore, the initiative seeks to build indigenous capabilities across quantum computing, communication, sensing, and materials development. By establishing specialized centres at premier academic institutions, the mission aims to foster an ecosystem that bridges fundamental research with practical applications in cryptography, healthcare, and climate modelling.

A notable development under this umbrella is the proposed Quantum Valley project in Andhra Pradesh, envisioned as a hub for cutting-edge research and industry collaboration. The project exemplifies a collaborative innovation model involving government, academia, and leading technology firms. It is expected to accelerate the development of scalable quantum processors, with ambitious targets for qubit systems in the coming years.

Complementing this, the government has partnered with global technology companies to provide researchers access to cloud-based quantum platforms, while simultaneously promoting domestic startups and indigenous language models. Earlier programmes such as QuEST have laid the groundwork, but the current mission adopts a more structured approach with clearly defined verticals and measurable outcomes.

Critics argue that success will depend on addressing challenges such as talent retention, adequate funding for basic research, and protection of intellectual property. Nevertheless, the mission aligns with India’s broader goal of technological self-reliance and positions the country to compete in the emerging quantum economy, where leadership in this domain could redefine global strategic balances in the coming decade.

clat-mock-26-p3.title: The Commonwealth Games
clat-mock-26-p3.text: The Commonwealth Games traces its roots to 1930. Originally styled as the British Empire Games, it was later renamed the Commonwealth Games and is today governed by the Commonwealth Games Federation. The closest edition, staged in a major Scottish city in 2026, was deliberately scaled down to a compact format of ten sports, dropping several disciplines that had appeared in earlier editions. A unicorn served as the official mascot, chosen in honour of the host nation's national animal. Competing against a much reduced roster that left out several of its strongest disciplines, the Indian contingent still delivered an efficient campaign, finishing in the middle of the leading pack with thirty-nine medals-thirteen gold, seventeen silver and nine bronze. A long-distance runner made history by becoming the first Indian to claim two medals in a single edition, and a weightlifter sealed three consecutive golds across as many Games. Looking ahead, the next edition, scheduled for 2030, is expected to celebrate the centenary of the event's founding and is set to be held in a country that hosted it once before, in its capital city.

clat-mock-28-p4.title: A Region Arranges Its Own Security
clat-mock-28-p4.text: West Asia is rearranging its own security. For decades the region's order rested on the promise of protection from a distant superpower, and much of it still does; but repeated rounds of escalation have made that promise look less dependable and have pushed several of its powers to hedge. The clearest expression of the mood came in 2026, when three regional states signed a joint defence agreement in the holy city of Makkah. The compact commits their armed forces to regular joint training and a structured exchange of intelligence and threat assessments — the machinery of closer military cooperation, not a declaration of war. The motives of the signatories are not identical, but they overlap. Attacks on shipping in the Red Sea, drone and missile fire that has exposed the limits of existing defences, and the fragility of the narrow sea passages through which the world's energy moves have fed a sense of exposure. One member, whose revenues rest heavily on energy exports, inward investment, tourism and an ambitious domestic transformation programme, has concluded that reliance on an outside patron is no longer enough and that independent defensive capability must be built. Analysts are careful, however, not to overstate the pact. Its operational provisions remain thin, its enforcement mechanisms unclear, and the alignments it creates cut across older rivalries in the region; it should therefore be read as a statement of intent rather than a formal treaty of the Western kind. Scepticism does not lessen its significance. The emergence of a self-arranged security compact among regional powers signals a slow shift in the balance of West Asia, and its consequences reach beyond the region — to India, whose energy security, defence exports, connectivity projects and standing in the Indian Ocean are all bound up in what happens there.

clat-mock-33-p0.title: Vande Mataram Bill passed
clat-mock-33-p0.text:
Parliament has passed the Prevention of Insults to National Honour (Amendment) Bill, 2026. Minister of State for Home Nityanand Rai  moved the bill to further amend the Prevention of Insults to National Honour Act, 1971. The legislation seeks to give Vande Mataram the same statutory protection as the national anthem, Jana Gana Mana. These offences are punishable with imprisonment up to three years, a fine, or both.

Earlier, replying to the discussion on the Bill, Minister of State for Home Nityanand Rai said, the bill is not merely a legislative amendment, but it represents India’s cultural heritage, national identity, and the ideals of the country’s freedom struggle. He said, in 1971, through the Prevention of Insults to National Honour Act, provisions were made to ensure respect for the National Anthem. The Minister said Vande Mataram is not just a song, but it is the voice of the nation’s soul. Mr Rai added the Vande Mataram song has been a source of inspiration for the country’s freedom fighters. He said, on 15th August 1947, Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel had asked Pandit Omkarnath Thakur to render the complete Vande Mataram on All India Radio at 6:30 in the morning, marking the beginning of the first Independence Day. The Minister said that through this bill, the ideals of unity, respect, and the immortal legacy of the nation’s freedom struggle will be further strengthened.

Participating in the discussion, K Kanimozhi of DMK opposed the legislation, claiming that the Bill divides people across the country. Supporting the bill, Sambit Patra of BJP said the legislation is very important. He said the central government is observing a year-long national commemoration for the 150th anniversary of the national song Vande Mataram from November last year. He said that through the bill, the Narendra Modi Government is giving legal protection to the National Song.

Extracted with edits and revisions from https://newsonair.gov.in/parliament-passes-bill-granting-vande- mataram-same-statutory-protection-as-national-anthem/

clat-aiom-mock-02-p0.text:
To align with its Net Zero 2070 targets, India has fundamentally overhauled its atomic energy governance. The President recently assented to the landmark SHANTI Act, a unified statute that ends the state’s long-standing monopoly and opens the sector to private capital and technology. This legislation replaces fragmented, Cold War-era laws that previously hindered capacity expansion.

A primary objective of the Act is to resolve the "Liability Dilemma" that deterred international suppliers. By restructuring liability norms to match global standards, the Act aims to facilitate the inflow of advanced technologies, particularly for Small Modular Reactors (SMRs).

Structurally, the Act addresses regulatory independence by granting statutory status to the Atomic Energy Regulatory Board (AERB), severing its subordination to the executive. It also streamlines dispute resolution by designating an existing appellate tribunal to adjudicate grievances. This legislative reform is synchronized with the Union Budget’s renewed focus on indigenous nuclear capabilities.

clat-mock-40-p3.title: 75 Years of India’s First Constitutional Amendment
clat-mock-40-p3.text: In 2026, India marked seventy-five years of its first amendment to the Constitution, an early intervention that continues to occupy an important place in debates on constitutional democracy. Adopted when the Constitution itself was barely a year and a half old, the amendment emerged from tensions between newly guaranteed fundamental rights and the social and economic policies being pursued by governments in the early years of the Republic. Several developments had brought these tensions into sharp focus. Courts were being called upon to examine restrictions imposed by the State, measures intended to benefit disadvantaged sections, and legislation designed to restructure agrarian relations. The Union government maintained that constitutional changes were necessary to ensure that elected governments retained sufficient space to pursue reform while operating within the framework of fundamental rights. The amendment consequently affected more than one field of constitutional governance. Its provisions had implications for freedom of expression, affirmative State action, economic regulation and land reform. Some of its innovations also sought to give specified legislation a degree of constitutional protection from fundamental- rights challenges. Its significance extended beyond the immediate policies of the 1950s. Soon after its enactment, its constitutional validity itself came before the Supreme Court, beginning a long judicial debate over Parliament’s power to amend the Constitution. In later decades, that debate would evolve considerably and become central to Indian constitutional law. [Adapted from the Statement of Objects and Reasons to the Constitution (First Amendment) Bill, 1951, and subsequent constitutional developments.]

clat-mock-26-p4.title: Komagata Maru Incident
clat-mock-26-p4.text: The incident involving a chartered steamship in the early twentieth century was a pivotal event in the global history of the Indian freedom struggle, highlighting the racial exclusion faced by Indian immigrants in British dominions and the subsequent radicalisation of transnational revolutionary movements. The vessel was chartered by a prominent activist to deliberately challenge exclusionary immigration laws. These regulations mandated that incoming immigrants arrive directly from their country of birth or nationality via a continuous journey on through-tickets. Because non-stop naval routes from India to North America were virtually non-existent, the law served as a hidden mechanism to restrict South Asian entry. Upon reaching its destination port in North America, the ship was denied permission to dock, and only a tiny fraction of passengers who could demonstrate previous legal residency were permitted to disembark. Local expatriate communities mobilized to form a dedicated body to offer relief and launch a legal battle, though local courts ultimately upheld the exclusionary mandates. The vessel was eventually forced to depart under armed naval escort. The crisis reached a tragic climax upon the vessel's return to India. When local colonial authorities attempted to restrict the passengers' movement, tensions escalated into open violence, resulting in multiple casualties and mass detentions. This confrontation acted as a major catalyst for overseas Indian revolutionaries, convincing many that constitutional agitation was ineffective and driving increased support for armed resistance against colonial rule.

clat-mock-17-p2.title: Remembering a Turning Point in Indian History
clat-mock-17-p2.text:
Recent discussions marking five centuries since a major military confrontation in northern India have renewed interest in the role of decisive battles in shaping political authority. Historians note that while battles often symbolize dramatic change, their long-term significance frequently lies in the administrative, military, and institutional transformations that follow rather than in the battlefield outcome itself.

The event has prompted renewed debate regarding the emergence of centralized political structures, the use of new military technologies, and the interaction between regional and transregional political traditions. Scholars have also emphasized the importance of examining historical events within their broader context, including patterns of state formation, revenue systems, elite alliances, and military organization.

The commemoration has encouraged reflection on how historical memory is constructed. Different communities and historians often interpret the same event through distinct lenses—viewing it as a military achievement, a dynastic transition, a technological turning point, or a moment within a larger process of political change. Consequently, contemporary discussions have focused not merely on the battle itself but on its wider historical consequences.

clat-mock-31-p2.title: India–UK Comprehensive Economic and Trade Agreement (CETA)
clat-mock-31-p2.text:
When the agreement finally entered into force on 15 July 2026, it ended a wait that had stretched across three British Prime Ministers and fourteen rounds of negotiations begun in January 2022. The pact itself had been signed almost a year earlier, during the Indian Prime Minister's visit to Britain, at the countryside retreat of his host — the two commerce ministers putting pen to paper as both leaders looked on, and a ten-year roadmap for the wider relationship was unveiled alongside.

India's Commerce Minister has called it the country's "most comprehensive" trade pact ever, and a "template" for those to come. The architecture explains the enthusiasm: nearly all of India's export lines enter Britain duty- free from day one, sweeping away the four-to-sixteen per cent handicap that Indian garments, footwear, carpets, marine and processed food products suffered against zero-duty competitors from Bangladesh, Pakistan and Cambodia an opening into a market worth over five hundred billion dollars, with bilateral trade, currently around fifty-six billion dollars, projected to double by the end of the decade.

Britain's prize lies in what India has historically defended hardest. Tariffs on its most celebrated spirit the bulk of which, ironically, is imported by Indian blenders themselves are halved at once, gliding down further over a decade above a minimum import price. For the first time in any Indian trade agreement, steep duty cuts were conceded on fully built foreign cars, though within calibrated quotas, and with electric vehicles shielded for the first five years. India also opened, for the first time, tens of thousands of high-value central government contracts to British bidders. Yet each side kept a jealously guarded exclusion list, and a companion convention on an entirely different subject travelled with the treaty into force the same day proof that modern trade deals are about far more than tariffs. (Extracted, with edits and revision, from reports of The Times of India, The New Indian Express and PIB, July 2026)

clat-additional-mock-01-p0.text: Debates surrounding the protection of women and children have significantly influenced the development of criminal and social laws in India. During British rule, efforts by the colonial administration to introduce social reforms often faced resistance from Indian political leaders and various social groups. A major example emerged in the late nineteenth century when the British government proposed legislation related to child marriage and the legally permissible age for marital relations. The proposal sparked widespread public controversy. Many social reformers supported the measure, considering it essential for the protection of young girls, while several nationalist leaders opposed it on the grounds that the colonial government should not interfere in the social traditions and religious practices of Indian society. This conflict highlighted the larger struggle between the need for social reform and opposition to colonial intervention. In present-day India, concerns regarding the safety and protection of minors have resulted in the introduction of specialised laws such as the Protection of Children from Sexual Offences Act, 2012, which establishes a detailed legal framework to deal with sexual crimes against children. However, the strict nature of this legal framework has increasingly become a subject of debate. In State of Uttar Pradesh versus Anurudh & Anr. (2026), the Supreme Court of India observed that the law is sometimes applied in cases involving consensual relationships between adolescents, especially when such relationships are opposed by families. The Court pointed out that although the legislation was intended to safeguard children from abuse and exploitation, it may also result in the criminalisation of consensual adolescent relationships in certain situations. This discussion reflects a broader challenge involving two important objectives: protecting children from sexual exploitation while also acknowledging the developing maturity and autonomy of adolescents. Policymakers, courts, and scholars continue to examine how these concerns can be balanced effectively while ensuring that the legal framework remains consistent with social realities and international standards relating to child rights.

clat-mock-03-p0.text:
In the wake of the recent Delhi bomb blast involving a medical professional, national security agencies have flagged the rise of a phenomenon now termed 'White-Collar Terrorism'. This disturbing trend, characterized by the weaponization of professional status for subversion, marks a resurgence of the foundational sociological concepts regarding crimes committed by individuals of high social respectability, which were first propounded in the 1930s. This shift has necessitated a significant overhaul of internal surveillance mechanisms to monitor high-risk professions.

Parallel to these internal security shifts, India’s foreign policy is undergoing a strategic recalibration. Due to the persistent obstructionism that has rendered SAARC initiatives ineffective, New Delhi is actively pivoting towards the BIMSTEC. This move aims to strengthen ties with eastern maritime neighbors while diplomatically isolating nations that utilize terror as state policy. Simultaneously, the government maintains a firm stance on territorial integrity and historical agreements. Security forces have intensified vigilance along the long-standing disputed 96-km estuary in the Rann of Kutch, which demarcates the boundary between the Indian state of Gujarat and the adjacent province of its western neighbor. Diplomatially, India has reiterated its commitment to the bilateral framework established in July 1972, which was signed in the aftermath of the war leading to the liberation of Bangladesh. Furthermore, to ensure energy and agricultural security, the administration has decided to fully exercise its rights under the Indus Waters Treaty of 1960, specifically accelerating projects to maximize the utilization of the 'Eastern Rivers' allocated for India’s unrestricted use.

clat-mock-23-p1.title: Constitutional Democracy and the Limits of Popular Will
clat-mock-23-p1.text: In a significant constitutional observation delivered recently, the Supreme Court reiterated that democratic governance cannot be reduced merely to the rule of the numerical majority. While elected governments derive legitimacy from the will of the people, the Court emphasized that constitutional democracies are founded upon principles that protect individual freedoms, institutional independence, and the rights of minorities irrespective of changing political preferences. According to the Court, public opinion, however overwhelming, cannot justify actions inconsistent with constitutional guarantees. The observations arose while the Court examined a challenge involving the relationship between governmental action and constitutional values. During the proceedings, the Bench highlighted that the Constitution establishes a framework in which every organ of the State is constrained by legal limitations, ensuring that political power remains accountable to constitutional norms rather than transient electoral mandates. Such limitations, the Court observed, preserve the balance between democratic governance and the rule of law. The judgment has renewed discussions on the distinction between electoral legitimacy and constitutional legitimacy. Constitutional experts note that while elections determine who governs, the Constitution determines how governance must be exercised. This distinction assumes particular significance in plural societies where competing social, religious, linguistic, and cultural identities coexist under a common constitutional framework. The observations also reinforce the continuing role of constitutional courts in reviewing legislative and executive action. Judicial review, separation of powers, and the protection of fundamental rights together function as institutional safeguards intended to prevent arbitrary exercise of authority while preserving democratic accountability within constitutional limits.

clat-mock-26-p0.title: Supreme Court of India — Judges, Jurisdiction and Constitutional Framework
clat-mock-26-p0.text: The constitutional design of India seeks to maintain an institutional balance among different organs of the State. The judiciary occupies a distinctive position within this framework because courts are entrusted not only with resolving disputes but also with interpreting constitutional provisions and protecting legally guaranteed rights. The higher judiciary therefore operates within a structure that combines judicial authority with safeguards intended to protect institutional independence. The Constitution establishes the Supreme Court as the highest judicial forum in the country and provides a framework concerning its composition, appointment of judges, conditions of service and jurisdiction. At the same time, several aspects of the Court's institutional functioning are capable of being regulated by Parliament through legislation. This arrangement allows the constitutional framework to remain relatively stable while permitting adjustments to respond to changing institutional requirements. Judicial independence does not imply that judges are beyond constitutional accountability. The Constitution establishes specific procedures concerning appointment, tenure and removal. These procedures are designed to prevent arbitrary interference while ensuring that constitutional office-holders remain subject to institutional checks. The process of appointment has also acquired a significant judicial dimension through constitutional interpretation over several decades. The jurisdiction of the Supreme Court is similarly diverse. It can adjudicate certain disputes involving constitutional entities, hear appeals from lower judicial and quasi-judicial bodies, and exercise powers intended to ensure substantial justice in appropriate cases. It may also perform an advisory function when constitutional conditions for seeking its opinion are fulfilled. The constitutional position of the judiciary must therefore be understood as a combination of authority and restraint.
