Courts exercise considerable powers, but these powers operate within procedures and institutional relationships established by the Constitution.

clat-mock-06-p3.text:
European integration is shaped by a combination of monetary coordination, treaty-based commitments, geographic realities, and security alliances. The countries that share the common European currency operate within a unified monetary framework governed by a central authority responsible for maintaining price stability, regulating liquidity, and guiding interest rate policy across participating states. This arrangement differs significantly from global financial institutions such as the International Monetary Fund and the World Bank, whose roles focus on international financial stability and development assistance rather than managing a regional currency.

The foundation of the Economic and Monetary Union was established through a landmark European treaty in the early 1990s, which introduced convergence standards and provided a structured path toward deeper economic integration. Subsequent treaty reforms strengthened coordination mechanisms within the European Union, enhancing institutional coherence without fundamentally altering the original monetary objectives.

In Southeast Europe, Bulgaria occupies a strategic position in the Balkan region, sharing borders with several neighboring states while remaining geographically distinct from others nearby. Beyond economic integration, the North Atlantic Treaty Organization reflects parallel patterns of cooperation, bringing together both EU and non-EU countries, under a shared security framework.

clat-mock-39-p3.title: India Australia Summit
clat-mock-39-p3.text:
India and Australia have steadily transformed their relationship from one centred largely on trade and education into a wider strategic partnership encompassing security, technology, energy and regional cooperation. Their latest annual summit reflected this evolution, with both sides seeking greater coordination in an Indo-Pacific increasingly shaped by supply-chain vulnerabilities, maritime security concerns and competition over critical technologies. Defence cooperation featured prominently. The two countries agreed to deepen operational coordination, information-sharing, military exchanges and defence-industrial collaboration. Maritime security received particular attention because both nations view secure sea lanes and adherence to international law as essential to regional stability. Cooperation now extends beyond bilateral exercises to capacity-building and coordination through regional institutions. Economic security formed another major pillar. The leaders discussed expanding bilateral trade, reducing non- tariff barriers and developing resilient supply chains for critical minerals and energy resources. Technology

cooperation was broadened to include cybersecurity, emerging technologies and trusted supply networks. Clean energy, renewable power and civil nuclear cooperation were also identified as important elements of long-term energy security. Education, skills, research and mobility continued to support strong people-to-people ties. The summit also highlighted growing cooperation in space, including support for India's human spaceflight programme, alongside new initiatives in sports and vocational training. The expanding agenda illustrates how India-Australia relations increasingly combine economic opportunity with strategic convergence. Their cooperation now operates bilaterally as well as through regional platforms, with both countries emphasising an open, stable and rules-based Indo-Pacific. Adapted from PIB and The Indian Express coverage of the 2026 India–Australia Annual Summit.

clat-additional-mock-01-p1.title: In January 2026, India and the European Union concluded a landmark Free Trade
clat-additional-mock-01-p1.text: Agreement after years of negotiations. The comprehensive deal represents one of the most ambitious trade openings undertaken by the EU in recent years, with significant implications for bilateral economic relations. The agreement establishes substantial tariff reductions across a wide range of goods, with elimination of duties on numerous industrial products. The deal is expected to generate significant annual savings for European exporters and create new opportunities for Indian businesses in the European market. The trade agreement addresses various sectors including automobiles, machinery, chemicals, and textiles. It includes provisions for addressing non-tariff barriers and establishing mechanisms for trade facilitation. The deal also incorporates safeguards and transition periods for sensitive sectors. Beyond tariffs, the agreement encompasses cooperation on digital trade, investment protection, and regulatory convergence. The framework establishes a foundation for deeper economic integration between the two major economies, with potential for significant expansion in bilateral trade volumes.

clat-mock-29-p4.title: Vikram-1 and India’s Private Space Launch Capability
clat-mock-29-p4.text: India’s space sector has witnessed rapid growth in private participation following reforms that opened several activities to non-governmental entities. This transformation has encouraged Indian start-ups to develop launch vehicles, satellites, propulsion systems and other space technologies, complementing the capabilities of the national space programme. A major milestone in this process came in July 2026, when a privately developed launch vehicle undertook its maiden orbital mission from an Indian launch facility. The mission successfully demonstrated the ability of an Indian private company to place payloads into Low Earth Orbit (LEO), marking an important step in the development of a commercially oriented launch ecosystem. The launch vehicle incorporates several advanced technologies aimed at reducing structural mass and improving manufacturing efficiency. Its design combines composite structures, solid propulsion and an additively manufactured liquid engine, reflecting the increasing use of innovative manufacturing techniques in India's private space industry. The maiden mission carried a range of payloads, including satellites and technology-demonstration experiments from different private-sector entities. These payloads illustrated the growing diversity of applications supported by small launch vehicles, including satellite deployment, technological experimentation and emerging orbital services. Beyond its technical objectives, the mission also carried symbolic elements intended to connect India's contemporary space ambitions with the country's scientific heritage. Such initiatives highlight the role of private space companies not merely in commercial launch services but also in promoting public engagement with science and India's broader space journey.

clat-mock-12-p1.title: ISRO
clat-mock-12-p1.text: Today, India stands at the forefront of the global space arena. This momentum becomes even more significant when we look at the ambitious roadmap laid out for the coming year. There was a time when space technology was restricted to a few nations. Today, India is not only mastering its own missions but becoming a trusted partner for the world. In this journey from being a participant to becoming a leader, the vision of Prime Minister Narendra Modi has played a major role. Today, you are taking 'Space Sector Reforms' from paper to reality. I have seen the confidence with which nine major launches are planned before the end of this financial year. On one hand is the reliability of our workhorse PSLV, while on the other hand is the power of the LVM3. Our LVM3 is continuously deploying satellites for the world. The collaboration with NASA, following the NISAR mission, and the launch of the Blue Bird Block2 for the USA, are indeed amazing. For the first time, a private industry consortium is realizing a launcher like the PSLV-N1. For the first time in the history of our space sector, the fruit of reform is visible where private industry will demonstrate more than 30 technologies, including electric propulsion and quantum communication. India has done the work of showing these capabilities to the world! All the scientists like you have done it. Today, the whole world is acknowledging the significance of India's manufacturing capability, our reform spirit, and our technological temperament. This surge in launches is a success not only for ISRO but for the entire nation.

clat-mock-32-p3.title: Foreign Contribution (Regulation) Amendment Bill, 2026
clat-mock-32-p3.text:
The Foreign Contribution (Regulation) Amendment Bill, 2026, proposes tighter rules for Indian organisations that receive foreign funds. The Bill seeks to change rules on registration, renewal and the handling of foreign- funded assets. It also proposes changes relating to organisations that receive foreign funds through the prior- permission route, the responsibilities of key functionaries and investigations into FCRA violations.

The Centre says the changes are meant to address gaps that have emerged in the administration of the existing law, improve transparency and ensure that foreign funds are used only for permitted purposes. But critics are concerned. Christian organisations, NGOs and minority groups fear that the new rules could increase paperwork and administrative demands. They also worry that officials may get wider powers to act against organisations and that mistakes or delays in compliance could have serious consequences for legitimate charitable and religious work.

The Bill was introduced in the Lok Sabha on March 25, 2026, and referred to a Joint Parliamentary Committee (JPC) on August 12 for examination. It is still under consideration. Separately, the revised FCRA Rules were notified on June 22 and are already in force. The Rules specify permitted purposes and States/Union Territories of operation, introduce new disclosure requirements and prescribe conditions for demonstrating reasonable activity.

Extracted with edits and revisions from https://www.newindianexpress.com/explainers/2026/Aug/24/fcra-bill- 2026-what-does-it-change-and-what-are-the-concerns

clat-mock-16-p3.title: New Series of GDP
clat-mock-16-p3.text:
The Ministry of Statistics and Programme Implementation (MoSPI) introduces a major structural revision to India's National Accounts by releasing a new Gross Domestic Product (GDP) series. In macroeconomics, periodic revisions of the benchmark timeline are essential to eliminate systemic measurement biases, clean out outdated data points, and capture structural shifts in consumer spending, industrial outputs, and informal sector contributions. The new series updates the central baseline from the outdated 2011–12 parameters to a more modern period, allowing policymakers to evaluate growth indicators against a post-pandemic economic landscape.

Methodologically, this revised framework introduces significant changes to data integration and inflation adjustment techniques. The updating of the series incorporates fresh, high-frequency datasets, including numbers from the Goods and Services Tax Network (GSTN), the Periodic Labour Force Survey (PLFS), and the Annual Survey of Unincorporated Sector Enterprises (ASUSE). This allows the state to better capture the output of informal workers and self-employed individuals. Furthermore, the updated series replaces aggregate-level price tracking with more granular, group-level indicators from the revised Consumer Price Index (CPI) and Wholesale Price Index (WPI) baskets. A key upgrade is the systemic adoption of techniques for specific sectors like manufacturing and agriculture, ensuring that changes in both input costs and output prices are independently adjusted for inflation. While these updates improve statistical accuracy, they present a major challenge for long- term historical comparison. To maintain a continuous timeline for econometric modeling, the government must reconstruct complex back-series data, translating past growth cycles into the newly established baseline without creating artificial statistical spikes.

clat-mock-06-p4.text:
Recent developments concerning the United States’ decision to withdraw from the World Health Organization have generated significant legal and constitutional debate. One of the primary concerns relates to unresolved financial obligations, as U.S. law ties participation in international bodies to the fulfillment of assessed contributions. Questions have therefore emerged about procedural compliance and whether all statutory requirements for withdrawal have been satisfied. The move was initiated through executive authority, sparking discussion over the balance of powers between the President and Congress in matters involving international institutional commitments.

The WHO, has long functioned as the central coordinating agency for global public health cooperation. Since its founding in 1948, it has led international campaigns on vaccination, disease surveillance, and health emergency response. One of its most notable historical achievements was the global elimination of a once-deadly infectious disease through coordinated immunization efforts, demonstrating the effectiveness of multilateral action. Each year, member states observe World Health Day to mark the establishment of the organization and to spotlight pressing global health priorities. These developments highlight the broader implications of shifting commitments within multilateral health governance frameworks.

clat-real-mock-01-p2.text: India’s grand geopolitical gambit, the India-Middle East-Europe Economic Corridor (IMEC), faces an existential crisis as regional volatility in West Asia indefinitely delays the rail-shipping network. Intended as a democratic counterweight to China’s Belt and Road Initiative (BRI), the project has hit a diplomatic wall with Saudi Arabia prioritizing immediate security concerns over long-term infrastructure integration. Compounding New Delhi’s woes, key European partner Greece has signaled a potential review of port logistics agreements, citing "fiscal realignment"—a move analysts suspect stems from subtle diplomatic pressure from Beijing. This double setback threatens Prime Minister Modi’s vision of India as a critical node in global supply chains, bypassing the traditional route. While the Ministry of External Affairs remains publicly optimistic, terming the delays "temporary operational pauses," internal reports suggest a scrambling for Plan B. The stalling of IMEC not only dampens India's trade aspirations but also exposes the fragility of US-backed minilateralism in a multipolar world. [Extracted from a Foreign Policy Analysis, October 15, 2025]

clat-mock-12-p0.title: 150 Years of Vande Mataram
clat-mock-12-p0.text:
On the 7th of November 2025, the Ministry of Culture organized the Inaugural Ceremony of the Commemoration of 150 Years of the National Song "Vande Mataram" at the Indira Gandhi Indoor Stadium in New Delhi. The occasion was graced by the Prime Minister Shri Narendra Modi as the Chief Guest, marking the formal launch of a year-long nationwide commemoration extending from 7th November 2025 to 7th November 2026. This event celebrated 150 years of the composition which inspired India's freedom movement and continues to evoke national pride. During that period, India was undergoing major social and political changes, and the song gave poetic expression to India's awakening spirit of unity. It was later published as a book in 1882. Dr. Rajendra Prasad, President of the Constituent Assembly, declared that "Vande Mataram" shall be accorded equal honour with the National Anthem.

The celebrations commenced at 10:00 AM with a Mass Singing of the full version of "Vande Mataram" spread across public places, involving all citizens, school children, officials, and stakeholders across all segments of society. In recognition of its historic importance, the Union Cabinet had approved the nationwide celebrations on 1st October 2025, and the year-long commemoration was subsequently approved by the National Implementation Committee on 24th October 2025. The salient features of the inaugural ceremony included a Cultural Programme, a Curated Exhibition tour on the history of the song, and a Concert on Culture Stage featuring approximately 75 musicians conducted by Violin Maestro Dr. Manjunath Mysore. A short documentary film was screened, and a Commemorative Stamp and Coin were released. All States and Union Ministries organized Mass Singing at 10:00 AM on 7th November 2025 at their respective premises, synchronised with the inaugural ceremony. A dedicated campaign website was launched wherein citizens were encouraged to participate in "Karaoke with Vande Mataram" and upload their own rendition of the song to express their devotion to the Motherland.

clat-mock-25-p3.text:
Political Stability and the Constitutional Framework Against Defection Representative democracy depends not only upon periodic elections but also upon the continued accountability of elected representatives to constitutional institutions and democratic principles. In parliamentary systems, frequent changes in party allegiance by legislators can affect governmental stability, legislative functioning and public confidence in the electoral process. To address such concerns, constitutional mechanisms have evolved to regulate circumstances under which legislators may lose their membership after changing political affiliations or acting contrary to prescribed legislative norms. The constitutional framework governing such matters seeks to balance two competing objectives. On the one hand, political parties require discipline to ensure that governments function effectively and legislative commitments made before elections are respected. On the other hand, democratic governance also recognises that legislators may, in exceptional circumstances, exercise independent judgment or participate in legitimate political realignments. Consequently, the law distinguishes between ordinary changes in political allegiance and certain institutional situations recognised under constitutional provisions. The authority to decide disputes arising under these provisions is ordinarily exercised within the legislature itself. However, constitutional experts have observed that decisions affecting the

membership of elected representatives involve questions extending beyond internal legislative procedure. As a result, courts have repeatedly examined the extent to which constitutional principles such as the rule of law, fairness and judicial oversight apply while respecting the autonomy of legislative institutions. The operation of these constitutional safeguards has generated continuing public debate. Some scholars argue that strict anti-defection rules strengthen stable governments by discouraging opportunistic political behaviour. Others contend that excessive party control may reduce the independence of legislators and weaken deliberative democracy by limiting dissent within political parties. Recent discussions have therefore focused on whether existing constitutional provisions appropriately balance political stability with democratic accountability and representative autonomy.

clat-mock-11-p1.title: Removal of CEC
clat-mock-11-p1.text: Constitutional provisions safeguarding the independence of electoral oversight bodies have drawn renewed parliamentary attention, with opposition mobilization seeking to initiate formal removal proceedings against current officeholders through mechanisms requiring rigorous evidentiary standards equivalent to those applied to judicial removals. Article 324's framework ensures that electoral commissioners can only be displaced through address-based proceedings in either legislative chamber, with threshold requirements of fifty members in the upper house or one hundred in the lower house, thereby insulating the institution from executive caprice. This procedural architecture mirrors the removal mechanisms for superior court judges under Article 124, reflecting the constitutional vision of electoral integrity as foundational to democratic legitimacy. Historical precedents reveal sporadic attempts to initiate such proceedings, though none have culminated in successful removal, underscoring the high evidentiary burden of proving misbehavior or incapacity. The current controversy involves allegations of electoral management irregularities in subnational jurisdictions, with opposition parties gathering signatures to formalize impeachment-style motions. Constitutional scholars emphasize that such procedural safeguards, while protecting institutional autonomy, also risk creating accountability gaps when commissioners face credible allegations of partisan bias. The debate illuminates persistent tensions between independence and accountability in electoral governance, with proposals for reform ranging from fixed tenure modifications to enhanced transparency in decision-making processes.

clat-mock-17-p3.title: Artificial Intelligence and Public Decision-Making
clat-mock-17-p3.text:
Governments around the world are increasingly exploring the use of artificial intelligence to improve public administration, policy implementation, and service delivery. AI systems are being deployed to process large datasets, assist in classification tasks, improve information retrieval, and support evidence-based decision- making. Advocates argue that such technologies can reduce administrative burdens, improve efficiency, and enhance the accessibility of public services.

At the same time, concerns remain regarding transparency, accountability, bias, and the quality of data used by AI systems. Policymakers have emphasized that technological tools should complement rather than replace human judgment, particularly in contexts where decisions may significantly affect individuals or communities. Experts have also highlighted the need for robust governance frameworks to ensure that innovation remains consistent with democratic values and public trust.

The growing use of AI in governance has generated broader discussions regarding data infrastructure, digital public goods, and the role of technology in strengthening state capacity. As governments continue to adopt new technologies, the challenge lies in balancing efficiency and innovation with safeguards that protect fairness, reliability, and accountability.

clat-mock-20-p1.title: Right to be Forgotten
clat-mock-20-p1.text:
The increasing digitisation of judicial records has transformed public access to legal information. Court judgments, orders, and case details that were once available only through physical archives are now searchable online, making them accessible to a far wider audience. While this development has improved transparency and strengthened public confidence in the administration of justice, it has also created new concerns regarding the long-term availability of personal information in the digital domain.

The Right to Informational Privacy, recognised by the Supreme Court judgment, affirms that individuals possess a legitimate interest in controlling the collection, use, and dissemination of personal information relating to them. As digital technology enables judicial records to remain permanently accessible through search engines and online databases, questions increasingly arise about whether continued public availability of such information always serves a legitimate purpose.

These concerns recently came before the Delhi High Court, which examined the tension between the permanent digital accessibility of court records and an individual's privacy interests. The Court observed that merely updating judicial records may not adequately protect privacy, since search engines can continue to display outdated or incomplete information even after subsequent judicial developments. Consequently, the Court emphasised that the issue extends beyond the accuracy of official records to the manner in which such records are discovered and presented in the digital environment. The Court further noted that the mere availability of judicial records does not necessarily require that every case should be readily discoverable through a simple search of an individual's name. Instead, it highlighted the distinction between preserving authentic public records and ensuring that digital search mechanisms do not disproportionately prejudice individuals by presenting incomplete or outdated information. To address these concerns, the Court suggested that judicial records should remain publicly accessible while also ensuring that significant subsequent developments are prominently reflected in digital databases. It further stressed the need for courts and online platforms to regularly update searchable records so that public access to judicial information remains accurate, contextual, and consistent with constitutional values. In doing so, the Court sought to protect individual privacy without compromising the integrity and accessibility of the judicial record.

clat-mock-08-p4.text:
The Global Risks Report 2026 presents an assessment of emerging challenges shaping national and global stability. It examines short-term and long-term threats across economic, technological, environmental, and geopolitical domains. The report highlights how risk perceptions vary between countries and at the global level, reflecting differences in exposure, preparedness, and strategic priorities. Technological vulnerabilities, geoeconomic tensions, and security-related concerns feature prominently in the evolving risk landscape.

India’s expanding digital infrastructure and rapid adoption of online services have increased the importance of cybersecurity resilience. The country faces a dynamic cyber threat environment involving multiple forms of malicious digital activity targeting institutions, businesses, and individuals. The growing scale and sophistication of cyber incidents underline the need for coordinated response mechanisms and capacity building. International cooperation remains central to addressing cybercrime, with global agreements seeking to harmonize legal frameworks and enhance cross-border investigative collaboration. Domestically, India has developed a multi-agency cybersecurity architecture involving specialised bodies responsible for incident response, infrastructure protection, cybercrime coordination, and defence preparedness.

The World Economic Forum, known for fostering public–private cooperation, publishes several influential global reports that shape policy discourse. These assessments contribute to informed decision-making in areas of economic stability, technological governance, and global risk management.

clat-mock-04-p4.text:
The global sporting community recently turned its eyes toward South Asia as the Commonwealth Sport General Assembly formally approved the host for the 2030 edition of the games. This upcoming event holds immense historical weight as it commemorates exactly one hundred years of the Commonwealth movement’s sporting tradition. The decision followed a rigorous selection process where the eventual winner was chosen over a competing bid from Abuja, Nigeria, which has instead been offered consideration for the 2034 cycle.

The successful bid process, initiated with an Expression of Interest in March 2025 and culminating in formal Cabinet approval in August, highlighted a shift in the nation's sporting strategy. The chosen venue city is being positioned as a world-class sporting hub, leveraging massive existing infrastructure such as the world’s largest cricket stadium and the developing Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel Sports Enclave. Planners have also outlined a dedicated Athletes’ Village capable of housing approximately 3,000 participants, ensuring a compact and efficient experience for visiting delegations.

A key aspect of this hosting rights victory is the proposed evolution of the sports programme. While core disciplines like Athletics, Swimming, Gymnastics, and Boxing remain central, the 2030 edition aims to blend modern popularity with cultural heritage. There is a strong push to integrate Para sports fully into the main schedule, covering Para Athletics, Swimming, and Powerlifting. Furthermore, the host nation is advocating for a mix of globally popular team sports—specifically the T20 format of cricket—alongside traditional regional games that reflect its rich cultural history, aiming to elevate them to international recognition.

This will be the second time the nation has welcomed the Commonwealth fraternity, the first being the 2010 edition held in its capital. That previous event is widely remembered for marking the country's peak performance in the medal tallies, setting a benchmark that subsequent contingents, such as the one at Birmingham 2022 have strived to emulate. The 2030 games are expected to build on traditional strengths in disciplines like shooting, wrestling, and weightlifting, while showcasing the country's growing capabilities in managing mega-events.

clat-mock-19-p3.title: India–Nepal Relations: New Momentum Amid Old Challenges
clat-mock-19-p3.text: Prime Minister of India and the Prime Minister of Nepal recently held bilateral talks in New Delhi focusing on economic cooperation, connectivity, energy security and regional stability. Both leaders reviewed progress under various infrastructure projects and emphasized the importance of people-to-people ties. They also discussed avenues for strengthening cooperation in digital payments, cross-border transport and renewable energy. The leaders reiterated their commitment to maintaining close coordination in regional and multilateral forums and agreed to enhance institutional mechanisms for addressing outstanding issues. The visit comes amid evolving geopolitical dynamics in the Himalayan region and renewed emphasis on connectivity and economic integration across South Asia. Both sides expressed confidence that stronger cooperation would contribute to prosperity, stability and sustainable development in the region.

clat-mock-12-p2.title: Israel –Iran Conflict
clat-mock-12-p2.text:
Following months of escalating tensions over Iran's nuclear programme and its support for regional proxy forces, the United States and Israel launched a coordinated military campaign against Iran, striking missile infrastructure, military installations, and senior leadership across the country. Within a week of the war's commencement, sustained aerial bombardment and active suppression efforts reduced Iran's missile attack capacity by approximately 90 percent, while the United States military claimed to have neutralised over 90 percent of Iran's naval fleet through direct strikes. Israel's forces killed more than 250 Iranian leaders, including the country's Supreme Leader and nearly the entirety of its senior military command — a scale of leadership elimination unprecedented in modern warfare. The United States designated its nuclear-site targeting operations under the codename Operation Midnight Hammer (June 2025), upon which Operation Epic Fury (February– April 2026), the broader military campaign, subsequently built.

Iran, unable to match conventional military superiority, pursued an asymmetric counter-strategy centred on economic disruption and alliance fracture. Tehran's closure of the Strait of Hormuz — a chokepoint carrying approximately a fifth of global oil supply — drove energy and fertiliser prices to levels not seen since 2022, straining economies from Southeast Asia to Australia to Europe and threatening to tip the global economy toward recession. Simultaneously, Iranian strikes on Gulf states hosting American military installations killed dozens, damaged major industrial sites, and eroded the region's reputation as a stable commercial environment. Despite the regime having survived a period of violent domestic repression in which thousands of protesters were killed, and despite the battlefield decimation of allied groups including Hezbollah and the Houthis, Tehran maintained governmental continuity — demonstrating that military attrition alone cannot guarantee the regime change that American strategic objectives had identified as among their most ambitious targets.

clat-mock-41-p0.text: In March 2026, the Supreme Court of India delivered a significant judgment in Harish Rana v. Union of India, bringing renewed attention to the constitutional and medical questions surrounding passive euthanasia and end-of-life care. Rana had remained in an irreversible vegetative condition for several years following a severe brain injury. His family approached the courts seeking legal permission concerning the continuation of medical interventions sustaining him. The case required the Supreme Court to examine its earlier jurisprudence on the right to die with dignity and the procedural safeguards governing withdrawal or withholding of life- sustaining treatment. A central issue concerned Clinically Assisted Nutrition and Hydration (CANH) and whether such intervention could fall within the category of medical treatment for the purposes of the existing passive-euthanasia framework. The Court also considered the principle of the “best interests of the patient”, particularly where the patient lacked the capacity to communicate an informed choice. The proceedings also highlighted the importance of medical boards, family consultation, advance medical directives and institutional safeguards in decisions involving end-of-life care. Following the Court's directions, Rana was placed under specialised care at AIIMS, New Delhi. The judgment consequently became an important development in the practical implementation of India's evolving legal framework governing patient autonomy, dignity and withdrawal of life- sustaining medical treatment.

clat-mock-31-p5.title: The Aravalli Ruling Defining a Mountain to Save It
clat-mock-31-p5.text:
How high must a hill be before the law will protect it? That deceptively simple question reached the Supreme Court because India's oldest mountain chain — a weathered spine of rock older than the Himalayas by well over a billion years — had for decades been governed by a patchwork of definitions across the states it traverses. In November 2025, a Bench headed by the then Chief Justice of India accepted a uniform, elevation-based formula proposed by a committee led by the Union Environment Ministry: a landform would qualify as a hill of the range if it rose at least one hundred metres above the surrounding local terrain, and two or more such hills within five hundred metres of each other would together constitute the range. One state, interestingly, had been following a similar height criterion since 2006.

The Court refused to impose a blanket ban on mining, reasoning as it had in an earlier judgment of 2021 that outright prohibition breeds illegality rather than protection. Instead, it froze all new mining leases until a comprehensive Management Plan for Sustainable Mining is prepared by a designated forestry research body, modelled on the plan earlier created for a forest in Jharkhand. Exceptions were carved for minerals bearing on strategic and national interests. The Court underscored what was at stake: the range is a green barrier holding back the eastward creep of a great desert, and a lung for the national capital region.

Then came the storm. Critics alleged the height threshold would strip protection from the vast majority of the range's lower hillocks, dismantling safeguards traceable to a 1992 notification. Within weeks, the Court took suo motu cognisance of the row, constituted a fresh expert body, and the Union ministry directed states to ban new leases across the entire landscape. In September 2026, the Court refused that body more time, demanding its report by the end of November.

clat-mock-35-p2.title: The "Creamy Layer" Concept in SC/ST Reservations
clat-mock-35-p2.text: The reservation debate travels in circles, but every few decades the circle widens. The doctrine of the "creamy layer" was born in the early nineties, when a nine-judge bench upheld job and college quotas for the Other Backward Classes and, in the same breath, ruled that the socially and economically advanced among them must be skimmed off the beneficiaries' list. For three decades that sieve filtered only OBC lists; the Scheduled Castes and Tribes stood apart, treated since a 2004 pronouncement as single, indivisible classes whose internal fortunes only Parliament could re-sort. That changed on the first of August two years ago, when a bench of seven judges declared — six voices strong — that States may slice the SC and ST quotas internally, prioritising the most backward among the backward, provided the carve-up rests on quantifiable, demonstrable data and not political whimsy. No sub-caste may swallow the whole pie; the Presidential lists themselves remain untouched. But it was a rider that set Delhi abuzz: one judge, himself from the community, asked whether a child in an elite metropolitan school and an elite college could honestly be bracketed with a child in a remote village school — and answered that the prosperous must step aside. Another pressed that benefits should end with the first generation to rise. The lone dissenter warned that State legislatures were creeping onto Parliament's turf over the designated lists, which only the Centre could define. Two monsoons later, the argument has sharpened again. Before a fresh larger bench weighing implementation, the Union has insisted that prosperity does not launder away the stigma of caste — that, whatever the judges mused, no "creamy layer" can legally be carved out of these communities. Meanwhile, one southern State has already written internal quotas into its statute book, and others are busy counting their castes.

clat-mock-13-p4.title: EL NINO
clat-mock-13-p4.text:
The El Niño-Southern Oscillation (ENSO) cycle represents one of the most consequential drivers of inter-annual climate variability, with cascading effects spanning oceanography, agriculture, hydrology, and energy systems across multiple continents. The phenomenon emerges from complex interactions between the surface temperatures of the equatorial Pacific Ocean and the atmospheric circulation systems that govern global weather distribution. These interactions operate through feedback mechanisms that can amplify or suppress regional precipitation, temperature anomalies, and storm activity with significant economic and ecological consequences.

The Peruvian coastal fisheries and associated marine ecosystems are among the most sensitive indicators of ENSO shifts, with changes in ocean surface conditions directly affecting the biological productivity of one of the world's most commercially significant fishing zones. In the Indo-Pacific region, ENSO cycles influence the timing, intensity, and geographic distribution of seasonal precipitation, with consequences for agricultural planning, reservoir management, and food security systems. Across the Americas, the redistribution of atmospheric moisture associated with these cycles produces markedly contrasting conditions — prolonged water deficits in some zones and dangerous precipitation surpluses in others.

The thermohaline circulation — the deep ocean conveyor system driven by differences in water density — interacts with surface ENSO dynamics in ways that climate scientists continue to study. The Southern Oscillation Index (SOI), measured as the pressure differential between Darwin, Australia and Tahiti, serves as the primary atmospheric indicator used by meteorological agencies to monitor and forecast the progression of ENSO cycles and their downstream regional impacts.

clat-mock-26-p2.title: Uttarakhand Becomes India’s Sixth Fully Literate State
clat-mock-26-p2.text: Uttarakhand has achieved an important milestone in adult education by becoming the sixth state in India to be declared fully literate under the country’s national adult literacy initiative. The achievement reflects the state’s efforts to provide learning opportunities to adults who were unable to acquire adequate education through the formal schooling system. The initiative adopts a broader understanding of literacy. Rather than limiting literacy to the ability to read and write, it seeks to develop foundational learning, numeracy and practical skills that enable adults to participate more effectively in everyday social and economic activities. Digital and financial awareness are also important components of this broader approach. The programme relies on the participation of volunteers, educators, local institutions and communities to identify learners and support their learning. Technology is used to facilitate registration, provide learning resources and monitor progress. The declaration of a state as fully literate is based on measurable learning outcomes, rather than simply counting the number of people enrolled in literacy programmes. This makes the achievement an indicator of actual progress in foundational learning. Uttarakhand’s achievement is significant in the wider context of India’s efforts to reduce adult illiteracy and expand opportunities for lifelong learning. It demonstrates how community participation, institutional support and technology-enabled education can contribute to improving literacy outcomes among adults who were previously excluded from formal education.

clat-mock-32-p4.title: Parliament Passes Bill to Rename Kerala as Keralam
clat-mock-32-p4.text:
The Parliament has passed the Kerala (Alteration of Name) Bill, 2026, with the Rajya Sabha approving it today. The Lok Sabha had passed the legislation yesterday. The Bill seeks to change the name of the state of Kerala to Keralam in the First Schedule of the Constitution.

Replying to a debate on the Bill, Minister of State for Home Nityanand Rai said the Kerala Legislative Assembly had passed a resolution in 2024, requesting the Centre to change the name of the State from Kerala to Keralam. He said the request in this regard was made because the name of the State in Malayalam is Keralam, while in the Constitution, it is written as Kerala. The Minister said that the Union Cabinet in February this year approved the proposal to change the name of the state to Keralam and to introduce the necessary legislation for amendment in this regard. He said the Union Government brought the Kerala (Alteration of Name) Bill, 2026 in the Parliament to honour the State’s request. Earlier, participating in the discussion, Tarun Chugh of BJP said the motto of this bill is to change the name from Kerala to Keralam and to erase the signs of slavery and restore the glory.

Jyoti Waghmare of Shiv Sena said the name is the first identity of any person or place and renaming Kerala to Keralam is a way to honour the Malayalam language. Participating in the discussion, Union Minister Suresh Gopi said, passage of the Bill is a celebratory moment for over four crore Malayalis around the globe. He alleged that in the presence of Congress and CPI (M) Members, the Bill was not allowed to be discussed in the Lok Sabha.

Extracted with edits and revisions from https://newsonair.gov.in/bill-altering-name-of-state-of-kerala-to- keralam-gets-nod-from-parliament/

clat-mock-05-p4.text:
Nipah virus outbreaks have periodically raised serious public-health concerns in South and Southeast Asia due to their high fatality rates and the absence of a definitive cure or widely available vaccine. The disease first gained international attention in the late 1990s and has since been associated with sporadic but severe outbreaks, often placing significant strain on local healthcare systems.

Public health investigations have shown that outbreaks frequently emerge in regions where human populations interact closely with animals and natural ecosystems. Factors such as changing land-use patterns, agricultural practices, and food-handling behaviors have been examined to understand how initial infections occur. Once cases appear, authorities focus on isolation, contact tracing, and community awareness to prevent further spread.

Clinically, the infection can progress rapidly, with symptoms ranging from fever and respiratory distress to acute neurological complications. In some outbreaks, secondary transmission among humans has been reported, highlighting the need for strict infection-control measures in healthcare settings. At the same time, scientists continue to study the virus’s biological characteristics to better understand its behavior, evolution, and potential for future outbreaks.

The recurrence of Nipah virus outbreaks underscores the broader challenge posed by zoonotic diseases and reinforces the importance of surveillance, early detection, and coordinated public-health responses to emerging infectious threats.

clat-mock-09-p0.title: India's Mineral Security and Strategic Resource Diplomacy
clat-mock-09-p0.text:
India's rapidly growing economy demands secure and diversified access to critical and strategic minerals essential for its clean energy transition, defence manufacturing, and industrial expansion. The country has emerged as a significant global player in mineral production, ranking among the top producers of key minerals including iron ore and aluminium, while simultaneously grappling with import dependence for several critical minerals vital for emerging technologies like electric vehicle batteries.

India's minerals diplomacy has evolved into a comprehensive strategy spanning the entire mineral value chain. This approach encompasses both domestic reforms and international partnerships, with bilateral memoranda and joint ventures established with multiple nations to promote collaborative extraction in third countries, building diversified supply chains that reduce concentration risks.

Domestically, the government has introduced significant legislative amendments to streamline the auctioning process for strategic minerals, ensuring transparent and efficient resource allocation. The revival of domestic smelting and refining capacity has shown promising results, with certain metals recording sharp production increases in recent fiscal years.

India's mineral security strategy is intrinsically linked to its climate commitments, announced at the COP26 Glasgow Summit in November 2021, which require massive deployment of mineral-intensive clean energy technologies.

clat-mock-27-p1.title: India's 100th Ramsar Site & The Ramsar Convention
clat-mock-27-p1.text: In 2026, India crossed a symbolic conservation milestone when the Prime Minister announced, that a bird sanctuary in a north-Indian state had been designated as the country's hundredth Ramsar site. The wetland, named after a local lake and home to rich avifaunal diversity attracting numerous migratory and resident birds, became the entry that took India's tally into three figures. Shortly afterwards, the count rose again when a lake in a hill state in the far north-east — the first wetland of that state to earn the designation — was added, taking the national total past one hundred. The Ramsar Convention, under which such sites are designated, is an international treaty for the conservation and sustainable use of wetlands, signed in a city of the same name in the early 1970s. India became a party to the treaty in 1982, and its network of designated wetlands has since grown from a handful of sites to become the largest such network in Asia and the third-largest in the world. The sites span everything from high-altitude Himalayan lakes and coastal mangroves to human-made reservoirs and bird sanctuaries. India's largest designated wetland is a vast mangrove ecosystem on the eastern coast, home to a famous tiger population. Several of the sites lie along a major migratory-bird flyway, and a few are listed on a special register of wetlands facing significant ecological stress.

clat-bootcamp-mock-01-p3.title: The Indus Waters Treaty — Abeyance and the Hague Answer
clat-bootcamp-mock-01-p3.text: When the boundary commission's pencil crossed Punjab, it severed barrages from the canals they fed: on an April day a year after independence, the upper riparian simply turned the water off, and a dominion's fields stood dry until an accord restored the flow — for a fee. Nine years of shuttling by a Washington development lender produced a signature in a port city on the Arabian Sea — a prime minister's handshake with a uniformed president. The bargain gave four-fifths of the flow, with the three western arteries, to the lower riparian; India took the three eastern rivers outright, yet kept a riverbanker's licence upstream — drink, modest fields, wheels that turn but may not store recklessly. A commission of two kept the ledger; technical grumbles climbed to a neutral engineer, legal quarrels to a court of arbitrators. It survived two wars, a mountain conflict and countless squabbles — the rivers kept their calendar while soldiers kept theirs. The strain came first as rhetoric, then as paperwork: a mid-winter notice in 2023 seeking renegotiation — two dispute processes, it complained, were being run at cross-purposes. Then a spring afternoon in a Kashmir meadow, bullets for unarmed tourists, and the next dawn the treaty was declared 'in abeyance' — a condition, the lender's chief said, nowhere found in its text. 'Circumstances have changed,' came the retort, 'beyond anything the signatories imagined.' The sequel unfolded at the Peace Palace. In March 2026 the lower riparian asked whether the treaty still lived; hearings ran in April, one chair empty. On August's last day, five arbitrators answered unanimously: the text lives, it knows no abeyance, and concrete on a Kishtwar dam wall must pause beyond specified heights until the technical expert's verdict. The empty chair called the court illegally constituted, its award void. The river, indifferent, kept flowing.

clat-aiom-mock-01-p0.text: The geopolitical tapestry of Asia is currently witnessing a complex interplay of historical grievances and modern economic pragmatism. As New Delhi and Beijing prepare to commemorate a Diamond Jubilee milestone in their diplomatic history, the relationship remains defined by a duality of friction and interdependence. On one hand, strategic anxieties persist, fueled by Beijing's assertive territorial concepts—such as the doctrine that views a specific autonomous region as a "palm" with five peripheral "fingers" to be liberated—and its dominance in critical supply chains, specifically the processing of minerals essential for high-tech industries. This has compelled India to deepen security architectures with like-minded maritime democracies in the Indo-Pacific. On the other hand, economic imperatives are driving a rethink. Recent high-level policy documents have advocated for decoupling from security concerns to attract foreign direct investment into India’s secondary sector, aiming to replicate the export-led growth model of its neighbor. This contemporary calibration echoes a much older tradition of exchange, reminiscent of the era when scholars and monks—not armies—traversed the Himalayas, fostering a civilizational dialogue between the courts of Kannauj and the monasteries of the East. The challenge now lies in navigating this "Dragon- Elephant" dynamic without compromising strategic autonomy.

clat-mock-04-p3.text:
In the final week of November 2025, world leaders gathered in a vibrant Amazonian city for the landmark 30th climate conference, exactly ten years after the historic Paris accord. The choice of venue itself sent a powerful message: the talks were happening in the lungs of the planet.

Throughout the fortnight, delegates repeatedly spoke of moving from grand promises to actual delivery, from words to measurable action. The host nation steered discussions with remarkable inclusivity, earning praise from developing countries for keeping fairness and historical responsibility at the heart of every negotiation.

India’s voice was particularly forceful on the need for real money – not loans disguised as aid – flowing from those who polluted first and prospered most. On the domestic front, one of India’s original 2030 pledges had already been met well ahead of time, a fact quietly celebrated in the corridors. A central outcome of the negotiations was the Global Mutirão Agreement, which prioritized deliverability and shared responsibility over the setting of new, loftier targets that nations might struggle to meet.

Even as ministers raced against the clock, an unforeseen emergency on the second-last day forced everyone to evacuate the main hall. Yet, the conference refused to break – it simply carried on, stronger and more determined than before.

When the final gavel fell, the world had not signed a dramatic new treaty, but something perhaps more valuable: a shared resolve to finally do what was promised a decade ago.

clat-mock-39-p1.title: Supreme Court (Number of Judges) Amendment Bill, 2026
clat-mock-39-p1.text:
Parliament’s decision in 2026 to expand the sanctioned judicial strength of the Supreme Court reopened a wider debate about institutional capacity, case pendency and the constitutional role of the country’s highest court. The government argued that additional judicial capacity could help the Court manage its growing docket and enable larger Benches to sit more regularly without excessively disrupting ordinary appellate work. The Supreme Court performs several functions simultaneously. It decides constitutional questions while also hearing civil and criminal appeals, writ petitions, special leave petitions and other matters. Constitution Benches

require several judges to sit together, temporarily reducing the number available for smaller Benches. Consequently, increasing judicial strength may give the Chief Justice greater flexibility in constituting different Bench combinations. However, commentators have cautioned that simply increasing sanctioned posts does not automatically reduce pendency; vacancies, case-management practices, institutional procedures and the volume of new litigation also matter. The legislative route chosen for the measure generated a separate constitutional debate. Because creating additional judicial posts involves expenditure from public funds, the legislation was processed through a category of Bill for which the two Houses of Parliament exercise different powers. Critics questioned whether this classification was appropriate, linking the controversy to a broader unresolved debate over the constitutional boundaries of such legislation. The episode therefore raises two distinct questions: whether increasing judicial capacity can meaningfully improve the functioning of the Supreme Court, and whether legislation affecting institutional expenditure should be enacted through a procedure that gives the Upper House a more limited role. Adapted from The Indian Express and Government of India coverage of the Supreme Court judge-strength legislation, 2026.

clat-mock-14-p2.title: Strategic Fiscal Responsibility: The Appeal to Curb Gold and Oil Imports
clat-mock-14-p2.text:
In a decisive move to safeguard macroeconomic stability, the Prime Minister has issued a crucial appeal to the nation to curb the excessive purchasing of gold and oil. India’s economic growth faces a persistent challenge from a widening Current Account Deficit (CAD), driven primarily by the inelastic demand for crude oil imports and an insatiable domestic appetite for gold. Because these two commodities dominate the nation’s import bill, they drain vital foreign exchange reserves and weaken the Indian Rupee against global benchmark currencies.

The Prime Minister’s appeal calls for a collective civic adjustment. By shifting personal savings from physical gold into productive financial instruments—such as Sovereign Gold Bonds—and adopting energy-efficient practices like public transit and renewable energy alternatives, citizens can directly fortify national economic resilience.

This strategic adjustment is not about enforcing austerity; it is about redirecting capital from unproductive assets into nation-building infrastructure. Reducing reliance on foreign oil and gold mitigates external economic shocks and strengthens fiscal sovereignty. Ultimately, this national push towards conscious consumption balances short- term individual desires with long-term macroeconomic health, ensuring steady economic growth.

clat-mock-40-p2.title: India–U.S. Cooperation in Lunar and Deep-Space Exploration
clat-mock-40-p2.text: India and the United States have steadily expanded cooperation in outer space from satellite applications and Earth observation to human spaceflight, planetary science and long-term lunar exploration. In 2026, this partnership gained fresh momentum as both sides explored possibilities for India to participate in future American-led efforts aimed at establishing a sustained human presence on the Moon. The discussions formed part of an established bilateral dialogue dedicated to civil space cooperation. Officials reviewed ongoing projects and examined opportunities in lunar science, human spaceflight, planetary exploration, scientific data sharing and commercial space activities. The interaction reflected India's growing role in international space collaboration and the increasing technological depth of its own space programme. Recent cooperation between the two countries has already produced a major joint Earth-observation satellite designed to study changes in forests, glaciers, agriculture and the Earth's surface with high precision. Experience gained from such technically complex collaboration has been viewed as a useful foundation for undertaking more ambitious ventures in the future. Lunar cooperation is also linked to a wider international framework that promotes peaceful, transparent and responsible exploration of the Moon and other celestial bodies. India joined this framework earlier in the decade, signalling its willingness to participate in rule-based international cooperation in outer space. India's expanding role in such initiatives also reflects the evolution of its own space programme. What began with a development-oriented vision focused on communication, meteorology and national needs has gradually expanded to include lunar exploration, Mars missions, solar observation and preparations for human spaceflight. The principles laid down by India's early space pioneers continue to influence this approach even as the country takes on increasingly complex missions. The emerging partnership therefore combines India's indigenous capabilities with international cooperation and may shape its role in the next phase of lunar and deep-space exploration.

clat-mock-10-p2.text:
The submission of the 16th Finance Commission’s report has reignited debates on the evolving contours of fiscal federalism in India. Chaired by Arvind Panagariya, the Commission has recommended maintaining the states’ share in the divisible pool of central taxes at 41 per cent, the same level set by its predecessor. However, it has introduced notable adjustments in the horizontal devolution formula, placing greater emphasis on economic contribution and demographic management while recalibrating the weight given to income distance.

Beyond tax devolution, the Commission has proposed a significant restructuring of grants, prioritising support for local bodies and disaster management while discontinuing several earlier categories of assistance. It has also outlined a fiscal roadmap, urging both the Centre and states to adhere to disciplined borrowing norms and reduce combined debt levels over the coming years. The report further advocates reforms in power distribution companies, subsidy rationalisation, and closure of loss-making public sector enterprises.

Critics argue that the revised formula may disadvantage states that have successfully controlled population growth and invested heavily in human development. Proponents, however, contend that linking devolution to economic performance will encourage competitive federalism and reward states contributing more to national GDP. In the broader context of cooperative federalism, the recommendations underscore the persistent tension between equity and efficiency in resource distribution. As India moves towards Viksit Bharat, the Commission’s emphasis on transparency, accountability, and sustainable public finance assumes added significance for long- term governance effectiveness.

clat-mock-16-p4.title: Nepal India Border Dispute
clat-mock-16-p4.text:
The diplomatic relationship between India and Nepal has faced renewed friction over the resumption of the high- altitude Yatra pilgrimage route. The core of the tension centers on the Himalayan Pass, a strategic mountain corridor at the tri-junction of India, Nepal, and China. While New Delhi and Beijing recently agreed to reopen the pass for trade and religious transit, Kathmandu issued a formal diplomatic protest note to both capitals, asserting that the route crosses sovereign Nepali territory.

This modern disagreement stems from conflicting interpretations of a nineteenth-century boundary treaty. India maintains that its position is consistent with administrative reality since the mid-twentieth century and points out that pilgrims have legally transited through this pass for decades. Conversely, Nepal’s current administration argues that any bilateral agreement concerning this specific territory requires Kathmandu’s explicit consent. The dispute has caused significant diplomatic ripples, impacting scheduled high-level bilateral visits and stalling joint technical mechanisms. While political leaders from both sides continue to engage in high-level talks in New Delhi to emphasize shared development goals and civilizational bonds, resolving the status of this Himalayan corridor remains a sensitive neighborhood policy challenge. (201 words)

clat-mock-41-p4.text:
National Sports Awards 2025 The Ministry of Youth Affairs and Sports announced the National Sports Awards 2025 in August 2026, recognising achievements across competitive sport, coaching and sports promotion. The honours covered multiple disciplines, including athletics, badminton, boxing, chess, hockey, kabaddi, shooting, para-sports, rowing and football.

The Arjuna Award formed the largest category, with recipients drawn from both Olympic and non-Olympic disciplines. Separate recognition was also provided under the Arjuna Award (Lifetime) category for contribution extending beyond an athlete's active sporting career. The Dronacharya Award were honoured under both regular and lifetime categories. The government's sports-promotion award was also conferred on an institution involved in developing sporting opportunities, including para-sport.

The selection process followed recommendations made by a committee comprising representatives from different areas of Indian sport. Applications had earlier been invited through a dedicated online mechanism, allowing eligible sportspersons, coaches and entities to apply directly.

The awards form part of India's wider system of national sporting honours administered by the Union government. Over time, this framework has evolved through changes in award categories and eligibility structures while retaining its broader objective of recognising sporting excellence, coaching achievement and contribution to India's sports ecosystem.

clat-mock-24-p2.title: Delimitation and Democratic Representation in India
clat-mock-24-p2.text: Representative democracy depends not only on periodic elections but also on ensuring that elected representatives speak for populations that are reasonably comparable in size. As demographic patterns change over time because of migration, urbanisation, and population growth, electoral boundaries may require periodic revision so that the principle of equal representation continues to be maintained. Such exercises are intended to strengthen democratic legitimacy while reflecting changes revealed through official population data. In India, the process of revising electoral boundaries is governed by constitutional and statutory provisions designed to ensure impartiality and transparency. An independent authority carries out this exercise after Parliament provides the necessary legal framework. Once the exercise is completed, the revised constituencies become the basis for future elections, contributing to a more balanced system of political representation. The legal framework also seeks to minimise prolonged disputes so that electoral processes are not disrupted by continuous litigation. Recent constitutional developments have renewed public discussion on the relationship between delimitation and political representation. In particular, debates concerning greater inclusiveness in legislatures have highlighted the importance of linking certain constitutional reforms with the completion of future delimitation exercises. These discussions have drawn attention to the broader objective of making representative institutions more inclusive while preserving the constitutional framework governing elections. As India prepares for future demographic changes, delimitation is expected to remain an important constitutional process balancing population shifts, federal considerations, and democratic representation. The subject therefore illustrates how constitutional design, electoral administration, and representative governance work together to sustain a functioning democracy.

clat-mock-11-p2.title: Artificial Intelligence and Linguistic Sovereignty
clat-mock-11-p2.text:
The confluence of technological nationalism and linguistic preservation has manifested through high-profile deliberations at the national capital's premier convention complex, where global stakeholders converged to examine artificial intelligence applications spanning citizen welfare, environmental sustainability, and economic advancement. The gathering emphasized indigenous language technologies, including platforms documenting oral traditions of tribal communities whose dialects face extinction pressures from dominant regional languages, and real-time translation systems bridging vernacular communication barriers. These initiatives align with broader digital governance frameworks seeking to democratize access to emerging technologies while preserving cultural heritage. The computational infrastructure supporting these applications—drawing conceptual foundations from the 1956 Dartmouth Conference that formalized artificial intelligence as a disciplinary field—

enables speech-to-text conversion across diverse linguistic registers, from endangered tribal tongues to major regional languages. Critical perspectives highlight the digital divide risks, noting that marginalized communities may lack infrastructure access despite technological availability, while proponents contend that AI-enabled preservation can reverse linguistic attrition through corpus building and digital archiving. The intersection of language technology with healthcare and environmental applications—ranging from AI-assisted diagnostics to climate modeling—demonstrates the integrative vision of inclusive innovation, though implementation challenges regarding data privacy, algorithmic bias, and digital literacy remain unresolved.

clat-mock-24-p1.title: India–Nepal Relations: Geography, Security and Contemporary Cooperation
clat-mock-24-p1.text: India and Nepal share one of South Asia's closest and most distinctive bilateral relationships, shaped by centuries of historical interaction, cultural affinity, and geographical proximity. Their open border facilitates the movement of people, trade, employment, and tourism, making the relationship unique among neighbouring countries. At the same time, certain historical agreements and differing interpretations of territorial boundaries have periodically generated diplomatic discussions, demonstrating the continuing relevance of history in contemporary international relations. Beyond historical ties, Nepal occupies considerable strategic importance in India's security and foreign policy. Situated between two major Asian powers, the country influences the broader geopolitical balance in the Himalayan region. Stability and cooperation between the two neighbours are viewed as essential for regional connectivity, border management, disaster response, and economic development. As a result, both governments maintain regular diplomatic dialogue on issues ranging from infrastructure and energy to security cooperation. Defence collaboration remains an important pillar of bilateral engagement. The armed forces of both countries maintain long-standing institutional ties through regular interactions, professional exchanges, and joint activities aimed at strengthening operational coordination and humanitarian capabilities. Such cooperation reflects the broader objective of enhancing mutual trust while responding effectively to common security and disaster- management challenges. In recent years, India and Nepal have also sought to expand cooperation in sectors such as cross-border connectivity, hydropower, trade, and digital infrastructure. Political developments within Nepal, including changes in government, continue to influence the direction of bilateral engagement, while both countries emphasise dialogue and cooperation as the preferred means of addressing differences. The relationship therefore represents a combination of historical continuity, strategic significance, and evolving regional partnerships.

clat-mock-26-p1.title: G7 Summit 2026 and India
clat-mock-26-p1.text: The 2026 G7 Summit brought together leaders of the major industrialised democracies to discuss contemporary global challenges. The summit included an Outreach Session, through which countries beyond the core grouping were invited to participate in discussions concerning international cooperation and global priorities. India used the platform to highlight concerns of the Global South, including the need for greater participation of developing and middle-income countries in global decision-making. It also emphasised the importance of strengthening international trust and developing partnerships based on mutual respect and shared responsibility. Alongside its participation in the summit discussions, India held bilateral meetings with several partner countries. These engagements covered areas such as trade, investment, security, energy and strategic cooperation. India and one of its major North American partners discussed strengthening their economic relationship and advancing negotiations for a comprehensive trade arrangement. The G7 has evolved considerably since its creation in the 1970s. It functions differently from treaty-based international organisations and operates through an annual presidency system. The country holding the presidency plays a significant role in determining priorities and organising meetings. The grouping also maintains engagement with countries outside its core membership through outreach mechanisms. The European Union participates in G7 proceedings through its institutional leadership, although its status differs from that of the individual countries constituting the grouping.

clat-mock-13-p2.title: Trump-China Visit
clat-mock-13-p2.text:
The Beijing summit of May 2026 between the leaders of the world's two largest economies drew intense global scrutiny, arriving against a backdrop of multiple simultaneous geopolitical pressures across the Middle East and the Taiwan Strait. The meeting was framed within a broader diplomatic context shaped by months of escalating economic friction, energy market volatility, and the approaching electoral calendar in the United States.

Prior to the summit, both nations had engaged in preliminary diplomatic exchanges aimed at stabilizing the bilateral relationship. The visit produced no formal signed agreements or joint declarations, yet the resumption of high-level direct communication was itself interpreted as a signal of mutual interest in preventing further deterioration. During formal proceedings, the Chinese leadership raised foundational questions about the structural nature of great-power rivalry, drawing on ancient historical precedents to frame the contemporary bilateral dynamic.

The Taiwan question featured prominently in the discussions, with the Chinese leadership characterizing it as a matter of exceptional sensitivity within the bilateral relationship. At a state banquet, the tone shifted toward identifying complementary national aspirations as a potential basis for managed coexistence. For regional observers — particularly middle powers in the Indo-Pacific — the summit's optics raised questions about how a consolidated bilateral understanding between Washington and Beijing might affect existing multilateral partnerships and the broader balance of influence across the region.

clat-mock-35-p4.title: India's Cultural Diplomacy — Soft Power through Global Engagement
clat-mock-35-p4.text: On a December evening, within the ramparts of a Mughal-era citadel on the Yamuna, the world formally adopted India's festival of lights as a jewel of humanity's living heritage — the first time the safeguarding committee met on Indian soil. Among sixty-odd nominations tabled that week, it was arguably the most luminous, and when the gavel fell, chants of celebration rang through the venue's ancient walls. For New Delhi, the moment was less an end than an exhibit: soft power in its natural habitat. Soft power — influence that seduces rather than compels, as a Harvard professor framed it in the nineties — India exercises through what it simply lives. A summer-solstice morning now bends plazas from Times Square to the Seine into yoga mats; a humble ancient grain once secured a whole calendar year from the world body; a WHO outpost for traditional medicine stands on Gujarat's coast; relics of the Buddha draw millions in Hanoi and Elista; a revived Nalanda enrols the world again; last year, a dozen sentinel forts — from Sahyadri crags to a lone southern outpost — marched into the heritage list at Paris; and several more tongues, Pali and Prakrit among them, now wear classical ribbons. None of this is accident. A cultural council founded in 1950 wires out teachers, troupes and scholarships across scores of countries; a six-decade-old training programme schoolmasters the Global South's bureaucracies; diaspora jamborees turn migration into memory. Coercion, the old argument goes, buys obedience; culture rents hearts. India's lease on that real estate, evidently, runs long.

clat-mock-05-p1.text:
On the 26th of January, 2026, the majestic expanse of Kartavya Path became the stage for a dual celebration of India's constitutional journey and its deep-rooted cultural nationalism. The annual parade, presided over by the President of India, was not merely a display of military might but a symbolic reiteration of the values enshrined in the supreme law of the land. This specific date holds immense historical weight, chosen deliberately by the Constituent Assembly to honor a pivotal declaration made decades prior by the Indian National Congress under the presidency of Jawaharlal Nehru—a declaration that shifted the freedom struggle's goalpost from dominion status to total independence.

The 2026 celebrations were distinguished by a unique diplomatic gesture, reflecting New Delhi's strengthening ties with the European bloc. For the first time, the dais was shared by two high-ranking European leaders, one of whom traces his lineage back to Goa, adding a personal dimension to the strategic partnership. The event's aesthetic and thematic elements were carefully curated to resonate with a significant cultural anniversary. The

path was lined with artistic installations featuring works from the early 20th century, specifically a rare series of illustrations from the "Bande Mataram Album," reviving the visual history of India's freedom struggle. Amidst the cultural tableaux and the rhythmic march of the armed forces—where the maritime service contingent notably outshone its peers—the parade underscored the resilience of the Indian Republic as it marched past the three- quarter-century mark of its constitutional existence.

clat-mock-15-p2.title: The Strait of Hormuz Crisis and India's Macroeconomic Vulnerabilities
clat-mock-15-p2.text:
The escalation of geopolitical tensions in West Asia has triggered an acute disruption along the Strait of Hormuz, a critical maritime chokepoint handling over one-fifth of the world’s petroleum consumption. As premium risk multipliers spiked global Brent crude prices past a multi-month threshold of ninety-five dollars per barrel, India's macroeconomic indicators experienced severe downward pressure. The surge in energy import costs instantly widened the national current account deficit (CAD). Because India relies on foreign sources for over eighty-five percent of its crude oil requirements, the domestic oil marketing companies aggressively ramped up their demand for greenbacks to settle commercial shipments.

This sudden, massive outflow of dollars systematically overwhelmed foreign exchange market matching systems, forcing a steep market-driven forces of the Indian Rupee (INR) against the United States Dollar (USD). To arrest an uncontrolled structural spiral and smooth out intraday volatility, the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) engaged in targeted interventions by drawing down its headline foreign currency assets. Concurrently, the financial ministry monitored peripheral trade metrics, evaluating the competitive benefits of a weaker currency on domestic merchandise exports against the immediate structural risks of imported inflation. Economists warn that if the Hormuz blockade persists, the combined impact of high energy inputs and currency devaluation will severely test the monetary policy framework's ability to maintain retail price stability.

clat-mock-25-p0.text: FIFA World Cup 2026: A New Era in Global Football The FIFA World Cup remains the most prestigious international football tournament, bringing together national teams from across the globe every four years under the aegis of the Fédération Internationale de Football Association (FIFA). Since its inception in the early twentieth century, the tournament has evolved from a relatively modest competition into one of the world's largest sporting events, attracting billions of viewers and serving as a symbol of sporting excellence, cultural exchange, and international cooperation. The 2026 edition marked a historic milestone in the evolution of the tournament. For the first time, the competition was jointly organized by Canada, Mexico, and the United States, reflecting FIFA's growing emphasis on multinational hosting and regional collaboration. The tournament also introduced an expanded competition structure, allowing broader participation from football associations across different confederations and increasing the total number of matches played. These reforms were intended to enhance the global reach of football while providing emerging nations with greater opportunities to compete at the highest level. The championship witnessed intense competition, with several traditional football powers and emerging teams producing memorable performances. The tournament concluded with a closely contested final that highlighted the importance of tactical discipline, defensive organisation, and resilience under pressure.
