Individual brilliance, collective teamwork, and consistent performances throughout the competition were recognised through FIFA's traditional tournament awards, while several long-standing records relating to player appearances and team achievements were also rewritten. Beyond the action on the field, the World Cup continued to demonstrate football's broader social, economic, and diplomatic significance. The event generated substantial tourism, infrastructure development, commercial investment, and international media engagement across the host nations. At the same time, FIFA reaffirmed its commitment to technological innovation through the use of advanced officiating systems and digital fan engagement initiatives. As football continues to expand its global footprint, the FIFA World Cup remains not merely a sporting competition but a platform for international cooperation, cultural interaction, and the celebration of excellence in the world's most popular sport.

clat-mock-18-p0.title: Rajya Sabha Elections and Parliamentary Representation
clat-mock-18-p0.text:
Recent Rajya Sabha elections in several states have once again drawn attention to the unique method through which members of the Upper House of Parliament are elected. Unlike Lok Sabha elections, which involve direct voting by citizens, Rajya Sabha members are generally elected by elected members of State Legislative Assemblies through a system designed to ensure proportional representation. Consequently, the outcome of Rajya Sabha elections often reflects not only numerical strength within state legislatures but also coalition dynamics, party discipline, and strategic voting patterns.

The elections have also highlighted the significance of the Rajya Sabha in India's parliamentary system. As a permanent House that is not subject to dissolution, it provides continuity in legislative functioning. At the same time, debates continue regarding the balance between representation of states, political accountability, and the role of the Upper House in the legislative process.

clat-aiom-mock-02-p1.text:
The 145th Report of the Parliamentary Standing Committee has flagged the "functional lethargy" of the Lokpal, India's apex anti-corruption ombudsman established under the 2013 Act. The report highlights that despite being a "sui generis" body, the institution remains structurally incomplete due to the non-operationalization of its Inquiry and Prosecution Wings.

The Lokpal’s architecture ensures independence through a high-powered Selection Committee and fixed tenure with age limits. It is a multi-member body requiring a balance of Judicial and Non-Judicial members along with mandatory social inclusivity. While its jurisdiction extends to the Prime Minister, the Act carves out specific subject-matter exclusions to protect sovereign functions. Functionally, the Lokpal holds superintendence over central investigating agencies for referred cases, exercises civil court powers for inquiries, and mandates reporting from vigilance bodies like the CVC.

clat-mock-33-p4.title: Centre Proposes Special Article 371 Framework for Ladakh
clat-mock-33-p4.text:
The Ladakh administration said Thursday that the new governance arrangement for the Union Territory will neither be statehood nor a UT with a legislature but a special constitutional amendment that will need the approval of Parliament.

A day after the meeting between representatives from Ladakh and officials of the Ministry of Home Affairs (MHA) in New Delhi, Ladakh Chief Secretary Ashish Kundra said that the agreement reached with the leadership here “is that a sui generis model, which does not exist anywhere in the country, will be crafted for Ladakh, where a legislative body will be created”.

“Ladakh was never a State. It was part of J&K, and later it became a UT. The aspiration of the people is to have legislative, executive, and financial powers. An agreement has been reached with the leadership here: a sui generis model, which does not exist anywhere in the country, will be crafted for Ladakh, where a legislative body will be created,” he said.

He added: “It is not going to be Statehood for sure or a UT with legislature, but it is some other body which will have these powers; the nomenclature of it is yet to be finalised, that is why discussions are on.” Kundra said that the framework proposed for Ladakh is a constitutional amendment and not the enactment of an “ordinary law”. For this, he said, a two-thirds majority is needed “and that requires political consensus across parties.” After this, he added, a detailed regulation to implement this decision will be needed. “These things have been transparently shared with the leadership yesterday.”

Extracted with edits and revisions from https://indianexpress.com/article/india/ladakh-governance-model- article-371k-sui-generis-mha-talks-10871906/

clat-mock-29-p1.title: Regulation of Mineral Rights and Mineral-Bearing Lands
clat-mock-29-p1.text: India's mineral sector is governed principally by the Mines and Minerals (Development and Regulation) Act, 1957, a statute that sits at the intersection of the Union and the States in India's fiscal federal structure. Mining- related subjects are distributed between the Union and State Lists of the Seventh Schedule, and questions repeatedly arise over which level of government may regulate which activity, and over which level may tax what. These questions have acquired sharpness in recent years because several States revised and multiplied the charges they assessed on the sector, and because a nine-judge Constitution Bench of the Supreme Court in 2024 examined the boundary between a tax and the other payments collected from the sector, and also addressed the recovery of outstanding dues. The Mines and Minerals (Development and Regulation) Amendment Bill, 2026 was passed by both Houses on 13 August 2026. It amends the 1957 Act on three related fronts: the reach of the Central regulatory framework, the power of State Governments to impose charges connected with mineral rights, and the legal position of claims that existed before the amendment came into force. On the first front, the amendment extends the range of subjects that fall within the framework laid down by the principal Act by adding a new category of land to the matters already regulated under it. The statute supplies a definition for this category, and the parameters used to identify it are to be settled through the framework that the Act itself provides. Supporters of the change argue that mineral resources are finite, that their exploitation carries national and strategic consequences, and that a single regulatory architecture produces better outcomes for exploration than a patchwork of arrangements. On the second front, the amendment introduces a fresh provision into the principal Act governing charges that State Governments may impose in connection with mineral rights or with the category of land brought within the Act's scope. The provision is drafted broadly as to the names such charges may be given, and it subjects them to a framework whose operation is governed elsewhere in the statutory scheme. The provision also engages with demands raised by States for periods before the amendment took effect. On the third front, the amendment prescribes transitional treatment for the claims that existed when it came into force. It separates such claims into categories and attaches a distinct legal consequence to each category, so that the status of past and outstanding demands is settled rather than left to litigation. Rule-making authority under the Act is correspondingly adjusted, so that the framework applicable to permissible State-level charges is furnished through a single mechanism rather than through separately drafted instruments in different States. Taken together, the amendment is presented as a measure intended to secure uniformity, predictability and stability in the fiscal and regulatory treatment of mineral resources, and thereby to support exploration and investment in the sector.

clat-mock-21-p2.text:
Assessing Grassroots Governance: The Panchayat Advancement Index India's commitment to grassroots governance and the localization of global development targets recently achieved a significant milestone with the modernization of its rural assessment frameworks. The nodal Union Ministry responsible for local self-government has evolved its measurement tools, releasing an upgraded version of its nationwide index—now referred to as the Panchayat Advancement Index (PAI) 2.0—to rigorously evaluate the socio-economic progress of over 2.5 lakh rural local bodies across the country. This robust multi-sectoral index shifts the administrative focus from mere fund utilization to actual outcome-based monitoring. It anchors its methodology on the framework of Localized Sustainable Development Goals (LSDGs), aggregating the 17 global SDGs into specific, actionable thematic areas meticulously tailored for rural realities. These parameters evaluate critical domains ranging from basic infrastructure self-sufficiency and water security to gender equity and administrative transparency.

To foster competitive and evidence-based planning, the index grades rural local bodies into distinct performance tiers based on their aggregate scores. The highest-scoring entities are recognized as top-tier models of rural development, while those at the lower end of the spectrum are identified as priority zones requiring targeted policy interventions and capacity building. By providing a granular, data-driven baseline, the index empowers policymakers, state governments, and local elected representatives to design strategic interventions, allocate resources efficiently, and ultimately drive sustainable, inclusive growth at the most foundational tier of Indian democracy.

clat-bootcamp-mock-37-p3.title: Union Budget 2026–27 The Budget of Three Duties
clat-bootcamp-mock-37-p3.text:
Presented on the first day of February from a ministry freshly moved into a new seat, the Budget announced itself through an idiom of duty: three duties, to be precise to quicken the economy and brace it for a volatile world; to make citizens partners, not passengers, in prosperity; and to leave no family, faith, region or trade outside the banquet. The arithmetic was stern but steady: receipts in the mid-thirties of lakh-crores met spending in the low-fifties, and the gap between them, measured as a share of the nation's product, bent a tenth of a point lower than the year gone by; the debt hill, fractionally, was set to shed rather than gain.

Growth got six levers. Manufacturing first: a health-industry moonshot named for strength, laboratories for clinical trials by the thousand; a semiconductor mission, second act; and corridors for rare earths mapped across four mineral-rich states of the peninsula's rim. Small industry would mint 'champions', aided by a new cohort of compliance comrades trained by the chartered institutes for tier-two towns. Then concrete and water: a fresh freight railway chained from the eastern rivers to a western port, twenty new waterways beginning on a coal-belt creek, and bullet-train spokes seven in number, three of which leave from one Deccan capital. The second duty built capacity: hospitals to attract the world's patients, a girls' hostel pledged to every district, a second citadel of mind-care for the north, and classrooms where gaming, animation and comics become a curriculum. The third duty reached the last mile: a multilingual farm companion that talks AI, a coconut promotion, and circuits of the Buddha woven through six Himalayan and hill-belt states. In Part B, quiet craft: honest travellers' bags made cheaper, a catch landed on foreign wharfs counted as exports, courier parcels capped no longer, and cloud empires lured to Indian data centres with a tax holiday longer than any CFO's career.

clat-mock-23-p3.title: UNIFIED PAYMENTS INTERFACE (UPI) AT 10 YEARS
clat-mock-23-p3.text: Few technological innovations have transformed everyday life in India as profoundly as the Unified Payments Interface (UPI). Introduced during a period when digital transactions constituted only a small fraction of retail payments, the platform has evolved into one of the world's largest real-time payment ecosystems. Its remarkable expansion has been driven by interoperability, ease of use, low transaction costs, and widespread smartphone adoption. Over the past decade, digital payments have increasingly replaced cash transactions for individuals, businesses, and government services, reshaping India's financial landscape. The growth of the platform has also become an important instrument of financial inclusion. By enabling seamless transactions across banks through a common interface, the system has expanded access to formal financial services while encouraging innovation among fintech companies. Its architecture has supported the emergence of QR-code based payments, merchant digitisation, and new financial products that rely upon secure digital authentication. The platform's influence now extends beyond India's borders. Through partnerships with foreign governments and payment networks, digital payment acceptance has gradually expanded across several regions including Asia, Europe, and the Middle East. This internationalisation has complemented India's broader objective of promoting digital public infrastructure as a global public good while strengthening cross-border payment connectivity. The tenth anniversary of the platform has therefore been viewed not merely as a technological milestone but also as an illustration of how public digital infrastructure can reshape governance, commerce, and financial inclusion. Even as new challenges relating to cybersecurity, digital literacy, and payment resilience continue to emerge, policymakers increasingly view interoperable digital payment systems as an essential component of future economic growth and global financial cooperation.

clat-mock-08-p1.text:
The emerging geopolitical landscape of the 21st century is increasingly shaped by control over semiconductor supply chains and artificial intelligence infrastructure. The Pax Silica Declaration, a U.S.- led initiative launched in December 2025, represents a coordinated effort among multiple nations to secure these critical technology supply chains through aligned policies and strategic cooperation.

The initiative brings together a select group of formal signatory nations, each contributing distinct technological and strategic capabilities to the alliance. These contributions range from advanced chip manufacturing and fabrication to AI research, semiconductor design, defence technology, sovereign wealth capital, and critical mineral reserves. The alliance follows a comprehensive "Full Stack" approach, encompassing every stage of the technology value chain.

However, the initiative has also generated geopolitical friction, particularly regarding critical mineral dependencies. Recent disruptions in critical input supplies between major economies have underscored these vulnerabilities, particularly affecting the automobile and electronics sectors.

The alliance operates with specific strategic, economic, and trade-related objectives, though its scope remains focused on technology supply chains rather than broader monetary or financial system restructuring.

clat-bootcamp-mock-01-p0.title: The PM CARES Fund — The Sleeping Treasury
clat-bootcamp-mock-01-p0.text: The first spring had rained cheques — overnight queues of corporations logging gifts against chartered benevolence quotas, a favour extended, critics noted, to no other relief coffer in the land — spent as feverishly as they arrived: breathing machines by the tens of thousands, pressure-swing oxygen forests, advances on little vials when there was not a shot to spare. Then the fever broke. The letters stopped; fresh gifts thinned to a fifth of their peak, the envelopes from overseas shrank to a lakh-scale trickle, and yet the ledger swelled to eight- thousand-odd crore by a recent March's close — fed less by giving than by the corpus's own quiet metabolism, and by refunds from contractors of the hectic years. Of that swollen lake, the year's outflow barely wet the shore: less than a crore, of which all but four-hundred- fifty-one rupees — the bank's charge for pings and messages — went to the orphans' covenant, whose wards number in the low thousands. Here the academicians of accountancy raised an eyebrow: the counted wards, at the scholarship promised to each, multiplied to a total that outran the year's actual release. The statement itself surfaced two rainy Augusts after the year it measured, signed by a new Mumbai firm of auditors — the earlier firm having retired after three seasons — and promptly drew fire: the accompanying explanatory notes were wanting, the guild's demanded document-marker was missing, nobody could say who had returned the hundred-crore packets, and sceptics asked why the vault should swell while calamities elsewhere are pleaded for. Nor is the storm only arithmetic. This winter, the capital's high court is to hear whether the vault may be juridically re-badged as the government itself — a badge that would swing the doors of the sunshine chapter open. The vault sleeps; the questions do not.

clat-mock-23-p2.title: Archaeology, Heritage and Judicial Adjudication
clat-mock-23-p2.text: A recent judicial proceeding concerning a historically significant monument in central India has once again highlighted. The Bhojshala–Kamal Maula complex at Dhar in Madhya Pradesh has long occupied a prominent place in debates concerning heritage, archaeology, and constitutional governance. The dispute centres on a centuries-old structure that has long been claimed by different communities, each relying on historical traditions, inscriptions, and documentary evidence to support competing assertions regarding its original character. During the proceedings, the High Court permitted a detailed archaeological survey to facilitate the collection of scientific evidence while emphasizing that questions relating to title and legal rights must ultimately be determined through due judicial process rather than public opinion or historical assertions alone. The case has renewed debates regarding the evidentiary value of archaeological findings in civil disputes involving places of worship and protected monuments. The controversy also illustrates the intersection of heritage conservation and constitutional rights. While archaeological agencies are entrusted with preserving monuments of national importance, courts are frequently required to balance conservation objectives with claims relating to religious practices, historical continuity, and public order. Legal experts have observed that archaeological evidence may assist courts in understanding the historical evolution of a site but does not, by itself, determine legal ownership or religious status. The proceedings have therefore attracted wider attention as an example of how constitutional institutions attempt to reconcile competing historical narratives within the framework of the rule of law, ensuring that disputes over cultural heritage are resolved through legal adjudication rather than political or majoritarian considerations.

clat-mock-21-p0.text:
The Global Blueprint for Apex Predator Conservation The International Big Cat Alliance (IBCA) represents a paradigm shift in global wildlife conservation, transitioning from isolated national efforts to a unified, transnational strategy. Spearheaded by India, this mega-coalition was instituted to secure the future of the world's most iconic apex predators. The alliance's mandate spans a comprehensive framework designed to protect natural habitats, mitigate human-wildlife conflict, and dismantle the illegal poaching networks threatening these species.

Rather than focusing on a single geographical region, the initiative casts a wide net, encompassing ecosystems ranging from the high-altitude Himalayas to the dense tropical wetlands of South America. It targets the preservation of seven primary feline species that serve as critical indicators of ecological health. By pooling financial resources, scientific research, and capacity-building protocols, the coalition aims to halt the rapid decline of global biodiversity.

Recently, the alliance has seen significant diplomatic momentum with the integration of major Middle Eastern economies, expanding its membership to over two dozen nations. This geopolitical expansion underscores a growing international consensus: safeguarding apex predators is not merely a regional environmental concern, but a shared global responsibility essential for maintaining the balance of the planet's broader ecological web.

clat-bootcamp-mock-01-p4.title: The Women's Cricket World Cup 2026 — A Lord's Summer of Records
clat-bootcamp-mock-01-p4.text: The Cricket teams, the format's largest-ever field, descended on England and Wales in midsummer 2026 for the tournament — a five-run defeat to the hosts in a curtained Cardiff friendly already filed away by the Indians as a warning. The champions of two years prior never made it to July. India arrived wearing an odd crown — ODI queens of barely eight months — and opened like empresses: Pakistan routed at Edgbaston in a sixty-four-run tumble beneath an off-spinner's five-for, then the batters of Utrecht's opposition scattered for 209, an Indian first in this tournament's ledger. A stumble in Manchester, though, made the last group game a decider — and deciders, fatefully, were to be played at Lord's. India's women had never played this format on that turf before; they may not wish to recall the first. A run-out mix-up silenced the left-handed opener in full flow, the skipper's 25-ball hurry — outstripping her own older mark — lifted them to a hundred and seventy, and three early wickets stirred hope before the all-rounder's counterpunch settled the pursuit with five balls unused. Two southern neighbours of that group thus passed instead into the semi-finals. The last Sunday belonged to the old rivalry under the pavilion's weather-vane: the hosts, six wins from six and never before beaten in a home World Cup, cobbled 150 for 4 behind their captain's fifty and a late, unbroken surge. The chase was no contest — a left-handed keeper of a veteran and a prodigy with a reverse-swept six raised a hundred stand, and the flagging runs came, half in triumph, half in wides, with overs to spare. Consolation postcards reached the departing Indians nonetheless: continental pre-eminence, it was agreed, would be stamped into the books as a passage to the five-ringed games of 2028.

clat-mock-23-p0.title: Russia–Ukraine Dispute: Beyond the Battlefield
clat-mock-23-p0.text: The conflict between Russia and Ukraine, which escalated into a full-scale war in 2022, has reshaped the strategic landscape of Europe and significantly altered global diplomacy. Although the immediate military confrontation is recent, the dispute is rooted in decades of political disagreements over sovereignty, security, and competing visions of the post-Cold War order. Successive developments—including constitutional changes within Ukraine, competing security arrangements in Europe, and disagreements over territorial status—gradually deepened mistrust between the two neighbours. The conflict has extended far beyond conventional warfare. International courts have been approached to examine allegations of war crimes and violations of humanitarian law, while economic sanctions imposed by several Western countries have attempted to restrict financial transactions, technology transfers, and energy exports. Simultaneously, Russia has sought to deepen economic engagement with partners outside the Western alliance system, reshaping patterns of global trade and energy flows. Maritime geography has also assumed strategic importance. Control over access routes linking enclosed regional seas with the wider Black Sea has influenced military logistics, commercial navigation, and international legal disputes. Infrastructure built across these waters has further intensified disagreements regarding sovereignty and freedom of navigation. The crisis has also revived broader debates over the expansion of military alliances, collective security arrangements, and the limits of international law in responding to armed conflict. As diplomatic negotiations continue intermittently, the dispute remains a defining test of the contemporary international order and the effectiveness of multilateral institutions in addressing prolonged interstate conflicts.

clat-mock-29-p3.title: Cauvery Water Dispute and Its Institutional Framework
clat-mock-29-p3.text: The Cauvery river water dispute is a major inter-State water-sharing issue involving Karnataka, Tamil Nadu, Kerala and Puducherry. Its constitutional foundation lies in the provisions concerning disputes over waters of inter-State rivers, while Parliament has enacted legislation to provide mechanisms for adjudication and implementation. Following the Supreme Court's 2018 judgment, the Union Government framed the Cauvery Water Management Scheme, 2018 under the existing statutory framework. The scheme established institutional arrangements for implementing the Tribunal's award as modified by the Court and for regulating water releases among the concerned parties. The Authority established under the scheme has a multi-member composition, with specified qualifications and tenure provisions for its leadership and members. It is intended to facilitate coordinated implementation and monitoring of water-sharing arrangements among the concerned States. The Supreme Court's 2018 decision also modified the earlier allocation of Cauvery waters, taking into account factors including drinking-water requirements and groundwater availability. The revised arrangement subsequently formed the basis for implementation and monitoring. The dispute continues to influence irrigation, drinking water, hydropower and infrastructure development in the basin. Proposals involving additional storage and water-supply infrastructure have therefore remained subject to scrutiny by relevant authorities. One such proposal has involved a proposed balancing reservoir and drinking- water project, for which the Central Water Commission sought inputs from the institutional mechanism established under the 2018 arrangement.

clat-mock-24-p0.title: Gaganyaan's Life Support System: Sustaining Human Life in Space
clat-mock-24-p0.text: Human spaceflight presents engineering challenges that extend far beyond launching a spacecraft into orbit. Once astronauts leave Earth's atmosphere, they enter an environment where breathable air, comfortable temperatures, and safe cabin pressure are unavailable. Unlike satellites, a crewed spacecraft must continuously maintain conditions that allow human beings to survive and perform routine activities throughout the mission. To meet these requirements, India's Gaganyaan programme incorporates an Environmental Control and Life Support System (ECLSS), a complex network of subsystems designed to regulate the spacecraft's internal environment. The system is responsible for maintaining cabin pressure, controlling temperature and humidity, supplying breathable air, and ensuring that contaminants generated during the mission do not accumulate to harmful levels. Continuous monitoring allows onboard conditions to remain within limits suitable for human habitation even as external conditions in space fluctuate dramatically. Given that Gaganyaan is intended as a short-duration mission, its life support architecture has been designed with simplicity, reliability, and safety as guiding principles. Rather than relying extensively on complex regenerative technologies, the system is expected to carry essential consumables for the planned duration of the flight while safely managing waste products until the crew returns to Earth. Such an approach reduces technical complexity and improves mission reliability for India's first human spaceflight programme. The development of the ECLSS represents a significant technological milestone for India's space programme. Beyond supporting the Gaganyaan mission, the experience gained from designing reliable life support technologies is expected to contribute to future long-duration human spaceflight, space stations, and other advanced exploration missions. As India expands its human spaceflight capabilities, mastering environmental control and life support systems will remain fundamental to ensuring crew safety and mission success.

clat-mock-39-p0.text: The approaching conclusion of the existing Ganga water-sharing arrangement has reopened a complex debate involving India, Bangladesh and Indian States situated along the river system. What began principally as a bilateral question of allocating dry-season river flows has increasingly become intertwined with concerns about federalism, climate change, sedimentation, ecological resilience and future water demand. Bihar has emerged as a significant domestic stakeholder in the debate. Its political leadership has argued that any future arrangement must take account of the State’s drinking-water, irrigation and industrial requirements, as well as problems associated with floods and sediment accumulation. Several Indian States have also sought greater consultation because domestic water requirements and river-management concerns are closely connected with the bilateral negotiations. This has made negotiations not merely an exercise in foreign policy but also one of internal federal consultation. Bangladesh, as the downstream country, has historically emphasised adequate dry-season availability and the environmental consequences of reduced flows. Meanwhile, changing rainfall patterns, upstream withdrawals and wider climatic pressures have made historical flow assumptions increasingly uncertain. Experts have therefore argued that a future agreement may need to go beyond a narrow allocation formula and incorporate ecological protection, data-sharing, flood forecasting, sediment management and stronger institutional cooperation. The controversy demonstrates how transboundary rivers create interdependence rather than a simple contest between upstream and downstream States. An enduring framework will therefore require India and Bangladesh to reconcile diplomatic obligations with domestic concerns while adapting river governance to ecological and hydrological conditions that have changed significantly since the existing arrangement was negotiated. Adapted from The Indian Express coverage and analysis of the Ganga Water-Sharing Treaty debate, July– September 2026.

clat-mock-12-p3.title: One Nation One Election
clat-mock-12-p3.text:
The Union Government has embarked on a historic constitutional journey to synchronize India's fragmented electoral calendar under the "One Nation, One Election" framework. At present, the country remains locked in an almost perpetual election cycle — with different states conducting polls at different times throughout the year. This creates a triple burden on the nation: enormous financial expenditure on repeated elections, persistent diversion of teachers, police officers, and civil servants from their core responsibilities to election duties, and recurring governance disruptions whenever the Model Code of Conduct freezes policy announcements across states.

The reform envisions two distinct phases. The first seeks to align Lok Sabha and State Assembly elections by modifying constitutional provisions that currently fix their independent five-year terms. The second phase aims to bring Panchayat and Municipality elections within a hundred-day window thereafter, requiring coordination between separate constitutional bodies that independently manage national and local polls.

While supporters highlight savings in public money and uninterrupted governance, opponents warn that merging electoral timelines could drown regional voices beneath national political narratives, thereby weakening India's federal architecture. As Parliament deliberates on the constitutional amendment bill introduced for this transformative purpose, the debate continues to test the delicate balance between administrative efficiency and democratic decentralization in the world's largest democracy.

clat-mock-34-p1.title: Money Bill Route to Increase Supreme Court Judges’ Strength
clat-mock-34-p1.text:
The Rajya Sabha Wednesday passed the Supreme Court (Number of Judges) Amendment Bill, 2026, which seeks to increase the sanctioned strength of Supreme Court judges from 34 to 38 including the Chief Justice of India.

The Bill, which cleared Lok Sabha Monday, was passed as a money Bill, a route it had also taken in 2019 when the Supre-me Court strength was raised to 34. In 2018, a key dissenting opinion in a Supreme Court ruling had described this route as a “fraud on the Constitution.”

The Statement of Objects and Reasons of the Bill cites the expenditure involved in creating four additional posts of judges, along with staff, residences and security.

“This will increase the expenditure on account of pay and allowances on creation of four additional posts of Judges in the Supreme Court along with required staff. The Judges will also be entitled to the use of a rent-free official residence. Each Judge will have to be provided with personal staff at residence and office. Expenditure would also be incurred in connection with the deployment of security for Judges. ⁠The estimated recurring expenditure on salaries of four Judges and their staff, conveyance and other miscellaneous expenses would be rupees 10,56,81,648 per annum and non-recurring expenditure towards car and furnishing of official residence and other miscellaneous expenses will be approximately rupees 3,47,36,000. Thus, the total expenditure on creation of additional four posts of Judges in the Supreme Court of India will be of rupees 14,04,17,648 approximately,” the Bill stated.

Extracted with edits and revisions from https://indianexpress.com/article/explained/explained-law/money-bill- route-pending-before-supreme-court-government-chooses-it-to-raise-strength-of-judges-10819849/

clat-mock-35-p0.title: The Mines and Minerals (Development and Regulation) Amendment Act, 2026
clat-mock-35-p0.text: The closing days of the Monsoon Session this August saw Parliament clear the Mines and Minerals (Development and Regulation) Amendment Bill, 2026 — passed by both Houses in mid-August — which has since become law with the President's assent. The parent statute has governed mines for nearly seven decades, but the provocation lay elsewhere: a 2024 Constitution Bench verdict holding that royalty is not really a tax, and recognising the power of State legislatures to tax mineral rights. Emboldened, some States levied cesses touching a fifth of a mineral's value, atop the fourteen-odd taxes, charges and fees miners already shoulder. Industry warned that every pithead rupee travels through steel, cement and electricity into the price of an ordinary family's home — even as mineral imports stood at ₹10.12 lakh crore in 2025-26. The Amendment rewrites this fiscal grammar. For the first time, the Union's reach extends expressly to the land that holds minerals, not merely to mines alone. A newly-inserted provision forbids State Governments from taxing mineral rights or mineral-bearing lands — by whatever name called — save under conditions and restrictions the Centre will prescribe through rules. Retrospective peace follows: demands raised but never recovered stand extinguished, while money already in State coffers stays put. The Centre's assurance is that nearly nine-tenths of the sector's revenues shall continue to accrue to States, whose writ over sand, gravel and some fifty minor minerals remains untouched, as do District Mineral Foundation collections under the PMKKKY. Beyond taxation, the country's exploration trust, hitherto confined to prospecting support, will now finance mine development as well, and be rechristened to match this wider role. Blocks with deep-seated deposits may expand once — by a tenth of a mining lease or three-tenths of a composite licence — and an authority shall register and regulate mineral exchanges.

clat-mock-41-p3.title: 26th SCO Summit & India
clat-mock-41-p3.text:
The 26th Meeting of the Council of Heads of State of the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO) was held in Bishkek, Kyrgyz Republic, from 31 August to 1 September 2026, coinciding with the organisation’s 25th anniversary. Leaders reviewed cooperation in regional security, economic development, connectivity, energy, technology and people-to-people exchanges. The meeting also considered institutional mechanisms for countering emerging security challenges and transnational crime.

Prime Minister Narendra Modi, representing India, called for translating the SCO’s long- standing dialogue into measurable outcomes. India emphasised three broad priorities— Security, Connectivity and Opportunity—while stressing that regional connectivity initiatives should respect sovereignty and territorial integrity. Counter-terrorism remained an important element of India's engagement with the grouping.

The summit adopted a major declaration along with several decisions and agreements relating to climate, nuclear safety, energy conservation, drug control and institutional cooperation. India also supported initiatives aimed at expanding civilisational and youth exchanges within the organisation. An SCO Plus meeting brought the grouping into dialogue with additional states and international organisations.

The summit concluded one country's rotational chairmanship and transferred responsibility for the organisation's next annual cycle to another member. For India, the SCO continues to provide a significant platform for engagement with Central Asia and the wider Eurasian region.

clat-mock-38-p3.text:
Commonwealth Games The 2026 Commonwealth Games represented an important experiment in the future organisation of large multi-sport events. Faced with rising hosting costs and growing concerns about the financial burden associated with major international competitions, organisers adopted a more compact model with fewer venues and a significantly reduced sporting programme. The streamlined format affected India in particular. Its contingent was considerably smaller than at previous editions because several disciplines in which Indian athletes have traditionally performed strongly were absent from the programme. As a result, India’s medal prospects depended more heavily on a narrower group of events, including athletics, weightlifting and other individual disciplines. Despite the reduced programme, the Games continued to emphasise integration between able-bodied and Para athletes, reinforcing a feature that has distinguished the Commonwealth sporting movement from many other international competitions.

The Commonwealth Games have undergone several transformations since their first edition in Canada in 1930. Their name and institutional identity changed as the political relationship among Britain and its former territories evolved. What began as a sporting gathering associated with the imperial structure gradually developed into a competition representing the modern Commonwealth. The 2026 edition also came at an important moment for the movement’s future. Organisers have increasingly sought flexible hosting arrangements, existing infrastructure and lower-cost delivery models rather than extensive construction programmes. With the centenary edition scheduled for 2030, the Commonwealth sporting movement is attempting to balance tradition with financial sustainability while retaining its distinctive emphasis on shared sporting competition among member nations and territories.

clat-bootcamp-mock-37-p0.title: The G7 A Club Born in a Library, Tested by a Tolling Strait
clat-bootcamp-mock-37-p0.text:
The club began as a murmur among finance men in a Washington library, graduated to a château outside Paris, admitted a northern neighbour in its second year, briefly tried becoming eight, and shrank back one large member having been shown the door over the seizure of a peninsula on a distant sea. It owns no charter, keeps no permanent office; the gavel simply travels, and wherever it lands, the host writes the menu.

This June the gavel came home, more than fifty years after that first French gathering, to a lakeside town whose spring water fills bottles on every continent. The timing was perfect: days earlier, a ceasefire-deal had been announced between Washington and Tehran, and the seven several of whom had bitterly criticized the launching of that war unanimously applauded the peace, praised the dealmaker-president, and agreed that no vessel should ever pay a toll to breathe through the strait below, with the host and a northern island ally offering mine-clearing frigates to help. The seven held their line, too, on the old eastern war: pressure on its aggressor's war-chest until a just peace returned the border.

There was, for the second year running, no single agreed communiqué. Instead the chef served the menu as nine separate platters geopolitics, minerals, rebalanced growth, health, smuggling letting each invited guest sign only the platters it relished; curiously, one dish united them all: guarding children in the digital space. Nor was China absent: a preparatory video-call, the first such broad gathering in over two decades, put global imbalances overcapacity there, twin deficits elsewhere onto the table for once. And the largest of the guests, the world's most populous democracy, spent the margins bartering: uranium supplies for its reactors, a trade pact to be sealed within the year, and a brand-new dialogue platform for the Americas.

clat-mock-40-p4.title: VB-G RAM G and the New Rural Employment Framework
clat-mock-40-p4.text: India’s rural employment architecture underwent a major transition in 2026 with the operationalisation of a new statutory framework aimed at combining wage employment with longer-term rural development. The new system retains the idea that eligible rural households may demand unskilled manual work, but seeks to connect such employment more closely with productive asset creation, livelihood security and infrastructure planning. The framework reflects a broader shift from viewing public employment primarily as short-term income support towards integrating it with village-level development. Greater emphasis has been placed on decentralised planning, convergence between government programmes, technology-enabled monitoring and the creation of assets capable of supporting agriculture, water security and resilience to extreme weather events. The new architecture also modifies the financial relationship between the Union and the States. Instead of following a uniform financing arrangement, the law provides differentiated cost-sharing patterns according to the category of State or Union Territory. State governments are also given responsibilities relating to implementation, unemployment support and identification of periods during which agricultural labour demand is particularly high. At the institutional level, Gram Panchayats and other local bodies continue to play an important role in translating the statutory guarantee into actual employment. The framework therefore operates at the intersection of several constitutional ideas: livelihood security, decentralised governance, cooperative federalism and the State’s responsibility to promote social and economic welfare. The reform has consequently become important not merely as a rural-development measure, but also for understanding the evolution of India's employment-guarantee policy and the constitutional architecture within which rural governance operates.

clat-mock-13-p3.title: UPI 10 YEARS
clat-mock-13-p3.text: The completion of a decade of operations marks a watershed moment for the Unified Payments Interface (UPI), a platform that has completely redefined the paradigm of retail commerce and accelerated financial inclusion. Launched as an ambitious experiment in digital public infrastructure, the ecosystem has steadily evolved into the undisputed anchor of the domestic digital economy. By seamlessly bridging the gap between traditional banking networks and informal daily transactions, it has democratized access to the financial system for millions of citizens, transforming small-ticket merchant checkouts into frictionless digital experiences. This deep nationwide adoption has fostered an unprecedented culture of trust, financial transparency, and economic agility across urban and rural landscapes alike. On the world stage, the platform has transcended its domestic origins to emerge as a global benchmark for real- time payment architectures. Recognizing its extraordinary scale, efficiency, and reliability, international financial institutions have lauded the infrastructure as a premier model for scalable and inclusive digital networks. Today, its expanding global footprint—characterized by cross-border system linkups and growing international merchant acceptance—has positioned the nation as a global leader in financial technology innovation, demonstrating to the world how a home-grown public utility can successfully challenge and surpass legacy global payment frameworks.

clat-mock-17-p4.title: Semiconductors and the New Geopolitics of Technology
clat-mock-17-p4.text:
Semiconductors are among the most important components of the modern economy. They are used in products ranging from smartphones and computers to automobiles, telecommunications equipment, defence systems, and advanced industrial machinery. As digital technologies become increasingly integrated into economic and strategic activities, access to semiconductor manufacturing capabilities has emerged as a significant policy concern for governments worldwide.

Recent years have witnessed growing efforts by countries to strengthen domestic semiconductor ecosystems. Policymakers have cited concerns relating to supply-chain resilience, technological competitiveness, economic security, and strategic autonomy. These efforts have included investments in manufacturing facilities, research and development, workforce development, and international partnerships. The issue has also acquired geopolitical significance. Concentration of advanced manufacturing capabilities in a limited number of locations has prompted debates regarding vulnerability to disruptions caused by natural disasters, political tensions, or economic restrictions. Consequently, many countries are seeking to diversify supply chains while simultaneously supporting innovation and industrial growth.

As governments compete to attract investment and build technological capabilities, semiconductors have become central to discussions concerning economic development, national security, and the future of global technological leadership.

clat-mock-31-p1.title: The Indus Waters Treaty & The Hague Ruling
clat-mock-31-p1.text:
Few treaties have survived what this one has — three full-scale wars, decades of frozen diplomacy, and repeated military crises — which is precisely why its present limbo is so consequential. Signed in Karachi more than six decades ago after nearly a decade of negotiations brokered by an international financial institution, the agreement performed a surgical division of a river system: the three eastern rivers for unrestricted use by India, the three western rivers largely for the lower riparian, leaving India roughly one-fifth of the system's waters along with narrowly defined rights to run-of-the-river hydroelectricity upstream.

That architecture cracked in the spring of 2025, when gunmen massacred twenty-six tourists in a Kashmir meadow. Within a day, New Delhi announced that the treaty would be held "in abeyance" until its neighbour "credibly and irrevocably" abjured support for cross-border terrorism a word, critics noted, that appears nowhere in the treaty or in the law of treaties. Islamabad moved the arbitral tribunal, which conducted hearings at the Peace Palace in April 2026 without India, which has consistently branded the forum "illegally constituted" and boycotted its proceedings since 2016-era objections hardened.

On 31 August 2026, the five-member court ruled unanimously that the treaty contains no exit hatch for one party alone: it can be modified or terminated only by another duly ratified treaty between the two states. Testing India's justifications against international law material breach, fundamental change of circumstances, armed conflict, countermeasures it found none sufficient. The treaty, it declared, "remains fully in force." Alongside the award came interim measures concerning a contested hydroelectric plant, crafted to prevent construction from creating irreversible facts on the ground before a parallel technical process, expected to conclude in mid-2027, delivers its verdict. New Delhi rejected the award within hours; the abeyance, it said, stands. (Extracted, with edits and revision, from reports of Reuters and legal commentaries, September 2026)

clat-mock-12-p4.title: Custodial Death
clat-mock-12-p4.text:
Custodial deaths, defined as fatalities resulting from torture or inhuman treatment while in police or judicial custody, remain a critical human rights challenge in India. Highlighting the severity, an Additional District and Sessions Court in Madurai imposed the death penalty on policemen in April 2026 for a 2020 custodial death case in Tamil Nadu. This landmark verdict underscores the judiciary's stance against abuse of power.

Despite constitutional safeguards like Article 20(3) and CrPC provisions mandating judicial inquiries into custody deaths, incidents persist. The National Human Rights Commission reported 2,739 custodial deaths in 2024. Key issues include lack of independent investigations, as police often probe their own departments, and the erosion of institutional integrity. Although India signed the UN Convention against Torture in 1997, ratification remains pending, and the Prevention of Torture Bill lapsed in 2014. The Supreme Court's 1996 D.K. Basu guidelines established arrest procedures and compensation norms, yet accountability gaps persist. Critics argue that without independent oversight and ratified international conventions, torture culture continues to violate human dignity. Recent statistics and judicial actions emphasize the urgent need for comprehensive legal reforms and stricter accountability mechanisms to protect detainees and restore faith in the justice system.

clat-mock-05-p0.text:
On the eve of Republic Day 2026, the Rashtrapati Bhavan portal lit up with the names of 131 individuals whose contributions have shaped modern India in ways big and small. From a veteran filmmaker who entertained generations to a violin maestro whose strings still echo in concert halls, from social reformers who spent decades in the shadows to scientists working quietly in distant lands, the list cut across age, region, and discipline.

For the first time in recent memory, the announcement carried an unusually high number of emotional moments as several families accepted the honour on behalf of those who were no longer present. The morning of 26 January saw the nation pause, reflect, and celebrate lives that touched millions, reminding everyone that civilian recognition remains the country’s highest form of gratitude.

The geographical distribution of the 2026 awards shows a concentration of recognition in states like Maharashtra and Tamil Nadu, which led the tally, while other large states like Uttar Pradesh and Karnataka also found representation. The selection committee’s choices often spark discussions regarding the categorization of fields. For instance, while the Sports category saw celebrated names from cricket and tennis being honored, observers noted specific trends regarding which tier of the Padma awards—Vibhushan, Bhushan, or Shri—was allocated to the sporting fraternity this year compared to fields like Art and Public Affairs.

clat-mock-27-p4.title: A Guarantee Reforged
clat-mock-27-p4.text: Replacing the old statute has meant rewriting the financial compact between Delhi and the states. Under the earlier law, the Centre alone paid the unskilled wage bill, and entitlements generated expenditure without limit. The new one makes the states partners in cost: for most states the wage bill is split three parts to two — the larger share borne by the Centre; for the hill states of the north-east and the Himalayas the split is nine parts to one; and for union territories without legislatures of their own, the Centre still pays the whole. The scheme thereby changes character — from a purely central scheme to a shared one, in which the Centre sets the standards and the states execute, within a predictable ceiling of central funds beyond which the state itself must pay. The works themselves have been pulled out of their old scattering into four named priority verticals: securing water — harvesting rain, recharging the ground; building the core of rural infrastructure, the roads and connectivity that open markets; raising livelihood assets — storage, markets, units of production; and, in the fourth, hardening the countryside against extreme weather, with flood drainage and soil conservation. Planning runs from the bottom up but is wired into national systems: every village panchayat prepares its own development plan, and every asset created is pooled into a single national register of rural infrastructure, connected with the country's grand spatial masterplan for connectivity. Oversight is being digitised — artificial intelligence and biometric checks to catch irregularities early, satellite tracking of works, live dashboards, weekly public disclosures, and social audits twice a year — while the worker's old protections survive: if work is not provided in time, an allowance must be paid.

clat-mock-20-p4.title: India–Nordic Summit 2026
clat-mock-20-p4.text: India's engagement with the Nordic region has emerged as an important pillar of its relations with Europe, reflecting growing cooperation in areas extending beyond traditional diplomacy and trade. The India–Nordic Summit provides a high-level platform for political dialogue between India and the other countries, enabling discussions on issues such as sustainable development, clean energy, digital transformation, innovation, maritime cooperation, Arctic affairs, resilient supply chains, and emerging technologies. The partnership has gained momentum amid changing geopolitical realities, with both sides seeking to diversify economic partnerships and strengthen cooperation in critical technologies and green transitions. The 2026 India–Nordic Summit, hosted in Norway, reaffirmed the commitment of both sides to deepen collaboration across multiple sectors. Maritime security, connectivity, innovation-led growth, and cooperation in multilateral institutions also featured prominently during the discussions. The summit further underlined the role of people-to-people exchanges, academic collaboration, and start-up partnerships in strengthening long-term ties. Although the Nordic countries represent relatively small populations individually, they collectively possess advanced technological capabilities, high innovation indices, and significant expertise in sustainable development. Consequently, India's engagement with the region increasingly reflects a convergence of strategic, economic, technological, and environmental interests rather than merely conventional diplomatic relations.

clat-mock-22-p0.title: GST 2.0
clat-mock-22-p0.text:
Nearly a decade after its historic inception, India's indirect tax architecture underwent a transformative structural overhaul to address persistent compliance friction and classification anomalies. The legacy system, burdened by a complex multi-tiered rate structure, frequently resulted in inverted duty challenges, legal ambiguities, and delayed input tax credit reconciliations. Recognizing the imperative to foster a frictionless, globally competitive business environment, the federal fiscal forum initiated a comprehensive modernization mandate, colloquially termed the next-generation overhaul.

This modernized framework functions by fundamentally rationalizing the tariff architecture. The previous complex matrices have been collapsed into a simplified, dual-slab core applied to the vast majority of goods and services, explicitly eliminating the intermediate and peak standard rates of the past. To sustain revenue buoyancy, this core is complemented by a specialized, higher punitive bracket strictly reserved for luxury commodities and socially detrimental goods, replacing previous compensation cess mechanisms. Beyond rate simplification, the new regime operates through aggressive technological integration—featuring automated e-invoicing, accelerated algorithmic refunds, and fully operationalized centralized appellate tribunals. Ultimately, this paradigm shift transitions the regulatory focus from policing evasion to proactively facilitating systemic economic formalization and transparent consumption.

clat-mock-33-p3.title: World Bank Income Classification: India Remains Lower-Middle-Income
clat-mock-33-p3.text:
In the World Bank’s classification of global economies, five countries moved from lower-middle to upper- middle income category this year. The World Bank’s classification is updated based on gross national income (GNI) per capita estimates from the previous calendar year.

India’s economy grew at 7.8% in the April-June quarter of 2026-27. But the country’s per capita income stood around US$ 2671 in the FY 2024-25. Where does India stand in the World Bank’s latest classification of global economies? The World Development Report 2024: The Middle-Income Trap identified a total of 108 countries, including India, facing challenges in moving away from the trap. Compared with the US, the report noted, these countries are trapped at modest income levels.

Using estimates based on the Solow-Swan model of growth, the report projects that these countries are likely to experience a significant slowdown between 2024 and 2100 if the drivers of growth remain as per their current and historic trends. The drivers of growth in this model are investment in human capital, total factor productivity, labour force participation, and the share of economic output accrued to public and private investment.

Extracted with edits and revisions from https://indianexpress.com/article/upsc-current-affairs/upsc-essentials/is- innovation-the-only-way-out-of-the-middle-income-trap-10870393/

clat-mock-06-p1.text:
The Panchayats (Extension to Scheduled Areas) Act represents a major constitutional effort to institutionalize self-governance in India’s tribal regions. Enacted in 1996, it extends Part IX of the Constitution to Scheduled Areas under the Fifth Schedule and recognizes the centrality of Gram Sabhas in local governance. The Act empowers village assemblies to safeguard customary practices, manage community resources, and participate in decisions regarding land acquisition and development projects. By placing communities at the heart of governance, it attempts to correct the historical marginalization of Adivasi populations.

In a significant development, Jharkhand recently operationalized PESA in January 2026, formally joining the group of states implementing the Act in Scheduled Areas. This move is particularly important for Jharkhand, a mineral-rich state with a substantial tribal population that has long experienced displacement due to mining and industrial expansion. The formal rollout aims to strengthen grassroots democracy by recognizing village assemblies as decision-making authorities in matters of land, minor forest produce, and local resource management. While effective implementation will depend on harmonizing state laws and administrative practices, the January 2026 step marks a crucial milestone in advancing tribal self-rule and participatory governance in Jharkhand.

clat-mock-18-p4.title: India's Quantum Leap in Secure Communications
clat-mock-18-p4.text:
India's efforts to build indigenous capabilities in emerging technologies have accelerated through mission-based programmes aimed at strengthening research, innovation, and strategic self-reliance. In recent years, policymakers have identified quantum technologies as a critical frontier with applications ranging from secure communications and advanced computing to precision sensing and defence systems. Government-backed initiatives have sought to foster collaboration among research institutions, industry, and startups to translate scientific advances into practical technologies.

A recent breakthrough demonstrated the growing maturity of India's quantum ecosystem. Officials noted that progress in secure communication technologies had advanced faster than initially anticipated, reflecting increasing participation from domestic startups and research organisations. Alongside technological achievements, efforts have also focused on expanding support for deep-tech enterprises, creating new financing mechanisms, and strengthening innovation pipelines in strategically important sectors. Experts believe that the success of such initiatives could influence India's long-term position in the global technology landscape.

clat-mock-08-p3.text:
The contemporary political landscape of Iran is witnessing significant turbulence, with deadly unrest erupting recently due to severe livelihood struggles and material deprivation. This instability has cast a spotlight on the exiled son of the last monarch, who is emerging as a symbolic figure for the opposition. His family’s rule ended when the previous regime’s ambitious, top-down modernization and land reform program of the 1960s backfired, alienating the clergy and paving the way for the 1979 revolution.

Following a pivotal national referendum held shortly after the monarchy’s fall, the nation was formally reconstituted as an Islamic Republic. The new governance model was built upon a specific theological doctrine conceptualized by the revolution's Supreme Leader, which grants ultimate authority to the clergy over the state. This unique synthesis of theocratic oversight and republican institutions continues to define the nation's politics, even as citizens return to the streets to voice grievances that echo the discontent of decades past.

Joint manufacturing of green hydrogen electrolyzers
questions.explanation: SHANTI is India's nuclear-energy framework (Sustainable Harnessing and Advancement of Nuclear Energy for Transforming India).

questions.question: The passage mentions the I2U2 grouping, a minilateral framework in which India and the UAE are founding members. Which other two nations complete this specific geopolitical bloc?
questions.explanation: I2U2 is India, Israel, the UAE and the US.

questions.question: Which of the following is a bilateral joint military exercise conducted between the land forces of India and the United Arab Emirates (UAE)?
questions.explanation: Desert Cyclone is the India–UAE army exercise. Desert Knight/Eagle are air exercises and Al Najah is with Oman.

questions.question: The 11th Schedule of the Indian Constitution lists functional items over which Panchayats may be granted administrative control. How many subjects are included in this schedule?
questions.explanation: The Eleventh Schedule lists 29 subjects.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT one of the official thematic areas used to assess Panchayats under the index's framework?
questions.explanation: The nine LSDG themes include Clean & Green, Women Friendly and Socially Just & Secured, but not 'Digitally Autonomous'.

questions.question: Under the grading mechanism of the Panchayat Advancement Index, what is the official designation given to the highest-performing Panchayats (those scoring 90 and above)?
questions.explanation: Panchayats scoring 90+ are 'Achievers'. Next come Front Runners (75–90), Performers, Aspirants and Beginners.

questions.question: The Panchayat Advancement Index evaluates grassroots progress by aggregating the 17 global Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) into how many specific Localized SDG (LSDG) themes?
questions.explanation: The 17 SDGs are grouped into 9 Localised SDG themes.

questions.question: Which state emerged as the standout leading performer, with a remarkable achievement of its Gram Panchayats rated in the "Front Runner" category?
questions.explanation: Tripura led PAI 2.0 with about 80% of its Gram Panchayats rated Front Runner.

questions.question: Which committee is widely considered the pioneer of the Panchayati Raj system in India for first recommending the establishment of a three-tier structure of local self-government?
questions.explanation: The Balwant Rai Mehta Committee (1957) recommended a three-tier Panchayati Raj.

questions.question: Which one of the following institutions acts as the nodal agency for the National Family Health Survey?
questions.explanation: The International Institute for Population Sciences (IIPS), Mumbai is the nodal agency for NFHS.

questions.question: Consider the following statements regarding the National Family Health Survey (NFHS): 1) It is a nationally representative household survey. 2) It provides district-level estimates for several health indicators. 3) It is conducted annually. Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.explanation: NFHS is a nationally representative household survey with district-level estimates (since NFHS-4). It runs in multi-year rounds, not every year.

questions.question: Which of the following indicators is NOT generally collected through the National Family Health Survey?
options: Anaemia prevalence among women and children
questions.explanation: Gross Enrolment Ratio comes from education data (UDISE+/AISHE), not NFHS.

questions.question: The Nagoya Protocol is primarily based on which of the following internationally recognised principles?
questions.explanation: The Nagoya Protocol (2010) is built on Access and Benefit Sharing for genetic resources.

questions.question: Consider the following statements regarding the Nagoya Protocol: 1) It is legally binding. 2) It supplements the Convention on Biological Diversity. 3) It entered into force before the Convention on Biological Diversity. Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
questions.explanation: It is legally binding and supplements the CBD. It came into force in 2014, long after the CBD (1993).

questions.question: Which protocol introduced legally binding greenhouse gas emission reduction targets for developed countries?
questions.explanation: The Kyoto Protocol (1997) set binding emission targets for developed (Annex I) countries.

questions.question: Consider the following statements regarding the Nagoya Protocol: 1) It creates a transparent legal framework governing access to genetic resources. 2) It seeks to ensure equitable sharing of benefits arising from the utilisation of such resources. 3) It establishes legally binding obligations relating to the transboundary movement of Living Modified Organisms. Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.explanation: Nagoya covers access to genetic resources and benefit sharing. Movement of LMOs is covered by the Cartagena Protocol.

questions.question: Consider the following statements about India’s biodiversity institutions: 1) The Biological Diversity Act, 2002 provides the legal basis for the framework. 2) Biodiversity Management Committees operate at the local level. 3) State Biodiversity Boards function below Biodiversity Management Committees. Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.explanation: The Biological Diversity Act, 2002 sets up a three-tier structure (NBA, SBBs, BMCs). BMCs work at the local level, below the State Biodiversity Boards.

questions.question: In which year was the inaugural FIFA World Cup hosted, and which nation won the title?
questions.explanation: Uruguay hosted and won the first World Cup in 1930.

questions.question: Which national team was awarded permanent possession of the original Jules Rimet Trophy after winning their third World Cup title in 1970?
questions.explanation: Brazil kept the Jules Rimet Trophy permanently after its third title in 1970.

questions.question: Consider the following statements regarding the 2026 FIFA World Cup format and hosts: 1) The 2026 FIFA World Cup will be jointly hosted across three nations: Canada, Mexico, and the United States. 2) It will be the first edition in tournament history to feature an expanded format of 48 national teams. 3) Mexico will become the first country in history to host or co-host the FIFA World Cup three times. Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.explanation: All three are correct. 2026 was co-hosted by Canada, Mexico and the US, was the first 48-team edition, and made Mexico the first three-time host (1970, 1986, 2026).

questions.question: Who scored the match-winning goal for Spain in the 106th minute of the 2026 FIFA World Cup final?
questions.explanation: Substitute Ferran Torres scored the 106th-minute winner against Argentina.

questions.question: Consider the following statements regarding the 2026 FIFA World Cup awards and milestones: 1) Rodri of Spain was awarded the FIFA Golden Ball as the best overall player of the tournament. 2) Unai Simón of Spain won the Golden Glove award for the best goalkeeper. 3) With this victory, Spain became the only nation in history to hold both the Men’s and Women’s FIFA World Cup titles simultaneously. Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.explanation: All three are correct. Rodri won the Golden Ball and Unai Simón the Golden Glove, and Spain, already women's champions (2023), held both world titles at once.

questions.question: Which player holds the record for the most all-time appearances (26 matches) in FIFA World Cup history?
questions.explanation: Lionel Messi set the record of 26 World Cup appearances in 2022, passing Lothar Matthäus's 25.

questions.question: According to global trends in military expenditure published by SIPRI, which nation carried the world's highest "military burden" (military expenditure measured as a percentage of GDP)?
questions.explanation: Ukraine has the world's highest military burden (over 30% of GDP) in SIPRI data.

sources.title: SIPRI: Trends in World Military Expenditure

questions.question: What significant strategic shift regarding India's nuclear warheads was highlighted for the first time in the SIPRI report?
options: India officially dismantled all land-based ballistic nuclear warheads.
India placed a portion of its nuclear warheads in an operationally "deployed" state.
India abandoned its long-standing "No First Use" (NFU) nuclear doctrine.
India signed the Comprehensive Nuclear-Test-Ban Treaty (CTBT).
questions.explanation: SIPRI Yearbook 2026 assessed for the first time that India has deployed warheads (about 12).

sources.title: Business Standard: India 5th largest military spender, deployed 12 warheads – SIPRI

questions.question: According to the SIPRI Yearbook, what is India's rank among the world's top military spenders, and what was its total defense expenditure?
questions.explanation: India was the 5th largest military spender in 2025, at about $92.1 billion.

sources.title: Angel One: India's defence spending reaches $92.1 billion in 2025 – SIPRI

questions.question:
Match the following key milestones in India's nuclear program with their correct historical details: 1) Operation Smiling Buddha (1974) A) Five underground tests at Pokhran under PM Atal Bihari Vajpayee; commemorated on National Technology Day (May 11). 2) Operation Shakti (1998) B) India's first "Peaceful Nuclear Explosion" (PNE) conducted on May 18 at Pokhran. 3) 2008 Civil Nuclear Agreement C) Landmark bilateral deal with the US that enabled India to enter global nuclear commerce without signing the NPT.

Which matching combination is correct?
questions.explanation: Smiling Buddha (1974) was the first 'peaceful nuclear explosion' on 18 May. Shakti (1998) was five tests under Vajpayee (National Technology Day, 11 May). The 2008 deal was the India–US civil nuclear agreement.

questions.question: Who serves as the Chairperson of the Executive Council of India's Nuclear Command Authority (NCA)?
questions.explanation: The NSA chairs the Executive Council of the Nuclear Command Authority. The PM chairs its Political Council.

questions.question: What was the codename of the May 2025 military confrontation between India and Pakistan highlighted by SIPRI for integrating cyber operations into active conflict?
questions.explanation: The May 2025 India–Pakistan conflict was Operation Sindoor.

questions.question: Regarding maritime security and trade, what crucial commitment did Iran make under the Islamabad MoU concerning the Strait of Hormuz?
options: Imposing a uniform 10% transit fee on all oil tankers entering the Persian Gulf
Allowing commercial transit strictly for ships flying non-Western flags
Granting absolute toll-free transit to all commercial vessels through the Strait of Hormuz
Transferring maritime traffic management of the strait of Hormuz to the United Nations
questions.explanation: Under the Islamabad MoU Iran committed to free passage of commercial vessels through Hormuz.

sources.title: Arms Control Association: Assessing the Islamabad MOU

questions.question: What is the duration of the interim negotiation window established under the Islamabad MoU for the US and Iran to finalize a comprehensive long-term agreement?
questions.explanation: The MoU set a 60-day window for negotiating a comprehensive agreement.

sources.title: Arms Control Association: Assessing the Islamabad MOU

questions.question: Which Constitutional Amendment Act of the Tenth Schedule, thereby removing protection for defections arising from a "split" (one-third of members breaking away)?

questions.question: In which landmark judgment did the Supreme Court hold that the Presiding Officer (Speaker/Chairman) acts as a tribunal while deciding disqualification petitions under the Tenth Schedule, making their decision subject to judicial review?
options: Shankari Prasad v. Union of India (1951)
Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973)
Kihoto Hollohan v. Zachillhu and Others (1992)
SR Bommai v. Union of India (1994)

questions.question: Under the rules of the Tenth Schedule, what is the timeframe within which a nominated member of a House can join a political party without facing disqualification?
options: Within 30 days from taking their seat
Within 3 months from taking their seat
Within 6 months from taking their seat
Nominated members can never join a political party

sources.title: Constitution of India, Tenth Schedule para 2(3)

questions.question: Which of the following situations would NOT attract disqualification under the Anti-Defection Law?
options: A member voluntarily gives up membership of his political party.
A member votes contrary to the party whip without prior permission and is not condoned within fifteen days.
Two-thirds of the legislators of a party agree to merge with another political party.
An independent member joins a political party after election.

sources.title: Constitution of India, Tenth Schedule para 4

questions.question: Which articles of the Indian Constitution directly lay down that a member shall be disqualified for being a member of either House of Parliament or State Legislature if they are disqualified under the Tenth Schedule?
questions.explanation: Articles 102(2) and 191(2) provide for disqualification under the Tenth Schedule.

questions.question: Which major life event of Gautama Buddha took place at Sarnath, marking the establishment of the Sangha (monastic order)?

questions.explanation: At Sarnath the Buddha gave his first sermon (Dhammachakkappavattana) and founded the Sangha.

questions.question: Which of the four principal holy sites associated with the Buddha's life are currently designated as UNESCO World Heritage Sites? 1) Lumbini (Birthplace) 2) Bodh Gaya (Enlightenment) 3) Sarnath (First Sermon) 4) Kushinagar (Mahaparinirvana) Select the correct answer using the code below:

44th site in India; 5th site in Uttar Pradesh
45th site in India; 4th site in Uttar Pradesh
48th site in India; 6th site in Uttar Pradesh

sources.title: Drishti IAS: Sarnath becomes India's 45th UNESCO World Heritage Site

questions.question: Which advisory body of UNESCO conducted the technical evaluation mission for Sarnath?
questions.explanation: ICOMOS evaluates cultural nominations. IUCN handles natural sites.

questions.explanation: Xuanzang (7th c.) described Sarnath's 200-ft vihara and the Ashokan pillar.

The tension between historical representation and contemporary social norms
The difficulty of establishing the chronology of Harappan metalworking
The disagreement over the geographical location of Mohenjo-daro

questions.explanation: The Dancing Girl is a bronze made by lost-wax casting.

questions.question: Consider the following pairs: Harappan Site Important Archaeological Evidence 1.     Kalibangan Ploughed agricultural field 2.     Dholavira Sophisticated water-management system 3.     Lothal Bead-making industry 4.     Mohenjo-daro Great Bath Which of the pairs given above are correctly matched?

questions.explanation: The Dancing Girl is in the National Museum, New Delhi.

questions.question: The Tribunals Reforms Bill, 2026 seeks to repeal which of the following existing laws?
questions.explanation: The 2026 Bill repeals the Tribunals Reforms Act, 2021.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a function assigned to the National Tribunals Commission under the Tribunals Reforms Act, 2026?
options: Conducting selection of members for tribunals
Maintaining the National Tribunals Data Grid
Hearing appeals against decisions of tribunals
questions.explanation: The National Tribunals Commission handles selection, performance review and data. It does not hear appeals against tribunal decisions.

questions.question: Who is eligible to serve as the Chairperson of the National Tribunals Commission?
options: A serving High Court Chief Justice only
A retired Supreme Court Judge or High Court Chief Justice
Any retired or serving civil servant with judicial experience
A serving Supreme Court Judge nominated by Parliament
questions.explanation: The Chairperson must have been a Supreme Court judge or a High Court Chief Justice.

questions.question: Which constitutional provisions provide the principal constitutional basis for the establishment of tribunals in India?
questions.explanation: Articles 323A and 323B (42nd Amendment) provide for tribunals.

questions.question: Under the Tribunals Reforms Bill, 2026, what is the proposed tenure of a Tribunal Member?"
options: Three years or until 65 years of age
Four years or until 67 years of age
Five years or until 67 years of age
Five years or until 70 years of age
